tasks.title: A refused write keeps the words and says what happened.
tasks.description: This task handles the two refusals a lease produces — someone else holds the card, or it changed while you were typing — without losing text.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

SCOPE
1. The field writes in `src/components/ItemPanel.tsx`.
2. The write adapter's error surface.

DEFINITIONS
- Held (423): another person holds the lease.
- Changed (409): the card moved on under the write.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Distinguishable
A held card and a changed card shall produce different messages.

R2 — Kept
The local text shall stay visible after a refusal.

R3 — Explained
The message shall name the holder, or the change that occurred.

R4 — Offered
The drawer shall offer to copy the local text and to reload the card.

R5 — Stopped
Further writes to that card shall be refused until the person reloads or the lease is released.

R6 — Never replayed
A refused write shall not be retried automatically.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-23
A refusal now says which refusal it was: **held** (423) names the holder, **changed** (409) carries
the version the server holds, and anything else is `other`.

What matters is what a refusal no longer does. The server's version is not written over the local
one — the words stay exactly as they were typed — and the card is frozen: no further request leaves
this tab for it until the person copies the words or takes the server's version. A refusal that was
only a lease ends when the lease does, so the card thaws by itself. Nothing refused is ever queued;
that rule was 118.4's and is unchanged.

The drawer shows the sentence above the fields and two doors: **Copy my words**, and **Take the
server's version** — or **Reload the card** when a lease, not a revision, was the reason.

Tests: the repository's three refusals; the store keeping the local title while offering the
server's; and a frozen card sending nothing further while still applying locally.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 — R1, R3: Force a 423; the holder is named. Force a 409; the change is named.
V2 — R2, R4: The text remains, and copy and reload both work.
V3 — R5: Keep typing; no further write is sent.
V4 — R6: Wait; no retry is attempted.
tasks.complexityReasoning: Two refusal states, a field that keeps its text, copy and reload, and no automatic retry.

tasks.title: A workspace has members, and a member's role decides what they may do.
tasks.description: This task adds workspaces, invitations, roles and removal.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

SCOPE
1. A workspace entity and the scoping of every persisted entity.
2. Membership and roles.
3. The invitation flow from the auth task.

DEFINITIONS
- Workspace: the container of boards, lanes, items, types, tags and objectives.
- Role: the recorded set of actions a member may take.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Scoped
Every board, lane, item, placement, edge, link, type, tag, objective and log entry shall belong to one workspace.

R2 — Sealed
A person shall see only the workspaces they are a member of.

R3 — Roles
At least owner, editor and viewer shall exist, with a recorded permission table.

R4 — Invitation
An invitation shall be accepted once, by the invited address.

R5 — Removal
Removing a member shall take effect on their next request.

R6 — No escalation
A member shall not grant themselves a higher role.

R7 — Ownership
The last owner shall not be removable while members remain.

RELATED WORKSTREAM
The admin/identity breakdown is tasks 131-149; docs/admin.md is the source. 131-136 and 142 deliver this task's role, invitation, removal and escalation clauses. R1/R2 (workspace scoping) remain task 118's job.

SPLIT — 2026-10-22
This task is an umbrella, so its split is not a second list of the same work. Roles, invitations,
removal and escalation stay with 131-136 and 142; the acceptance pass is 122.3 because nobody else
owns "these add up together". What 118 left undone is the container itself, and that is 122.1 and
122.2.

COMPLETE — 2026-10-24
The workspace is a container: a row, and a `workspace_id` on every entity (122.1); every read and
write sealed to the workspace the session resolved, with a source guard that finds an unscoped
query (122.2); and the acceptance pass that proves the clauses of this task and of 131-146 add up
(122.3). Roles, invitations, removal and escalation were delivered by 131-136 and 142.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 — R1, R2: Two workspaces; each member sees only their own, in the UI and the API.
V2 — R3: A viewer attempts an edit; refused.
V3 — R5: Remove a member; their session loses access on the next request.
V4 — R6: Attempt to raise your own role; refused.
V5 — R7: Attempt to remove the last owner; refused.

subtasks.title: The workspace is a row, and every entity names it.
subtasks.description: SYSTEM
subtasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/admin.md section 3.1.

This is the part of task 122 that no other task owns. Roles, invitations and removal are delivered
by 131-136 and 142; what remains here is the container those roles are about — because task 118.1
deliberately stored one workspace per instance and left the boundary to 122.

ORDER
This follows task 132.1: the two axes exist before anything is scoped by them.

SCOPE
1. `migrations/` (the next free number): a `workspaces` row, and a `workspace_id` on every entity
   table that holds work.
2. The read and the writer, carrying the id without the client having to know it.
3. A backfill that puts today's single workspace into one row.

DEFINITIONS
- Workspace: the container of boards, lanes, items, placements, edges, links, people, types, tags,
  objectives, key results, templates, settings and logs.
- The instance's workspace: the one a fresh instance creates, named for the instance.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Every entity belongs to exactly one
Boards, lanes, items, placements, edges, links, people, issue types, objectives, key results, board
templates and the settings row shall each carry `workspace_id`, not null, with a foreign key.

R2 — Backfilled, not guessed
The migration shall create one workspace and assign every existing row to it. It shall not drop
anything, and it shall be safe to run on a database that already has rows.

R3 — The client does not carry it
The workspace shall be chosen by the server from the session, not sent by the browser. No URL, no
header and no body shall be able to point a read at another workspace.

R4 — One, for now
A fresh instance shall create exactly one workspace, named for the instance, and the first person to
sign in shall be its administrator (task 132's first run).

R5 — Both runtimes
The migration shall run through `Database.batch` on D1 and on the Node file driver, and the whole
read shall still round-trip on both.

VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: a fresh database has the column on every table; a board row cannot be written without it.
V2 — R2: a fixture at the old shape, with rows, migrates; every row keeps its id and gains the one
workspace.
V3 — R3: a request that names another workspace is served the session's, or refused; it is never
served the other.
V4 — R5: the round-trip test from 118.1 passes unchanged, and the Node smoke test passes.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-24
**R1 — every entity names it.** A `workspaces` row (migration 0018) and `workspace_id` on the twelve
tables that hold work: people, issue types, boards, lanes, items, item log, placements, edges, links,
objectives, key results and board templates. The children — a checklist, a log's rows, a board's
kinds and tags, a template's lanes — belong **through their parent** and are scoped by it; a second
column there would be a second thing to keep true. The settings row is keyed by the workspace id, so
it carries the workspace as its identity rather than as a second column saying the same thing. Both
choices are in the migration's own comment.

**R2 — backfilled, not guessed.** One workspace, named for the instance, and every existing row
assigned to it: `UPDATE … SET workspace_id = 'workspace'` per table, nothing dropped. The
`people.test` fixture — a database at the old shape with rows in it — migrates, keeps every id and
every value, and gains the scope on every row.

**R3 — the client does not carry it.** The read and the write take the id from
`WorkspaceCaller.workspaceId`, which `requireWorkspace` resolves; nothing reads a workspace from a
URL, a header or a body. `readWorkspace`, `readItem`, `readItemsByIds`, `writeWorkspace` and
`writeItem` all take it as a parameter, so a call site cannot forget it and still compile.

**R4 — one, for now.** A fresh instance creates exactly one workspace and the first person to sign in
is its administrator — task 132's first run, unchanged.

**R5 — both runtimes.** The migration is plain SQL run through `Database.batch`, the round trip passes
on the file driver, and the Node smoke test passes.

**A constraint, honestly stated.** SQLite will not add a `REFERENCES` column that has a non-NULL
default, and `Database.batch` runs each migration inside one transaction — so the thirteen-table
rebuild that would give a literal `NOT NULL` cannot be done with foreign keys enforced, on either
runtime. What the migration does instead: the column with its **foreign key**, a backfill of every
row, and **triggers** that refuse an insert or an update which leaves it empty. The behaviour the task
asks for is enforced ("a board row cannot be written without it" is a test), and only the
`PRAGMA`-visible word differs. It is recorded here rather than left to be discovered.

**What is not here.** 122.2 — sealing every route to the resolved scope, and refusing a workspace you
are not a member of — is the next subtask. Today there is one workspace per instance and every route
resolves it from the session, so nothing leaks; what 122.2 adds is the guarantee that stays true when
there are two.

Tests: the column on every table and not on the settings row, an insert without it refused by the
trigger, an insert naming a workspace that does not exist refused by the foreign key, another
workspace's board absent from a scoped read and present in its own, and an import replacing only its
own workspace's rows.

subtasks.title: Every read and write is sealed to the workspace.
subtasks.description: SYSTEM
subtasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/admin.md sections 3.1 and 3.3.

SCOPE
1. The server's queries: one scoping helper, used everywhere.
2. The guard: membership is asked per request, never cached on the client's word.
3. The refusal: a workspace you are not in is not an empty workspace.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — One door
Every query that reads or writes work shall be scoped by the workspace the session resolved. The
scope shall be a parameter of one helper, not a clause each author remembers to add.

R2 — Sealed, not filtered
A person who is not a member of a workspace shall be refused — 403 with the reason, or 404 where
naming it would leak its existence — never served an empty board list.

R3 — Asked every request
Membership and role shall be read live on each request, so a removal or a role change takes effect
on the next one without a re-login. No session shall carry a cached role.

R4 — The instance administrator may enter
An instance administrator shall be able to read and administer any workspace without being listed as
one of its members, which is the rule that lets somebody repair a workspace they are not on.

R5 — The write path agrees
`PATCH /api/items/:id` and every later write shall resolve the same scope as the read, so a card id
that belongs elsewhere is a refusal rather than an update.

VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: a search for an unscoped `SELECT`/`UPDATE` in `server/` finds none.
V2 — R2: a signed-in non-member asks for the workspace; 403 or 404, and no rows.
V3 — R3: remove a member mid-session; their next request is refused.
V4 — R4: an instance admin who is not a member reads the workspace and may administer it.
V5 — R5: patch a card id from another workspace; refused, and the row is unchanged.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-24
**R1 — one door.** `resolveWorkspace` is the only place a request's workspace is decided, and every
route reaches it through `requireWorkspace` (or, for the socket, `workspaceCallerFromCookie`, which
calls the same function). It answers the workspace **and** the role and its source, so a route cannot
get one without the other. `workspaceId(c)` — the helper that returned a path parameter or a
constant — is gone; there is no second way to ask.

**R2 — sealed, not filtered.** A person who belongs to no workspace, or asks for one they are not in,
gets **404 `no such workspace`** — the same answer for "it does not exist" and "it is not yours",
because naming the difference would confirm it exists. A member asking is served; nobody is ever
handed an empty board list in place of a refusal.

**R3 — asked every request.** Membership comes from `workspace_members` on each request and the role
from `effectiveRole` (direct + active groups); nothing is cached in the session. Removing a member
takes effect on their **next** request, with no re-login — asserted by deleting the row mid-session
and watching the next read become a 404.

**R4 — the instance administrator may enter.** A caller with `instance_role = admin` reaches a
workspace they are not on, and may administer it (`workspace.members` through the same door), which is
the rule that lets somebody repair a team they do not belong to. It still has to exist.

**R5 — the write path agrees.** A card id that exists in **another** workspace is a **404**, not a
creation: `itemBelongsElsewhere` tells "no such item here" from "such an item, and not yours", and the
pen refuses it too — a lease on somebody else's card is a write waiting to happen. The row is
untouched and no copy appears (asserted). The writer's own deletes are scoped as well
(`DELETE FROM items … AND workspace_id = ?`, the lane parent fixup likewise), so the guard is in the
query rather than only in the route.

**The feed is the workspace's.** `GET /api/workspace/changes` now filters to this workspace's items,
so a second workspace's change ids do not appear in somebody's cursor.

**V1, as a test.** `server/scope.test.ts` searches the server's own source for a statement touching a
table of work without naming a workspace, and fails the build if one appears. It cannot see SQL built
out of a variable (`add()` in `write.ts` is the one that is), and it says so; what it does catch is
the query somebody adds next month in a hurry. Six statements were flagged when it was written: four
were genuinely unscoped and are fixed, two are children reached through their parent (`item_log` by
`item_id`) or a count of the whole instance for a backup, and each carries a comment saying so on the
line above it.

Tests: the source guard; a non-member refused with 404 while a member is served; an administrator with
no membership row reading and administering; a removal taking effect on the next request; a foreign
card id refused for both the write and the pen, with the row unchanged and no copy made; and the feed
carrying only this workspace's changes.

subtasks.title: The workstream holds together: the acceptance pass.
subtasks.description: SYSTEM
subtasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/admin.md section 7, "Acceptance tests".

The clauses 122 states are delivered by 131-145 across several tasks. This subtask is the one that
proves they add up — because every one of them is a rule about a second person, and a single-person
test cannot see any of them.

SCOPE
1. The acceptance list from the document, as tests.
2. Two people, two roles, one instance, through the real entry points.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — The matrix
Every role × action pair shall be asserted once against `can()`, and every pair that a route enforces
shall be asserted through the route as well. A hidden control is not a permission check.

R2 — The second person
A Viewer shall sign in, read a board, and be refused a write with 403 while no row changes. An
Editor shall write work and be refused board design.

R3 — The lifecycle
An inactive account shall not complete sign-in and shall have no live session afterwards. A role
change shall take effect on the next request. A removal shall end access immediately.

R4 — The safe guards
The last administrator shall not be demotable, deactivatable, deletable or removable; a second
administrator shall make all four possible. A person shall not deactivate or delete themselves.

R5 — The static build is untouched
With no server, the app shall still boot and show what it shows today. None of this may make a board
need an account.

VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: the table is generated from the role list, so a new action without a decision fails.
V2 — R2: two real sessions; the Viewer's `PATCH` is 403 and the stored row is byte-identical.
V3 — R3: deactivate, change a role, remove; each takes effect on the next request.
V4 — R4: the last administrator's four attempts all refuse; with two, all four succeed.
V5 — R5: the e2e suite against the static build passes unchanged.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-24
**R1 — the matrix, twice.** `src/domain/roles.test.ts` already asserts every role × action pair,
one test per pair, and fails when an action arrives without a decision. What was missing is the
second half: the same table **through the routes**. `server/acceptance.test.ts` drives the five routes
that enforce an action — `board.read`, `item.write`, `workspace.import`, `workspace.settings`,
`workspace.members` — for all three roles, and asserts that a refusal is **403 and nothing else**:
any other answer means the permission passed, whatever the interface would have shown.

Most actions have no route, and that is not an omission: a board, a lane and an objective are part of
the workspace payload, whose only server-side write is the import. The table says so where it matters
— "an editor may not redesign the board" is asserted at `workspace.import`, which is the route that
would carry it.

**R2 — the second person.** A Viewer signs in, reads the board (200), and is refused a write (403)
with the stored row **byte-identical** — no field, no revision, no timestamp. An Editor writes the
same card (200) and is refused the import (403), with no board created.

**R3 — the lifecycle.** A role change takes effect on the **next request**, with no re-login and no
new session (editor writes, then is a viewer and is refused, and still reads). A removal is the door
itself: the same cookie becomes 404. Deactivation revokes every session in the same transaction — the
old cookie is 401, no live session remains, and the door refuses to issue a new one.

**R4 — the safe guards.** All four ways to lose the last workspace administrator — demote, deactivate,
delete, remove — are **409** when they would leave nobody, and all four **succeed** with a peer
administrator standing (a fresh pair per act, because two of the four remove the person they are
applied to). A person's own deactivation and deletion are refused regardless.

**R5 — the static build.** Untouched, and proved by the lane that already exists: the e2e suite runs
the shipped `dist/` against the static preview and passes unchanged (47 tests), with no server
involved for any of them.

**What this file is for.** Every rule in 122 is about a second person, and a test with one signed-in
user can see none of them. These 21 tests sign several people in and drive the real routes, so the
clauses are proved to *add up* rather than each holding in isolation.

tasks.expansionPrompt: (1) the workspace entity and the scoping change for every table; (2) membership and the invitation acceptance path; (3) the role table and its enforcement at the API; (4) removal, the last-owner guard and tests.
tasks.complexityReasoning: Workspaces scope every entity already in the schema, which is a schema-wide change, plus roles, invitations, removal and escalation guards.

tasks.title: A board can be shared as a read-only link, and the link can be revoked.
tasks.description: This task adds signed, revocable links that show a board without an account.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

SCOPE
1. A share token bound to a board.
2. The read-only mode of the board view.

DEFINITIONS
- Share token: an unguessable value naming one board.
- Revoked: a token that no longer resolves.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Token
A share link shall carry an unguessable token bound to one board.

R2 — Read-only
The link shall render the board and its cards, and shall offer no editing control.

R3 — No writes
The API shall refuse every write reached with a share token.

R4 — Revoked
Revoking shall stop the link at once.

R5 — Expiry
A link may carry an expiry, after which it shall refuse.

R6 — No account
Opening the link shall not create an account or a session.

NOTE — 2026-10-24: unaffected by the identity work
A share link carries no identity, so OIDC-only sign-in (task 154) and SCIM (task 168) change nothing
here — which is why this one can be taken at any time.

CANCELLED — 2026-10-25: read-only access is a role, not a second kind of link
A share link would have been a parallel identity system — a token that names one board, a separate
read path, a separate revocation, and a rendering mode that is nobody's job to keep true. The product
already has the right shape for this: **Viewer**, one of the three workspace roles, which the server
already enforces on every route (`src/domain/roles.ts`: read and comment, nothing else).

The access a share link was invented for is what an invitation as a Viewer is. So this task is
cancelled, and what remains is not a new mechanism but making the existing one visible in the
interface — task 171.

A link that carries no identity is still unbuilt, deliberately: it would be a fourth door with its own
lifetime, and this product has one door and three roles.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 — R2: Open the link in a private window; the board renders and no editing control appears.
V2 — R3: Attempt a write with the token; refused.
V3 — R4: Revoke; the link no longer resolves.
V4 — R5: Expire a link; refused.
V5 — R6: Check that no user or session was created.
tasks.complexityReasoning: A signed token, a read-only render, an API guard and revocation.

tasks.title: The flows that make the product work are tested end to end.
tasks.description: This task adds a browser suite over the seams that unit tests cannot see — drag and drop, the drawer, board design and import.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

SCOPE
1. A new end-to-end suite (Playwright), run in the CI workflow.
2. The preview deployment.

DEFINITIONS
- Seam: a place where two store actions are composed by a component, which unit tests do not reach.
- Deterministic: the suite seeds its own workspace and does not depend on the clock.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Drag and drop
A card shall be dragged between lanes and keep the position it was dropped at.

R2 — WIP
On a justify board, cancelling the reason prompt shall leave the card where it was, and answering shall land it where it was dropped.

R3 — Drawer
A test shall edit a title, add a tag, add a person and set a parent.

R4 — Board design
A test shall split a lane, add a cell and remove it, in edit mode.

R5 — Import and export
A test shall export a workspace, import it into a clean state, and compare the boards.

R6 — Deterministic
The suite shall not depend on wall-clock time or on the demo's current contents.

R7 — Gated
The suite shall run on every pull request and fail the workflow.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-21
Seventeen tests over six flows: drag (three), the WIP prompt (two), the drawer (four), board
design (four), the workspace file (two), and the harness itself (two). They run against the built
app, each in a fresh origin, and finish in about ten seconds locally and eighty in CI, where the
browser install dominates.

The job is named `e2e`, waits on `checks`, and publishing waits on it: a red test never reaches
the live app. A failure keeps its traces and screenshots for a week. The ceiling is recorded at
five minutes — generous against eighty seconds, and to be raised deliberately.

R2's evidence is real: putting the WIP drop bug back made both WIP tests fail, and restoring the
line made them pass.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 — R1–R5: The suite passes locally and in CI.
V2 — R2: The cancel case fails when the drop is made to write its position regardless of the seam's answer.
V3 — R7: The workflow runs the suite and blocks on failure.
V4 — R6: Run the suite twice; the results are identical.

subtasks.title: The harness: each test starts from an empty origin, against the built app.
subtasks.description: This subtask adds Playwright, a config, a seeded workspace and one command that builds, serves and runs.
subtasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

SCOPE
1. `e2e/` — a Playwright suite, its config, and a fixture that seeds a workspace.
2. `package.json` — a `test:e2e` script.

DEFINITIONS
- Seeded workspace: the demo the app creates for a fresh origin — deterministic, and free of the wall clock.
- Fresh context: Playwright's per-test browser context, so storage starts empty every time.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Isolated
Each test shall start from an empty origin, so the app seeds its own workspace and no test sees another's edits.

R2 — The shipped build
The suite shall run against the production build (`vite preview`), not the dev server, so what it tests is what ships.

R3 — No clock
No assertion shall depend on the current date. The demo's dates are relative, so tests read titles, positions and counts.

R4 — One command
`npm run test:e2e` shall build, serve and run, and answer non-zero on failure.

R5 — No false green
A failing assertion shall fail the run, and a server that cannot start shall fail it too rather than skipping silently.

subtasks.title: A card dragged between lanes lands where it was dropped.
subtasks.description: This subtask covers the drag: across lanes and within one, asserting the position rather than just the lane.
subtasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Between lanes
A card dragged from one lane to another shall appear in the target lane.

R2 — Where it was dropped
The card shall sit at the dropped position: above the card it was dropped above, below the one it was dropped below.

R3 — Within a lane
A card dragged within its own lane shall reorder, and the order shall survive a reload.

R4 — The real gesture
The test shall drive the pointer the way a person does — press, several moves, release — because the app's lift is pointer-driven and a synthetic drag drops the lift.

subtasks.title: The WIP prompt: cancelling leaves the card, answering lands it where it was dropped.
subtasks.description: This subtask covers the justify policy — the case that once failed while every unit test passed.
subtasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

DEFINITIONS
- Justify board: a board whose WIP policy asks for a reason before a move that would exceed a lane's limit.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Cancelled
Dropping a card into an over-limit lane shall raise the reason dialog; cancelling shall leave the card exactly where it was.

R2 — Answered
Giving a reason shall land the card in the target lane, at the position it was dropped.

R3 — Recorded
The reason shall be on the card's Activity and on the card itself.

R4 — The regression this exists for
R1 is the case that once failed while every unit test passed: the drop wrote its position regardless of the policy's answer. The test is named after that, so a future refactor of the drop reads it.

subtasks.title: The drawer edits: title, tag, person, parent.
subtasks.description: This subtask covers the four edits the drawer is opened for, and that each reaches the card.
subtasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Title
Editing the title shall change the card's title on the board once the drawer closes.

R2 — Tag
Adding a tag from the board's vocabulary shall show that tag on the card.

R3 — Person
Adding a name shall show the person's initials on the card.

R4 — Parent
Setting a parent shall show the lineage on the card.

subtasks.title: Board design: split a lane, add a cell, remove it.
subtasks.description: This subtask covers design mode, and that the controls stay out of the working board.
subtasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Split
In edit mode, splitting a lane shall produce the cells it promised.

R2 — Add
A cell added to a container shall accept a card.

R3 — Remove
Removing that cell shall leave the cards it held somewhere valid, by the store's rule — not lost.

R4 — Outside edit mode
The design controls shall not be present on the working board.

subtasks.title: Import and export: a file out, the same workspace back.
subtasks.description: This subtask covers the round trip, and the refusal of a file that is not a workspace.
subtasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Export
The Export control shall download a JSON file carrying the workspace's boards and items.

R2 — Round trip
Importing that file into a clean origin shall reproduce the boards and the item count.

R3 — Refusal
Importing a file that is not a workspace shall be refused with a message, and change nothing.

subtasks.title: The suite runs in CI and a failure stops the workflow.
subtasks.description: This subtask wires the suite into the workflow, with a trace left behind when it fails.
subtasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Trigger
The suite shall run on every push to `main` and every pull request.

R2 — Gate
A failing test shall fail the workflow, in a job named `e2e`.

R3 — Evidence
A failure shall leave a trace — screenshot or video — so the run can be read rather than guessed at.

R4 — Ceiling
The suite shall finish inside a recorded ceiling (proposed five minutes). If it does not, the ceiling is wrong and shall be raised deliberately.

tasks.title: The app is usable with a keyboard and a screen reader.
tasks.description: This task closes the accessibility gaps left by the visual work: focus, announcements, keyboard paths and motion.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

SCOPE
1. The drawer and dialogs.
2. The board, its lanes and the drag gesture.
3. The CI workflow.

DEFINITIONS
- Focus trap: focus may not leave an open modal surface until it closes.
- Live region: a polite announcement of a change a sighted user sees.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Focus
An open drawer or dialog shall contain focus, and Escape shall return it to the control that opened it.

R2 — Announced
A completed drag, a refused drop and a raised warning shall be announced.

R3 — Keyboard paths
Every action available by drag shall have a keyboard path: move to lane, set parent, reorder.

R4 — Motion
`prefers-reduced-motion` shall be respected.

R5 — Names
Every control shall have an accessible name, and the lane tree shall read as a tree.

R6 — Contrast
The legibility tests shall remain green.

R7 — Automated
An axe check shall run over the key views in CI.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-24
**R1 — focus.** One hook, `useDialogFocus`, is now the only way a modal is opened: the caret starts
inside it (a named control where one is the natural answer — the confirm button, the reason field,
the invitation link), Tab and Shift+Tab cycle within it, Escape closes it, and the caret returns to
the control that opened it once the surface is gone. It is applied to every dialog in the app —
confirmation, WIP reason, board settings, template editor, new board, palette, profile, the people
drawer and the invitations pair — and a **source guard** in `src/lib/a11y.test.ts` fails the build if
a file with `role="dialog"` does not use it, or omits `aria-modal` or a name. The card panel is
deliberately **not** trapped: it sits beside the board rather than over it, so trapping focus would
take the board away; it restores the caret to the card that opened it (`useReturnFocus`).

**R2 — announced.** `src/lib/announce.ts` plus one `Announcer` live region (`role="status"`,
`aria-live="polite"`) mounted at the app root. The announcements are made **at the seam that writes**
— `moveCard`, `moveInitiative`, `setParent`, `moveCardsToLane`, `reorderCard` — so the pointer, the
menu, the keyboard and the bulk bar speak the same sentence and cannot disagree. A completed move
says the card's **title** and the lane's **path**, never an id. A refused drop says which lane and
which limit (`block`), or that the move is held for a reason (`justify`); a refused hierarchy edit
says why; a section-crossing initiative move says its section is derived. A **raised warning** is
detected by reading `uncommittedBelow` before and after the write, so only a warning that actually
arrived is announced.

**R3 — keyboard paths.** *Move to lane*, *set parent* and *remove parent* were already in the card
menu (Shift+F10 on a focused card). **Reorder** was the missing one: `reorderCard` is a new store
action, offered as *Move earlier* / *Move later*, moving one place and saying where it landed
("… is now 2 of 5 in In Progress / Dev") — and stating the end of the list rather than doing nothing.

**R4 — motion.** A `prefers-reduced-motion` block in `index.css` zeroes every animation and
transition, so it covers components added later. Verified in a browser with the preference set.

**R5 — names and the tree.** The cards lane tree is now a `tree`: `role="tree"` named after the
board, `role="treeitem"` per lane with `aria-level` and `aria-expanded`, and `role="group"` for a
container's children. The lanes deliberately carry **no `aria-label`**: a lane contains its cards,
and a name on a container whose visible text is not part of it is what WCAG 2.5.3 forbids — axe
found exactly that. Controls that lacked a name were given one where axe found them; the add-card
footer is now "Add card to …", so its visible words are part of its name.

**R6 — legibility.** Unchanged and still green. Three real contrast failures found by the new check
were fixed rather than waived: the band chips (white on a 500 was 2.5:1 → the 700s), the card's
rollup percentage (slate-400 at 2.6:1 → slate-600, and emerald-600 → emerald-700), and two
explanatory lines at 4.4:1 on their own tinted ground (→ slate-600).

**R7 — automated.** `@axe-core/playwright` runs over the board, a card's panel and the admin screen
in `e2e/a11y.spec.ts`, failing on any **serious or critical** violation. One rule is disabled on the
board by name, `nested-interactive`: a `treeitem` is an interactive role, and a lane's item contains
the cards and their menus — the alternative is to stop saying the nesting at all, which is worse for
the person the role exists for.

**What is not here.** The **initiatives flow** keeps its named regions rather than becoming a tree:
it is a grid of sections and cells whose every cell already names its path and count. Giving it
`treeitem` semantics is a change to that surface rather than to this one, and worth doing when
someone next works on it.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 — R1: Tab through the drawer; focus does not escape, and Escape returns it.
V2 — R2: With a screen reader, complete a drag; it is announced.
V3 — R3: Move a card using only the keyboard.
V4 — R7: The axe job runs and passes.
V5 — R4: With reduced motion enabled, transitions do not run.

tasks.title: A workspace can be deleted — by its own administrator, and nobody else’s hands reach it.
tasks.description: The workspace is the tenant: it holds many people’s accounts, its boards and its cards, and it is the thing that is charged. Its owner is a field on the workspace, its administrator may end it, a member may not, and the deletion stops at that workspace. The instance-wide destroy is gone from the product.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/admin.md §3.1 (the two axes) and task 144's
delete-versus-erase decision.

SCOPE
1. The **Account Admin**: the instance administrator, named for what the role now carries.
2. Deleting a **workspace** — its boards, lanes, items, placements, settings.
3. Closing the **account** — the whole instance, verified.
4. Billing details as a record the Account Admin keeps, not a payment system.

NOT IN SCOPE
- Deleting an individual **person**: task 144 delivered delete versus erase, and this task does not
  revisit it.
- The privacy notice, terms, support address and changelog: split into their own task (150), because
  they are about the public site rather than about authority and deletion.

DEFINITIONS
- **Account**: the instance — one deployment, its people, its workspaces, its audit.
- **Account Admin**: today's `instance_members.role = 'admin'`. No third axis and no new table; the
  name is what changes, because the role now carries billing and deletion as well as the door.
- **Workspace**: the container of boards, lanes, items and placements (task 122.1).

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — One role, named honestly
`instance_members.role = 'admin'` **is** the Account Admin. `member` is everybody else. The
interface, the docs and the audit sentences say "Account Admin" where they used to say "instance
administrator", and nothing about who may sign in changes. A third authority axis is deliberately not
introduced: it would be a second answer to "who runs this deployment".

R2 — The four powers, in the matrix
`src/domain/roles.ts` gains the account-level actions — `account.rename`, `account.billing`,
`account.admins`, `account.delete`, `workspace.delete` — each decided for both instance roles
(admin: yes; member: no) so that a new action cannot arrive without a decision, the same completeness
rule the workspace matrix already has. `requireInstanceAdmin` asks the matrix rather than keeping a
second list.

R3 — Delegation
An Account Admin may make another person one, and take it away again, with the last-administrator
guard that already exists (`mayAdminister`, task 144): the last one cannot be demoted, deactivated,
deleted or removed. The act is audited.

R4 — Billing, as a record
The account holds what billing needs to be *arranged*: a billing email, a company name, an external
customer reference and a plan label. **Never a card number, a CVC or a bank detail** — those belong
to the payment provider, and a database that holds them is a liability with no upside; the record
points at the provider's customer instead. Editing is `account.billing`, audited, and each field is
validated (an address must look like one; a reference is bounded).

R5 — Rename
The **account's** name is the Account Admin's (`account.rename`), audited. The **workspace's** name
stays the workspace administrator's existing `workspace.settings`. Today they are the same string;
the task keeps them two fields so that "rename the account" and "rename this workspace" cannot
silently become one act.

R6 — Deleting a workspace
`DELETE /api/workspace` (the resolved workspace, task 122.2) removes that workspace's rows — boards,
lanes, items, placements, edges, links, objectives, key results, templates, the workspace's people and
its settings — in **one transaction**. It is `workspace.delete`: the Account Admin's, or the
workspace administrator's if the decision is taken that way — one of them, stated once in the matrix.
- A workspace the caller may not administer is **404**, never a refusal that confirms it exists.
- The account's **only** workspace is refused with a sentence that names the alternative: closing the
  account is what deleting the last one means.
- The audit row is written **in the same transaction, to the account's trail**, which survives the
  workspace: somebody has to be able to say afterwards that it was deleted and by whom.

R7 — Closing the account
`DELETE /api/account` removes **everything this instance holds**: every workspace and its work, the
members and their invitations, sessions, groups and their grants, audit events, error reports, and the
instance's own settings. The answer is only given after the deletion has happened; a verification
query per table runs first, in the same transaction, and a mismatch rolls it back rather than leaving
a half-closed account.
- The confirmation is the account's **name typed**, as the destructive acts already require (task
  140's drawer, 144's erase).
- The last-account-admin guard does **not** apply here, and that is deliberate: the guard exists to
  keep the deployment administrable, and closing it is the act of ending it. A single Account Admin
  may close it; the confirmation is what stands in for the second person.
- After it, a fresh sign-in creates a new account (the first-run path, task 132) — the e2e proves it.

R8 — Export offered before either
The confirmation offers the file first: a workspace export for R6 (the existing `exportWorkspace`,
proved by `e2e/workspace.spec.ts`) and a full backup for R7 (task 119's `backup.ts`). Offering it is
the interface's duty; requiring it is not, because an operator closing a deployment may already have
the file.

R9 — Both runtimes
The deletions are `Database.batch` transactions — the same statements on D1 and the Node file driver.
The e2e runs against the Node entry: delete a workspace, read it back as gone; close an account,
sign in again, and find a new one.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION

V1 — R2: the matrix decides every account action for both roles, and a new action without a decision
     fails the guard test.
V2 — R1/R3: a member is refused rename, billing, promotion and deletion (403); an Account Admin is
     allowed each; the last Account Admin cannot be demoted.
V3 — R6: delete a workspace with work in it; its rows are gone, the account's other workspace is
     untouched, and the trail names the act.
V4 — R6: the only workspace refuses, and the refusal points at closing the account.
V5 — R7: close the account; a query per table finds no rows; a second sign-in creates a fresh account.
V6 — R4: the billing record has exactly the four fields, and no column anywhere can hold a card
     number (asserted against the schema).
V7 — R9: the Node entry performs both deletions and the smoke test still passes.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-24
**R1 — one role, named honestly.** The Account Admin **is** `instance_members.role = 'admin'` — no new
table, no third axis. What changed is that the role now carries the account's own record and its
destruction, and the code says so: `canAccount` is the second matrix, and `requireInstanceAdmin` takes
the action it is guarding. Who may sign in is untouched.

**R2 — the matrix, completed.** `ACCOUNT_ACTIONS` (`account.rename`, `account.billing`,
`account.admins`, `account.delete`, `workspace.delete`) is decided for both instance roles in
`src/domain/roles.ts`, and `roles.test.ts` asserts every pair plus the completeness check, so a new
account action without a decision fails the build. A member is granted nothing at this level, and the
tests drive each power through the route to prove it (403, not a hidden control).

**R3 — delegation.** `PATCH /api/admin/account/admins/:id` appoints and unappoints, audited, with the
last-account-admin rule: the last one cannot step down, and the refusal names what to do first. The
People drawer carries the control ("Account" — Member or Account Admin).

**R4 — billing as a record.** Five columns on `instance_settings`: the account's `name`, and
`billing_email`, `company_name`, `billing_reference`, `plan`. **No card number, no CVC, no bank
detail** — the reference points at the payment provider's customer, and a test asserts the table's
shape so "just one more column" has to justify itself. Addresses are validated; the audit records the
**field names**, never their values.

**R5 — rename.** `account.rename` on the account; the workspace's own name stays the workspace
administrator's `workspace.settings`. They are two fields, so "rename the account" and "rename this
workspace" cannot silently become one act.

**R6 — deleting a workspace.** `DELETE /api/admin/account/workspaces/:id`: its boards, lanes, items,
placements, edges, links, objectives, key results, templates, people, settings, members, group grants
and its pending invitations — one transaction. The **audit row is written in that transaction to a
table with no workspace id**, so it outlives the thing it describes. The account's **only** workspace
is refused with a sentence that names the alternative (close the account), and a workspace that does
not exist is a 404.

**R7 — closing the account.** `DELETE /api/admin/account` removes **every table this database holds**,
read from `sqlite_master` rather than listed by hand — a table added next year is closed with the
rest. Foreign keys are **deferred** for the transaction rather than switched off, so the deletes can
arrive in catalogue order and a violation still fails the commit. The answer is given only after
`remainingRows` confirms nothing is left. `schema_migrations` stays, because it describes the shape
rather than anybody's data.
- The confirmation is the **name typed**, checked **on the server** as well as in the panel — a
  confirmation only the client enforces is a suggestion.
- The last-account-admin guard deliberately does **not** apply: it exists to keep a deployment
  administrable, and this is the act of ending it. The confirmation stands in for the second person.
- After it, the app returns to the sign-in surface carrying the reason, and the **first person to
  sign in creates the account again** — `identify`'s first-run batch re-inserts the instance's
  workspace row, which membership needs and closure removed. Proved by e2e.

**R8 — the file first.** Both destructive panels offer the export before the act: the workspace export
beside the workspace, and again beside the account's closure.

**R9 — both runtimes.** Everything is `Database.batch`; the round trip, the Node smoke test and the
e2e all pass.

**The screen.** Admin → **Account**: name and the four billing fields, then **Ending things** — the
workspace list with *Export first* and *Delete this workspace*, and the closure with its typed
confirmation. Deleting the only workspace is refused by the server and explained in the panel.

**A note on the e2e.** Closing an account deletes everything, so it cannot share an instance with the
rest of the suite: a **fourth webServer** (port 4176, its own database) exists for exactly this spec,
and the spec ends by proving a new sign-in begins a new account.

Tests: the table's shape and the absence of card data; rename and billing recorded with field names
only; a member refused every power; delegation and the last-admin refusal; a workspace deleted with
its work while the account and the trail survive; the only workspace refused; the account closed
leaving no rows; and the four e2e acts on their own instance.

REVISED — 2026-10-24, after review
The model above put the account where the deployment is. It is the other way round, and the code now
says so:

- an **account** is a person;
- a **workspace** is the tenant — it holds many accounts, its boards and its cards, and it is the
  thing that is charged;
- the **owner** is the account that pays, and it is a **field on the workspace**
  (`workspaces.owner_id`), not a role: a workspace may have several administrators and exactly one
  payer. Ownership is set by an administrator, and the owner must be a member.

So:

**Moved.** The billing record (`billing_email`, `company_name`, `billing_reference`, `plan`) moved from
`instance_settings` to `workspaces` (migration 0020), and `instance_settings.name` went with it: the
deployment is not a thing anybody names in the product, and the workspace's own name already lived in
`workspace` (settings).

**Granted to the right role.** `workspace.delete` left the account matrix and joined the workspace
matrix: **the workspace administrator may delete the workspace, and a member may not**. It is a
`DELETE /api/workspace` on the workspace the session resolved, so it cannot name another one.

**Narrowed.** Deleting a workspace takes that workspace and nothing else — its boards, lanes, items,
placements, edges, links, objectives, results, templates, people-in-workspace, settings, members, group
grants and pending invitations — in one transaction. Another workspace, the people's **accounts** and
the instance survive. The audit entry is written in that transaction to a table with no workspace id,
so it outlives the thing it describes.

**Removed.** The instance-wide destroy is gone from the product entirely: no route, no screen, no
`canAccount` matrix, no "Account Admin". Tearing a deployment down is an operator's act with the backup
tooling, not a button a user has. The instance administrator is what it always was — the door, the
people, the invitations, the groups — and nothing at the account level.

**After the deletion.** The person keeps their account and has no workspace to open: `/api/workspace`
answers **404**, the session reports no workspaces (the payload now asks the same `resolveWorkspace`
door every request uses, rather than inventing one for an instance administrator), and the app says so
— "No workspace" — while the board keeps drawing this browser's own copy. Creating another workspace
is a separate piece of work, and the interface is honest about the absence until it exists.

**The screen.** Admin → **Workspace account** (workspace administrator only): the owner, the four
billing fields, and **Delete this workspace** behind the workspace's name typed — checked on the server
as well as in the panel, because a confirmation only the client enforces is a suggestion. The export is
offered beside it.

**Still true from the first pass.** No card number, CVC or bank detail anywhere — the reference points
at the payment provider's customer, and a test asserts the table's shape. Every deletion is one
`Database.batch`, on both runtimes.

Tests: the owner and the bill on the workspace and not on the deployment; the four fields and the
absence of anything chargeable; a member refused every power; an owner who is not a member refused;
deleting a workspace leaving another workspace, the people's accounts and the trail intact; a member
refused the deletion; the typed name enforced by the server; and the e2e on an instance of its own —
owner and bill set, the workspace deleted, and the person left signed in with nothing to open.

CORRECTED AGAIN — 2026-10-24, on review
The workspace and its accounts end together, and arrival no longer seats anybody.

**The accounts go with it.** Deleting a workspace deletes the accounts that belong to it — the
`users` rows, with their sign-in identities, sessions and instance memberships cascading. There is
no "member without access" state afterwards: the person's account existed for that workspace, and it
ends with it. A user who wants to come back signs up again and creates a new workspace, which is the
same act as the first time.

**The trail outlives both.** The `workspace.delete` entry is written in the same transaction, before
the accounts go; `audit_events.actor_id` is `ON DELETE SET NULL`, so the row keeps the sentence and
the data carries the name of whoever did it (`{ name, by }`), because their id is about to disappear.

**One refusal, and the way out of it.** If the workspace's people include the deployment's **last**
administrator, the deletion refuses (409): an account going with the workspace must not leave a
deployment nobody can administer. That made the instance role unappointable, which the first pass of
126 had removed with the account matrix, so it comes back where it belongs — the **people screen**,
not an account panel: `PATCH /api/admin/users/:id/instance`, audited (`user.instance`), with the last
one protected. Deleting a workspace is then possible as soon as somebody outside it administers the
deployment.

**Arrival is an account, not a seat.** `identify` no longer joins a stranger to the deployment's
workspace. The first person on a fresh deployment still gets it — that is the self-hosted first run —
and an invitation still joins the workspace it is for. Everybody else arrives with **no workspace**,
which is the state the sign-up page (162) and the in-app "Create a workspace" both address. Two
consequences rippled through the tests and are now asserted as the rule:
- an open door admits a **member of the instance** and grants no seat on any board;
- a **group** that carries a role is a way *into* a workspace (membership, not just a role on one),
  so closing the group removes the seat with it.

**What is still true.** One workspace per account. The owner is a field on the workspace and is the
account that created it. The workspace's administrator may delete it and a member may not. Nothing a
deletion does reaches another workspace, and the deployment has no account of its own.

REVISED — 2026-10-24: the bill goes, the deletion stays
The deletion semantics stand — one workspace, its accounts with it, the trail kept. The **billing
record** and the **owner as payer** do not: nothing is sold (task 163), so the panel loses its four
billing fields and the owner picker, and the schema loses the columns (task 166).
tasks.testStrategy: The matrix completeness guard; a member refused and an Account Admin allowed each power; a workspace deleted with its work and the trail kept; the only workspace refused; an account closed leaving no rows; and the billing schema asserted to hold no card data.
tasks.complexityReasoning: A reframed role with a matrix entry, a billing record that must not become a payment system, and two deletions — one scoped to a workspace, one verified across every table.

tasks.title: A board has a history of its own: what moved, what changed, and who.
tasks.description: This task gives every board a history view, derived from the entries the workspace already holds.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

Task 116 put an author on every new entry, and a move has always carried the board it happened on.
Between them the entries already describe a board's life; what is missing is a screen that reads
them, and one honest decision about what a board can and cannot know.

SCOPE
1. A board view — `components/BoardHistory.tsx`, the view switch, and `view=history` in `lib/url.ts`.
2. `domain/history.ts` — deriving one board's entries from the items it holds, newest first.
3. The lane actions in the store, for R4 (board-design events are not recorded today).

DEFINITIONS
- Board history: the entries that concern one board — its moves, and the changes to the items it
  holds — newest first.
- Move entry: a log entry of kind `moved`, which carries the board it happened on, the lanes and
  the stages as they were.
- Item change: any other entry on an item. It carries a time, a kind, a note and (since task 116)
  an author — but not a board.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — A place
The board's history shall be a view of the board, at its own URL (`view=history`), reachable from
the board's navigation, and board-specific like every other board view.

R2 — Moves, exactly
Every move recorded on this board shall appear, with the lanes and stages as they were. The entry
carries them, so a lane renamed or removed later cannot rewrite the past.

R3 — Changes, honestly bounded
Changes to the items this board holds shall appear too, and the screen shall say what it cannot
know: an item can sit on several boards, and an edit records no board. The task shall choose one of
two honest answers and write down why: record the board on new entries (so the future is exact),
or label changes as the item's own history rather than the board's.

R4 — The board's own design
Splitting, adding, renaming or removing a lane, and changing a WIP limit, are not recorded at all
today. A board's history that omits them is missing its most consequential events. They shall be
recorded, with the same who and when, and shown in the same view.

R5 — Nothing invented
An entry from before identities existed shall show no author. A deleted item takes its history
with it. The screen shall show what exists rather than filling the gaps.

R6 — Derived, not stored
The view shall read the items' logs. It shall not add a second place where history lives: one
workspace, one record, however many ways it is read.

VERIFICATION

V1 — R1: A deep link to `view=history` opens it, and the board's navigation names it.
V2 — R2: Move a card, rename the lane it left, then open the history: the entry names the lane as
it was, with the person's name beside it.
V3 — R3: With an item on two boards, a change made while the other board was in front appears —
and is described in the terms the task chose.
V4 — R4: Split a lane; the split appears in the history with its author and time.
V5 — R5: An old entry renders without an author; delete an item and its entries leave with it.
V6 — R6: `localStorage` gains no history key; the view reads what the workspace already holds.

CANCELLED — 2026-10-21
A card can sit on several boards, so its history is the card's, not the board's. A board-level view
would have to attribute an edit to a board the person may not have been looking at — a record that
lies about what it saw. The entries are already per item, and the card's own Activity tab is where
the model puts them: the feature this task was reaching for already exists in the right place.

What the task noticed along the way is a separate question and not a task: a board's own design
changes — splitting, renaming or removing a lane, changing a WIP limit — are recorded nowhere. That
is a gap in the *board's* record, not the card's, and it should be decided on its own terms.

tasks.title: The project runs on a machine its owner controls.
tasks.description: This task packages the portable server as something a team can run: a Docker image, a compose file, a first run that makes the first account the owner, and the environment it documents.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

SCOPE
1. A multi-stage Dockerfile: build the client, copy the server, run the Node entry on a small base
   image.
2. A compose file: one service, one volume, one port.
3. A first run that applies the migrations, makes the first account the owner, and needs no manual
   SQL.
4. Configuration by environment, documented in one place: the database path, the public URL, the
   providers, the mail relay.
5. A health endpoint, and a README section a self-hoster can follow without reading this repository.

DEFINITIONS
- Self-hosted instance: one deployment a team runs, on a machine they own, with one workspace.
- First run: the state an instance is in before anyone has signed in.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — One command
Bringing an instance up shall be one command after a checkout, and the image shall build from the
repository alone.

R2 — No manual setup
The first run shall apply the migrations, create the storage the server needs and start answering —
no SQL typed by hand, no seed script to remember.

R3 — The first account owns the instance
The first person to sign in shall become the owner, and the instance shall refuse a second owner
without an explicit handover.

R4 — Configuration is environment
Every deployment-specific value shall arrive as an environment variable and be documented in one
place: the database, the public URL, the providers, the mail relay.

R5 — Data outlives the container
The database and any uploaded file shall live on a volume, and removing the container shall not
remove them.

R6 — Honest readiness
A health endpoint shall say whether the instance can serve, and the app shall say when it cannot —
the honesty `persist()` already gives the browser.

R7 — Nothing hostile by default
The image shall run as a non-root user, expose no debugging port, and ship no default credentials.

R8 — Say what SQLite means
The documentation shall say plainly that a file-backed database serves one instance: scaling out
means Postgres, not a second container on the same file, and backing up means copying the volume.

REVISED — 2026-10-24: the operator’s path, and it is the main path
Raise to **high**. This is no longer the self-hoster's optional lane: every deployment is an operator's.
The scope grows from "a machine its owner controls" to **install, upgrade, back up, restore**: a
container or a systemd unit, the environment reference, TLS behind a proxy, the migration step on
upgrade, and a restore drill that is run rather than described.

DONE — 2026-10-24 (commit `fe2a91a`, CI green: `checks`, `e2e`, `image`, `deploy`)
`Dockerfile` builds in two stages — the client and the site compiled, then `dist/`, the server, the
migrations and `src/domain` carried into a runtime that installs production dependencies only. It
runs as `flowline` (uid 10001), exposes one port, ships no credentials, and its `HEALTHCHECK` is the
same `/api/health` an operator would curl. `compose.yaml` is one service, one volume, one loopback
port. `docs/docker.md` is the road, `install.md` gains a container section, and `configure.md` says
plainly that there is no mail relay.

Two findings from building it, both fixed rather than worked around:

- **`tsx` is a runtime dependency**, not a dev one: the shipped server is TypeScript, and `--omit=dev`
  produced an image that started and could not answer. Moved, with the lock. The image went from
  1.48 GB to 441 MB, and `node_modules` from 528 MB to 79 MB.
- **`.dockerignore` cannot exclude `e2e/`**: `tsconfig.json` references its tsconfig, and the
  typecheck is the first thing `npm run build` does.

R3 is superseded by task 163: the first account **administers** the instance and its workspace, and
there is no owner to hand over — nothing is sold (task 166). R4's "mail relay" does not exist by
design: invitations are links, and the server never writes to an address.

CI now builds the image and runs it through compose on every push: health, the unprivileged uid, the
database it creates itself, the first sign-in becoming the workspace under `WORKSPACE_NAME`, and the
container replaced with the work still there. Verified locally the same way, plus a backup taken
inside the container.

R8 is written down in `install.md` and `docs/docker.md`: one file serves one instance, two containers
on the same file is corruption rather than scaling, and scaling out means Postgres behind
`server/db.ts`.

VERIFICATION

V1 — R1: from a clean clone, build and start with one command; the app answers.
V2 — R2, R5: stop and remove the container; start it again on the same volume; the workspace is there.
V3 — R3: sign in as the first person; the admin surface is theirs. Invite a second; they are not an owner.
V4 — R4: change the public URL and a provider through the environment; both take effect.
V5 — R6: break the database path; the health endpoint says so rather than the app failing quietly.
V6 — R7: inspect the running container; its user is not root.
V7 — R8: read the README as someone who has only just heard of the project; the limit and the backup are stated, not implied.
tasks.expansionPrompt: (1) the Dockerfile and the Node entry in the image; (2) compose, the volume and the config; (3) first run, migrations and the owner; (4) the health endpoint and the README a self-hoster follows.
tasks.complexityReasoning: Packaging rather than invention: the server and schema already exist, so the work is an image, a volume, a first run, a health check and documentation honest enough to follow without the repository open.

tasks.title: The server has a shape before it has a route.
tasks.description: This task builds the portable HTTP seam — one Hono app, two entry files, one database interface — so that 117's first route and 118's first table are written once and run in both places.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

SCOPE
1. A Hono application in `server/` that is the whole API: one `fetch` handler, no bindings.
2. A `Database` interface, with two implementations — D1, and a driver over a SQLite file.
3. `worker/index.ts` as the Cloudflare entry: bindings in, `app.fetch` out, nothing else.
4. `server/index.node.ts` as the Node entry: a port, a database path, `serve(app.fetch)`.
5. A health route that answers on both, and static assets served by both.
6. A second CI job that boots the Node entry and replays the API paths the e2e suite uses.
7. The existing `/api/errors` endpoint moved onto the seam — the first route proven in both places —
   with the pure parser beside it in `server/`.

DEFINITIONS
- Entry: the only file that knows which runtime it is on.
- Seam: the four things that differ between deployments — the entry file, the database binding,
  static assets, and the live channel.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — One handler
The API shall be one `fetch` handler. A Worker shall export it; a Node process shall serve it.

R2 — Bindings at the edge of the code
`cloudflare:*` imports, `D1Database`, `env.ASSETS` and `cf-connecting-ip` shall appear only in
`worker/`. `server/` shall compile and run without them.

R3 — The database behind an interface
Every statement shall go through `Database` — `all`, `get`, `run`, `batch` — with two
implementations: D1, and a SQLite file in the Node entry. No statement shall depend on an API only
one of them has.

R4 — Assets on both
The built client shall be served by the Worker's asset router and by the Node entry, with the same
single-page fallback, so every place in the app is a URL on both.

R5 — Health
`GET /api/health` shall answer on both entries, and shall say whether the database can be reached
rather than answering 200 regardless.

R6 — The second runtime is tested
CI shall boot the Node entry against a temporary database and replay the API paths the e2e suite
uses, so a route that works on one runtime and not the other fails the build.

R7 — No behaviour change
The app shall behave exactly as it does today. This task adds a shape, not a feature.

R8 — The endpoint that exists comes with us
`/api/errors` shall move onto the seam rather than sit beside it: the same statuses — 204, 400, 413,
429, 503 when the database is absent — the same hourly cap, and the same salted address hash. It
shall lose its direct D1 access and reach the database through `Database`. Because it is the first
route, it shall gain the test it never had: today only its parser is tested, not the endpoint.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-21
`server/` holds the whole API as one Hono handler. `Runtime` names the three things that are
genuinely per-runtime — the database, the client's address, and the salt — so no route reads a
binding. `worker/index.ts` is the Cloudflare entry over `worker/d1.ts`; `server/index.node.ts` is the
Node entry over `node:sqlite`, serving the built client with the SPA fallback.

`/api/errors` moved onto the seam and gained the test it never had: seven cases against a real
database built from the real migrations. `/api/health` asks the database rather than assuming it.

`npm run portable` fails the build if a Cloudflare binding appears in `server/`, and
`npm run smoke:node` boots the Node entry on a temporary database and uses the API. CI runs both.
Hono is the framework; the contract underneath it is `Request` to `Response`, as
`docs/server-runtime.md` argues, so the framework stays replaceable.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 — R1, R4: open the built app on both entries; the board works on each, deep links included.
V2 — R2: CI searches `server/` for `cloudflare:` and binding types; it finds nothing.
V3 — R3: point each implementation at a temporary database; the same statement answers the same on both.
V4 — R5: `GET /api/health` on both; remove the database and it says so rather than answering 200.
V5 — R6: break one route on the Node entry only; CI fails.
V6 — R7: the existing unit and e2e suites pass unchanged.
V7 — R8: a report is accepted on both entries and stored; an oversized body is refused with 413; with no
database configured it answers 503; the hourly cap still answers 429.
tasks.expansionPrompt: (1) the Hono app and the health route in `server/`; (2) the `Database` interface with a D1 implementation; (3) the SQLite-file implementation and the Node entry; (4) static assets and the SPA fallback on both; (5) the CI job that boots Node and replays the API paths.
tasks.complexityReasoning: A small amount of code with a large blast radius: every later route and table is written on this seam, so getting the boundary wrong is expensive and getting it right is cheap. The CI lane is what keeps it honest.

tasks.title: A board's dashboard leads with the work that needs attention, and the cards behind every number.
tasks.description: The dashboard's first section becomes a count band of attention signals over the board's unfinished work — overdue, stale, unassigned, no priority, no estimate — with a review list beneath it holding exactly the items behind those counts, so a reader can go from a number to the card in one click.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

The dashboard today is an initiative table and a time-in-column table. A team board usually has no initiatives placed on it, so its dashboard is nearly empty, and the first question anyone opens a dashboard with — "what is at risk of being forgotten?" — has no answer on any board. This task gives every board dashboard a first section, modelled on the "Needs attention" band and "Items to review" list in the supplied reference: a count band over the work the board renders, and a review list of exactly the items behind those counts.

SCOPE
1. `src/domain/attention.ts` — the derivation, pure and unit tested.
2. `src/domain/attention.test.ts` — the boundaries and the invariants.
3. `src/components/ManagementDashboard.tsx` — the band and the list at the top of the dashboard, above the initiative table.
4. `src/lib/colors.ts` — only if a genuine reuse gap appears. The badge set is not to be reinvented.

DEFINITIONS
- Attention item: an item this board renders and has not finished — not archived, and not in a Done stage.
- Signal: one reason an attention item deserves a closer look. The set is closed in this task; nothing else is invented.
- The board's work: the cards placed on a board that renders a cards workflow; the initiatives placed on a board that does not.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Derived, never stored
Every signal shall be computed from state the model already keeps — the placements, the lane stamps, the assignees, the priority, the size and the target dates. Nothing shall be written onto an item, no persisted field shall be added, and there shall be no persist version bump or migration. `attention.ts` shall take the graph, the board id, the issue types and `now`, and return the items and the counts; the component shall compute nothing of its own.

R2 — Six signals, each defined once
The band shall carry these tiles, in this order:

- **Unfinished** — the population itself: cards placed on this board, not archived, whose stage is not Done. Every other count is a subset of this one, which is an invariant to test.
- **Overdue** — `isOverdue(item, resolved)` from `filters.ts`, the same predicate the filter panel uses. A finished or archived card is never overdue.
- **Stale** — committed work (Not Started or In Progress) whose placement carries a `laneEnteredAt` older than `STALE_AFTER_DAYS`. A card with no stamp is *not* stale: an unknown last movement is not the same as no movement, exactly as `initiativeHealth` already argues. The threshold shall be read from the constant, never typed into the component; the subtitle shall name the real threshold ("No movement for 7+ days"), not the 30 in the reference screenshot.
- **Unassigned** — no assignees, matching the `unassigned` filter exactly, so the number and the filtered board cannot disagree.
- **No priority** — `priority` is undefined. Priority is a judgement the team makes, so its absence is a reviewable gap rather than an error.
- **No estimate** — `size` is undefined, on **cards only**. An initiative has no estimate by design, so an initiative is never counted against one; on a board with no cards workflow the tile is absent, not zero.

R3 — Coordination boards read their own work
A board with no cards workflow shall run the same section over its own initiatives rather than over cards: Overdue from the target date against the derived rollup bucket, Stale and Unowned from `initiativeHealth` (whose `stale` and `unowned` rules already read the work below), No priority from the item, and no No estimate tile at all. The shape, the ordering, the band and the list shall be identical, so the dashboard reads the same way on a team board and a programme board.

R4 — One computation, two surfaces
The band and the review list shall read one array. A tile's number shall always equal the number of rows carrying that signal, and a row's signal chips shall be the same objects the counts were taken from. This is asserted in a unit test, so the heading and the list can never tell different stories.

R5 — Every count is a door
Clicking a tile shall narrow the review list to the items carrying that signal — view state only, never the board's saved filters and never a store write. Choosing the selected tile again, or an "All" affordance, shall restore the full list. Clicking a row shall open that item with the store's existing `openItem`, so a number can become the card in one click. The tiles shall be real buttons with accessible names, not divs with click handlers.

R6 — Order that puts the worst first
Rows shall be ordered by number of signals, descending; then by known age, descending, with unknown ages last; then by title, case-insensitively. Nothing else. A reader should be able to stop after the first row and still have seen the worst item.

R7 — Quiet, honest, and never nagging
When no item carries a signal, the section shall say so in one calm sentence and draw no band. An unknown age shall render as an em dash, never `0d` and never "new". Nothing shall be auto-flagged, auto-moved, auto-assigned or notified; this surface only reports what is already true, which is the same contract as the health column and the aging cue.

R8 — One vocabulary
The signal chips shall reuse `FLAG_BADGE_SHAPE` and `FLAG_BADGE` from `lib/colors.ts` — risk for Overdue, watch for the rest — and `STAGE_LABELS` for any fallback status. Age and overdue shall come from `ageDays` and `isOverdue`, not a second implementation. Each chip shall carry its rule's own `why` as a `title`, the way `HealthFlagInfo` already does, so a badge explains itself in words. No new badge palette, no second notion of stale.

R9 — The list's own columns
The review table shall carry Item (type colour and title), Status (the lane the card sits in, falling back to the stage's label), Age (whole days in the current lane), and Signals (the chips). It shall sit directly beneath the band, titled "Items to review", and wear the same bordered white card as the tables already there.

R10 — The export does not change
`dashboardCsv` shall keep exporting the initiative rows exactly as it does today. The attention section is a reading surface, not a second export; adding attention rows would change the meaning of a file that already has one.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-21
`src/domain/attention.ts` derives the band and the review list from one row array: each row is an item the board renders and has not finished, with its lane path, its known age, and the signals it carries. The counts are taken from that array, so a tile and the rows behind it cannot disagree, and `hasEstimate` says whether the No estimate tile exists at all.

The population follows the app's own rule rather than the presence of a lane tree: `isAggregating` decides, so a programme or portfolio board reads its initiatives through `initiativeHealth` — stale and unowned in that rule's own words — and a team board reads its cards. Staleness reuses `STALE_AFTER_DAYS` and says nothing without a lane stamp; overdue reuses `isOverdue`; the list's status is the lane path, with the stage as fallback. No store field, no migration, and `dashboardCsv` is untouched.

The dashboard leads with Needs attention: tile buttons (`aria-pressed`) narrow the Items to review table, Show all clears them, Unfinished shows the whole population, and a row opens the item. A board with no signals draws a sentence instead of a band, and an unknown age is an em dash.

`attention.test.ts` covers each signal's boundary, unknown stamps, Done and archived exclusions, the counts-equal-rows invariant, ordering, the initiative path, and the absent estimate tile. The full suite (430 tests), typecheck, lint, scan, build and the bundle-size check pass.

FOLLOW-UP — 2026-10-22
The initiative overview now sits between the Needs attention band and Items to review. Each review row also carries an Open on board action (an external-link button in its own column): the row still opens the drawer, while the action leaves the dashboard for the board with that item open.

FOLLOW-UP — 2026-10-22 (Time in column)
Time in column now reads as a four-cell band in the same shape as Needs attention: one cell per typed column, left to right, carrying the stage dot and column name, the oldest age as the headline, and the card count and median beneath. The staleness threshold colours the oldest number, and the empty-column sentence replaces the table when the cards workflow has no columns.

FOLLOW-UP — 2026-10-22 (reading order)
The dashboard now reads high level first: Time in column (with the card count in each column as the headline, oldest and median beneath), then the initiative overview, then Needs attention, then Items to review directly beneath its band.

FOLLOW-UP — 2026-10-22 (filter connection)
The band and the review table now share one card: the tiles sit directly above an Items to review toolbar that states what the selection is doing ("8 items need a look", "Overdue · 3 of 8 items"), with a Clear filter action and an aria-live summary. The selected tile is ringed, and the section subtitle says the tiles filter the items below, so the relationship is visible rather than inferred from two headings.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 — R1: unit tests in `attention.test.ts` build a graph by hand and assert every signal from it. Nothing on an item changes after the computation.

V2 — R2: boundaries, one test each — a card due yesterday is overdue and one due tomorrow is not; a card exactly `STALE_AFTER_DAYS` old is stale and one day short is not; a card with no `laneEnteredAt` is never stale; a Done or archived card appears in no count; a Backlog card is not stale but can be unassigned; a card with `size: 0` has an estimate while one with `size: undefined` does not.

V3 — R3: a graph with no cards workflow yields initiative rows; the estimate tile is absent rather than 0, and the stale count agrees with `initiativeHealth` for the same graph.

V4 — R4: for each tile, the number equals the length of the rows selecting it, and every count is at most Unfinished.

V5 — R5: clicking a tile narrows the list and clicking it again restores it; the board's saved filters are unchanged; clicking a row sets the store's selected item.

V6 — R6: a fixture with equal and unequal signal counts, known and unknown ages, and two same-aged titles asserts the exact row order.

V7 — R7: an empty board renders the sentence and no tiles; a card without a placement stamp shows an em dash.
