never changes a row optimistically, and a selection is dropped when the filters change so a bulk
action can only ever touch rows the operator can see.

**CSV.** `GET /api/admin/users.csv` serves the documented columns — name, email, role, status, last
active, joined — quoted per **RFC 4180** (a name with a comma stays one field), with the date in the
filename. No token, no session, no hash: nothing that could authenticate anybody. It honours the
list's search and status filters, capped at 10,000 rows.

Tests: exactness against lookalikes, the viewer role a domain grants, the audited change, the
whole-selection refusal leaving every row untouched, the successful bulk change, and the file's
header, quoting and absence of secrets. E2E: a domain admitted into a fresh browser context, a
lookalike refused, the CSV downloaded and read, and a bulk deactivation driven from the table.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - An allowed domain admits a verified address as Viewer only.
V2 - A lookalike domain does not match.
V3 - The domain list is visible and audited.
V4 - A bulk operation refuses as a whole when one row is protected.
V5 - Bulk success reports the number changed.
V6 - CSV has the documented columns, correct quoting and no secrets.
V7 - Page and export are server-side and do not download the directory.

tasks.title: Groups: a role granted once to many.
tasks.description: A group is a named set of users so a workspace role is granted once. Inactive groups grant nothing. This is deliberately deferred until there is more than one workspace and a customer asks for it.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md section 3.1 (the v1 decision) and section 7 (P3).

SCOPE
1. groups and group_members tables.
2. group_workspace_roles, joining the existing workspace_members permission check.
3. Active/inactive groups.
4. Admin UI, behind the same instance-admin door.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Model
groups(id, name, description, active, created_by, created_at). group_members(group_id, user_id, added_by, added_at). group_workspace_roles(group_id, workspace_id, role).

R2 - Effective role
A person's workspace role is the union of their direct workspace_members row and every active group role. The highest role wins. The guard function names the source (direct or group) so the UI can explain it.

R3 - Inactive group
Grants nothing, immediately. Its members keep any direct role.

R4 - Last administrator
A group granting admin counts toward the last-administrator calculation. Removing the last admin-bearing group assignment is refused just like removing the last person.

R5 - No recursion
Groups do not nest. Add nesting only with a cycle guard and a real requirement.

R6 - Versioning
Every assignment and membership change is audited.

TESTS
Two people in a group with Editor can edit. Deactivate the group; both lose Editor but keep a direct Viewer. Removing the last admin group is refused. A group role cannot exceed the assigning administrator's authority.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-24
**R1 — the model.** `groups`, `group_members`, `group_workspace_roles` (migration 0017), exactly as
specified: a name and what it is for, the people in it, and the role it carries per workspace. Names
are unique case-insensitively, so two "Platform Leads" cannot both exist.

**R2 — the effective role.** `effectiveRole` reads the union of the direct `workspace_members` row
and every **active** group's grant for the workspace, in one statement, and answers the highest role
**with the source it came from** — `direct`, `instance`, or `group:<name>`. Every path that asks goes
through it: the permission middleware, the workspace member list, the people screen, and the client's
own `/api/auth/session` (so a person whose editor role comes from a group is not shown a read-only
board). On screen the People table and the drawer say **"via group"** and name it — a role nobody can
explain is a role nobody can change.

**R3 — an inactive group** grants nothing, immediately, and the test takes the pen away on the next
request. The list of people and the grant are kept, so it can be turned back on.

**R4 — the last administrator.** `workspaceAdminIds` answers *who administers this workspace* —
directly or through a group — and it accepts a simulated change, so the refusal is about who would be
left rather than who is there now. It is the count behind all three forms of the rule: deactivating a
group, deleting one, changing its role away from admin, and removing its last admin-bearing member
are each **409** with a sentence, and nothing is written. The people and workspace rosters use the
same count, so a group-granted administrator cannot be demoted through the person screen either.

**R5 — no recursion.** A group has no parent column at all, so nesting is not prevented but
impossible; a test asserts the table's columns so the absence stays deliberate.

**R6 — the trail.** `group.create`, `group.edit`, `group.delete`, `group.member` and `group.role`,
with the workspace and the role in the data. Every one of them is asserted in the test.

**The screen.** Admin → **Groups**: the list with its people and the role it carries here, a role
select, **turn off / turn on**, delete behind a confirmation that says what is lost, an "add person"
picker, and a create form. The People table is told to read the directory again when a group changes,
so one screen never shows two answers.

**One thing worth saying.** The door is the instance administrator's, so the rule in the tests — *a
group role cannot exceed the assigning administrator's authority* — is implemented (`grantable`
reads the caller's own effective role) but cannot be reached today: an instance administrator holds
admin everywhere. It is there for the day a workspace administrator is given the door.

Tests: the grant applies to every member and disappears when the group is turned off; the highest of
direct and group wins, and the client is told the effective one; all three refusals of the last
administrator, with the grant still intact afterwards; the schema has no place to nest; every change
in the trail; and the list naming each person's source. E2E: a group created on screen, given a role
and a person, showing "via group" in the People table, turned off and gone from the server's answer.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - A group role applies to every active member.
V2 - An inactive group grants nothing.
V3 - The highest direct or group role wins.
V4 - The last administrator rule counts group-granted admins.
V5 - Groups do not nest, or nesting is cycle-safe.
V6 - Every change is audited.

tasks.title: A custom role label that grants nothing.
tasks.description: An administrator can name a role for routing approvals or describing a team, but the label carries no permissions. Windshift's deliberate choice, and the only safe way to offer custom roles.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md section 8 (custom roles).

SCOPE
1. A label entity, separate from the permission role.
2. Assignment to a person, per workspace.
3. No permission path from the label.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Separate fields
workspace_members.role stays the closed set. A new custom_label_id (nullable) or a separate person_labels table carries the display name. It is never read by can().

R2 - Label only
The UI shows the label beside the role, and says in one sentence that it does not grant access. Creating, renaming and deleting labels is workspace-administrator work.

R3 - No escalation by naming
A label called "Administrator" grants nothing. The permission role is the only authority. Test this by naming a label Administrator and confirming a viewer stays a viewer.

R4 - Deletion
Deleting a label does not remove anyone's permission role and does not delete a person.

R5 - Audit
Label assignment and removal are audited, because they route people.

TESTS
Create a label called Administrator, assign it to a Viewer; every write is still 403. Delete the label; the person's role is unchanged. A label cannot be used in the role guard.

CANCELLED — 2026-10-24
Decided by the product owner: **custom roles are not wanted.** The closed set of three is the whole
vocabulary — a label that grants nothing would add a field to every role question and answer none of
them, and the thing it exists for (a name for "what this person does") is already carried by the
group's name and the card's own words.

Nothing depended on this task. `workspace_members.role` stays a closed set of viewer / editor /
administrator, `can()` stays the only permission path, and `docs/admin.md` §8's note on custom roles
stays a note rather than a plan. If a deployment ever asks for one, it comes back as a new task with
the reason it was asked for.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - A custom label is never consulted by can().
V2 - A label named Administrator grants no authority.
V3 - Deleting a label leaves roles and accounts intact.
V4 - Assignment and removal are audited.
V5 - Only a workspace administrator manages labels.

tasks.title: A machine proves who it is, and the tool acquires the credential.
tasks.description: A scoped, revocable token that a script or an agent obtains for itself — by browser approval, or one click from Admin — rather than copying a secret out of a settings page. Administrator-minted tokens remain for CI and daemons.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md sections 5 and 8.

SCOPE
1. api_tokens table: id, user_id, name, token_hash, scopes, expires_at, last_used_at, revoked_at.
2. Create/list/revoke endpoints and a Security page section.
3. Scope enforcement on the API routes that exist.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Secret handling
32 random bytes, shown once, stored as SHA-256. Never logged, never returned by list, never in audit data.

R2 - Scopes
resource:action strings, at least boards:read, boards:write, items:read, items:write, admin:users:read. A token can never exceed its owner's role: both the scope and the role are checked.

R3 - Expiry
Optional expiry, default 90 days. An expired or revoked token is 401 on the next request.

R4 - Identity
A token authenticates as its owner. Its last_used_at updates at most hourly. The UI shows the last use and a Revoke button.

R5 - Admin visibility
An instance administrator can list and revoke tokens for an account in the People drawer, with audit. The token value is never available to the administrator.

R6 - No privilege escalation
Minting a token with a scope the owner's role cannot exercise is refused at mint time, not silently at use.

TESTS
Mint a read-only token; write is 403, read is 200. Revoke; next request 401. Expire; 401. A viewer cannot mint an items:write token. A list response never contains a token or hash. Admin revoke is audited.

DEFERRED — 2026-10-24
Decided by the product owner: **Flowline is for human users for now**, so it issues no machine
credentials. Deferred rather than cancelled, because nothing about the design is wrong — it is
parked until something needs it.

WHY IT IS PARKED
A token exists for a client that is not a person: a script, a CI job, an importer, a bot. There is no
such client today. The only consumer of this API is the app, and it uses a session like a person
does. `docs/admin.md` already filed this under P3 with the reason attached — *"needs an API worth
calling"* — and that has not changed.

WHAT WOULD BRING IT BACK
- a real integration somebody asks for (an importer, a chat bot that files cards, a dashboard);
- a read-only share link (123) growing into "let a script read this board too";
- a self-hoster wanting to script backups or imports against their own instance (128).

IF IT RETURNS, DO THIS FIRST
Settle the scope vocabulary against `src/domain/roles.ts` before writing any code. The matrix has
twenty actions and splits `board.design` / `board.settings` / `board.delete` into administrator-only
acts, so a coarse `boards:write` either smuggles admin powers into a token or needs more scopes than
the old requirement listed. That is an hour of design, it costs nothing now, and it is the only part
that gets harder with time.

WHAT IS UNCHANGED
The session remains the only way to be a caller: one door, one `Caller` shape, and every rule —
roles, workspace resolution, the seal — applies to it alone. Nothing in the code assumes tokens
exist, so nothing needs undoing.

REVIVED — 2026-10-24: scripts and agents are users too
The deferral was right for the product it was written for — a board a person opens in a browser, on a
service nobody else can reach. It stops being right now that Flowline is software a team installs and
runs: a self-hoster wants a cron job that files a card, a script that exports a board, and an agent
that reads the board to answer a question. Tasks **169** (the REST API) and **170** (the MCP server)
are the clients this was parked for, and both depend on this one.

Back to pending, and unchanged otherwise: the token is minted once, stored hashed, scoped, expiring
and revocable, and it can never exceed its owner's role. The one thing this task must do first is the
thing its own note says — settle the scope vocabulary against `src/domain/roles.ts` (twenty actions,
with `board.design`, `board.settings` and `board.delete` administrator-only) before a single route is
written, because a coarse `boards:write` either smuggles administrator powers into a token or needs
more scopes than the old text listed.

DECIDED — 2026-10-24: yes, a credential is needed — but the *acquisition* was the bad part
The question was whether the REST API (task 169) and the MCP server (task 170) could avoid tokens
altogether. They cannot, and the reason is worth keeping:

- **A session cookie is not a machine credential.** It exists only after an interactive OIDC redirect,
  it carries no scopes, and it drags browser assumptions (SameSite, CSRF) into clients those
  assumptions were never written for.
- **An OIDC ID token is not an API credential** either: it is proof of a sign-in *to this server*, for
  this client id, and must never be accepted as a bearer token.
- **Without a credential there is no identity**, and then the audit cannot say who filed a card, a
  token cannot be read-only, and revocation becomes "restart the instance".

What was wrong was making a person go and copy a secret. The remedy is acquisition, not a different
kind of token. Everything above stands — hashed at rest, scoped from `src/domain/roles.ts`, expiring,
revocable, never exceeding its owner's role — and these are added:

R7 — The tool acquires it
`flowline login` (and the MCP server's equivalent) prints a short code and a URL. The person approves
in the browser they are already signed in to; the instance mints a token with the scopes the approval
screen named; the tool stores it in the operating system's keychain, or in a `0600` file where there
is none. The secret never passes through a clipboard, a shell history or a chat message.

R8 — One click from Admin
"Connect an agent" mints a scoped token and writes the MCP client config (task 170), so adding
Flowline to an agent is a button rather than a JSON snippet somebody has to fill in correctly.

R9 — Administrator-minted stays, as the exception
CI jobs, daemons and a script on a machine nobody will ever open a browser on. Same scopes, same
expiry, same revocation, and the list screen says which were minted this way.

R10 — The approval screen is the consent
It names the tool, the scopes and the expiry, in words: "read boards and cards, for 90 days". The code
is single-use, short-lived, bound to the person who approved it, and useless if they did not. A
credential nobody can explain is one nobody will revoke.

Out of scope, recorded rather than implied
- **Flowline is not an OAuth authorization server** for MCP clients: no dynamic client registration,
  no token endpoint. If an agent exists that cannot run a local command, that is the task that adds
  it.
- **An IdP's access token is not accepted as a bearer credential.** Google's are opaque and would need
  per-request introspection with a client secret; Entra and Keycloak issue usable JWTs but need an
  API/audience registered per deployment, plus JWKS caching, rotation and clock skew. That is a
  second credential model, and it belongs in its own task if a deployment asks for it.
- **No unauthenticated mode, including on stdio.** A local agent still says who it is, or the trail
  cannot say who filed the card.

DONE — 2026-10-25 (CI green: checks, image, e2e, publish, deploy)
The design the note demanded was settled before a route was written, and it changed the old text in
three places.

**The vocabulary — nine scopes, one action each, all twenty-one actions reached.** `boards:read`,
`items:read`, `people:read`, `items:comment`, `boards:write`, `items:write`, `objectives:write`,
`workspace:admin`, `instance:admin`. `src/domain/scopes.ts` holds the table; `src/domain/scopes.test.ts`
asserts (a) every action in the matrix is reached by exactly one scope, so a new action cannot arrive
unreachable or doubly reachable, and (b) which roles may hold which scope.

Three decisions the old requirement did not anticipate:
- **`items:comment` is its own scope.** The matrix gives a Viewer `item.comment` and nothing else in
  that group, so with commenting inside `items:write` a Viewer could mint the writing scope. Split, a
  Viewer gains a commenting token and `items:write` stays out of reach. `items:write` *includes*
  `items:comment` (`includes` in the table), because a writer obviously comments.
- **`admin:users:read` became `instance:admin`.** The instance's own administration is not a workspace
  action, so it cannot be expressed as a subset of the matrix; it is answered by the other axis and
  checked in `requireInstanceAdmin`. Coarse, and it cannot escalate: the person must already be an
  instance administrator.
- **A scope is judged by "any action the role can exercise", not "all".** Otherwise an editor could
  never hold `boards:write` (creation yes, design no). The role still refuses the design action at use,
  which is the second ceiling below.

**Two ceilings, both read per request.** The token's scopes (`covers`) and the owner's role from
`workspace_members` (`can`). Demoting an editor tightens every token they hold with nothing to revoke;
a token can only narrow a role, never widen it. The two refusals have different sentences on purpose —
"a viewer may not item.write" and "this credential may not item.write" — because a person and a script
author need different answers. `refusalFor` is that one place, and the item PATCH now uses it too:
its door is `item.comment` (task 171), so the *change* asks again for `item.write` when it is not a
note.

**The credential (R1–R4, R9).** 32 random bytes behind a `flt_` prefix, SHA-256 at rest, shown once,
never in a list or in audit data. `GET/POST /api/tokens`, `DELETE /api/tokens/:id`,
`GET /api/tokens/self`. 90 days by default; `expiresInDays: null` is never, for a daemon nobody will
revisit. Revoked or expired answers 401 — not a person short of authority — and the row stays, marked,
because "which credential was this" is asked afterwards. `last_used_at` is written at most hourly.
Administrator routes list, mint and revoke somebody else's, with audit, and mint within **that
person's** role: an administrator cannot hand a Viewer a writing token.

**The acquisition (R7, R10).** A device flow: the tool asks (`POST /api/tokens/device`), the person
opens `/app?approve=…` and sees the tool's name, the scopes in words and the expiry, approves or
narrows, and the tool exchanges once. The code lives ten minutes, is single-use in both directions,
and is rate-limited per address. `scripts/flowline.mjs` (`npm run flowline -- login`) is the client,
dependency-free: it prints eight characters, polls, and writes the secret to
`~/.config/flowline/token` with mode 0600 (or `FLOWLINE_TOKEN_FILE`). `flowline whoami` and
`flowline token` round it out. Verified against a real server end to end: login → approval → read 200
→ write 403 "this credential may not workspace.import".

**R8 is not done here and not forgotten.** "Connect an agent" writes the MCP client config, which is
task 170's shape; there is nothing correct to write until that task defines it. The scopes, the
minting route and the approval screen it needs all exist.

**Screens.** The profile dialog gained *Machines and agents* (list, mint with scope checkboxes and
expiry, the secret once with a copy button, revoke). The People drawer shows the same panel for one
person, which is where an administrator revokes a credential (R5) or mints one for a daemon (R9). The
consent screen is a lazy chunk (`?approve=…`), because a board must not carry a dialog about
credentials it will not show — the first download is 161.6 KB against 162, and the code is read at
module load, before `useUrl` normalises the query.

**Tests.** 11 server tests (`server/tokens.test.ts`): scope ceiling, revoke, expiry, the role ceiling
after a demotion, viewer refusals at mint, the device flow (pending 428, approve, exchange once, 410),
scope narrowing, administrator mint/revoke with the audit row, and a non-administrator refused.
9 domain tests on the vocabulary. One e2e added to `e2e/setup.spec.ts` — a tool asks, Ada approves in
the browser, the exchange buys the secret, the credential reads `/api/workspace`, the code is spent,
and the list on her account carries no secret.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - The token is shown once and only a hash is stored.
V2 - Scope and role are both enforced.
V3 - An expired or revoked token is 401.
V4 - A token cannot exceed its owner's authority.
V5 - Listing never reveals a token or hash.
V6 - An administrator can revoke but never read a token.
V7 - Admin revocation is audited.

tasks.title: A second factor, if a deployment ever needs one.
tasks.description: TOTP and recovery codes, at the password door only: enrolled from the profile, single-use codes shown once, and nothing added to the OIDC door (the issuer owns that factor). Reopened because task 154 gave a deployment without an identity provider a real password to protect.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md sections 1.4 and 8.

SCOPE
1. An instance policy: provider only (default), or provider plus a registered second factor.
2. WebAuthn registration and verification for the second factor.
3. Recovery, or an explicit administrator fallback.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Trigger
Do not build this until a real deployment requires it. The provider's own MFA already covers most teams and costs nothing to support.

R2 - Policy
One instance-wide policy with preview mode, as Windshift does: warn first, enforce later, list affected users before enforcing.

R3 - Credential
WebAuthn only. No TOTP secret, no password, no SSH key, because none of those exist elsewhere in Flowline.

R4 - Recovery
An administrator fallback that is explicitly enabled, audited, and shown as a banner while it is on. Losing the only factor must not lock the last administrator out permanently.

R5 - Sessions
A second-factor change revokes other sessions and writes audit.

TESTS
Preview mode warns without blocking. Enforced mode refuses a session without the factor. Recovery works only when enabled and is audited. The last administrator cannot enrol into a state with no recovery path.

DEFERRED — 2026-10-24: the second factor belongs to the identity provider
Under task 154 the only way in is OIDC, so MFA is the issuer's job — and the issuer is the one place a
team can require it for every application at once. The one deployment left without an issuer has no
accounts at all (the development switch), so there is nothing here to protect. Deferred rather than
cancelled: a future local-account mode, or a deployment that wants a second factor *inside* the app,
would bring it back with a reason.

REOPENED — 2026-10-24: passwords give it something to protect
The deferral said the second factor belongs to the identity provider, and that the only deployment
without one had no accounts at all. Task 154 changes the second half: passwords and magic links mean a
deployment with no IdP now holds real accounts, and a password is one factor. So the deferral's reason
no longer holds.

Not folded into 154: that task adds the doors, this one adds a lock to the door. The shape when it is
taken: TOTP (an authenticator app), enrolled from the profile, ten single-use recovery codes shown
once, and a step at the password door only — an OIDC sign-in is the issuer's business, and a magic
link is already a second proof of the address. Rate-limit the second-factor prompt like the password.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - The default policy is provider-only and changes nothing today.
V2 - Preview warns; enforce blocks.
V3 - Only WebAuthn is accepted as the second factor.
V4 - Recovery is explicit, audited and bannered.
V5 - Enrolment revokes other sessions.
V6 - The last administrator cannot be locked out.

tasks.title: The public pages: what we do with your data, and how to reach us.
tasks.description: The privacy notice, the terms, a support address and a changelog — and links to the export and the closure that 119 and 126 actually build.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

SCOPE
1. The public pages a person reads before trusting the product: the privacy notice and the terms.
2. A support address, with the response expectation stated.
3. A changelog of user-visible changes.

WHAT THIS IS NOT
Deletion and account authority left this task when 126 was refocused: it now covers only what a
visitor reads. Export is not built here either — the workspace export already exists
(`src/lib/exportWorkspace.ts`, proved by `e2e/workspace.spec.ts`) and the full backup is task 119's;
this task **links** them from the notice rather than writing another.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Notice
A privacy notice shall name the processors actually used, and nothing that is not: the identity
providers, the host, and the error log. A processor list that is out of date is worse than none,
because it reads as a promise.

R2 — Terms
Terms shall be published, and linked from every surface that offers a way in (sign-in, invitation
acceptance).

R3 — Support
A support address and a response expectation shall be published, and reachable from the app.

R4 — Changes recorded
A changelog shall record user-visible changes, newest first, in the words a person would use rather
than in commit subjects.

R5 — Yours to take
The notice shall say how to export a workspace and how an account is closed, with links to the acts
themselves (tasks 119 and 126) — a promise that points at a form is a promise nobody keeps.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION

V1 — R1: the notice's processor list is generated from, or checked against, the configuration the
     deployment actually has (a test that fails when a provider is configured and unlisted).
V2 — R2: the sign-in surface links the terms; the e2e asserts the link exists and resolves.
V3 — R3: the support address appears on the same page, and is a `mailto:` that opens.
V4 — R4: the changelog parses and its newest entry is dated; a page with no entries fails the test.
V5 — R5: the notice's export and closure links both resolve to pages that exist.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-24
**R1 — the notice names the processors, and only them.** `site/processors.json` is the one list: the
identity providers (Google and Microsoft, or an operator's own OIDC), the host, and the error log,
each with a sentence about *what it sees* and why it is there. The page renders that list rather than
carrying a copy of it, and `server/site.test.ts` fails when `server/config.ts` knows a provider the
list does not — a notice that drifts from the code is worse than none.

**R2 — the terms stand beside the door.** The account menu's sign-in surface says, under the provider
buttons, "By continuing you agree to the terms and the privacy notice", with both links live. The e2e
opens it on the instance and checks the link resolves to the page that exists.

**R3 — support, with the promise.** `support@flowline.example` on the help page, the notice and the
terms, with "answered within two working days" beside it; security reports have their own address and
a faster promise. The signed-in account menu gained **Help & support**, so somebody already inside
reaches a person without leaving the app.

**R4 — the changelog.** Dated entries with `<time datetime>`, newest first, in the words a person
would use — what changed and what it means, not commit subjects. `check-site.mjs` fails on a changelog
with no dated entries or one that is out of order, and the e2e asserts the same over the served page.

**R5 — the acts, not a form.** The notice links `/help/#export` and `/help/#closing`, and the help
page carries both sections: **Export** (the board menu, the file is the workspace) and **Closing**
(Admin → Workspace account → Delete, administrator only, name typed, accounts deleted with it). The
site check now resolves **every internal link on every page** against the build, so a promise that
points nowhere fails the build rather than the reader.

**What the notice says that the code decided.** No analytics, no advertising, no third-party scripts;
sessions as hashes with a twelve-hour (or thirty-day) life; the audit kept 90 days and pruned; an
address stored only as a salted hash; no card number, CVC or bank detail anywhere. A removed member's
work stays and says **"Former member"**; a deleted workspace takes its accounts with it.

Tests: `server/site.test.ts` (provider coverage against the code, a sentence per processor, no
duplicates, the placeholder rather than a second copy, the two help anchors, support and changelog
shape); `check-site.mjs` (every internal link resolves, the notice names each processor, the support
address is a `mailto:`, the changelog is dated and ordered); and the e2e (the terms beside the door
resolving, the support address opening, the changelog newest-first).

REVISED — 2026-10-24: no payment processor to name
The processor list keeps the identity providers, the host and the error log, and loses the payment
provider — there is none. The terms lose the plan and refund language and become the terms of
open-source software you run yourself, and the notice says plainly that a self-hoster is the
controller of their own instance's data.

NOTE — 2026-10-24: the changelog page was removed
`/changelog/` was deleted with `/status/` and `/help/` after shipping. A change log on the site
duplicates the repository's own history and its releases, and the site is not where a person reads
what changed — the tag is. `CONTRIBUTING.md` now asks for a release note at the tag instead of a line
in the page, and `docs/public-site.md` records the removal.

NOTE — 2026-10-25: privacy and terms rewritten in a scannable shape
Both pages were rebuilt as a standfirst, a *Last updated* date, an **In short** panel of five bullets,
and numbered sections — the shape good project sites use (mindwtr.app, super-productivity.com) rather
than a page of prose. `/privacy` is now explicitly about *this site and the demo* and says that an
instance you run is yours, with you as the controller; `/terms` leads with the AGPL doing the heavy
lifting and adds the parts a licence does not cover (the site, the builds we publish, no warranty,
liability). The support address and the "answered within two working days" promise stayed; the tests
that asserted their old sentences were updated with them.
tasks.testStrategy: The processor list checked against configuration; the terms linked at sign-in; a support address that opens; a changelog with a dated newest entry; and every link in the notice resolving.
tasks.complexityReasoning: Public pages and a list kept honest by a test; no server work of its own.

tasks.title: The site is static, and `/` is the front door: the app moves to `/app`.
tasks.description: A build that emits real HTML pages for the public site, the application moved to `/app` without losing a single existing link, a 404 that is a 404, and a crawler policy that indexes the site and not the app.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/public-site.md §The shape and §The pages.

SCOPE
1. `site/` — one file per public page, a shared layout, and the site's own stylesheet.
2. `scripts/build-site.ts` — renders the pages into `dist/`, writes `sitemap.xml`, `robots.txt` and the
   404, and copies nothing the app already builds.
3. The app's entry moves to `app/index.html`, served under `/app`; the home page takes `/`.
4. The legacy query redirect, so every link that exists today still lands where it did.
5. `public/_headers`, `wrangler.jsonc`'s not-found handling, and the Node entry's static fallback.
6. The e2e and size gates that hold the line afterwards.

DEFINITIONS
- **Public page**: a page anyone may read, with no session and no JavaScript.
- **The app**: the React board, under `/app`, with its query grammar unchanged.
- **Canonical origin**: `SITE_URL`, the one value used by canonical tags, Open Graph and the sitemap.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — The build emits the site
`npm run build` shall be typecheck, `vite build`, then `node scripts/build-site.ts`, and shall finish
with `dist/index.html`, one HTML file per public page at its own path, `dist/app/index.html`, and the
site's CSS. No public page shall need JavaScript to be read: with scripting disabled its text, links
and images are all there. The app's bundle shall be unchanged and `npm run size` shall still measure
the app rather than the site.

R2 — The app has its own place
The app shall be served under `/app` and only there, with its query intact
(`/app?board=b-atlas&view=dashboard&item=…`). `/?board=…` and every other query the app reads
(`view`, `item`, `q`, `filters`, `lens`, `boundary`, `select`, `collapse`, `stress`, `edit`) shall
land on the same place under `/app` with the query preserved — on every host, including a plain
static one, so an inline head script on the home page is the mechanism and it shall fire before the
home page paints. `useUrl` shall keep the path it was loaded on; the app shall not rewrite itself
back to `/`. `README.md`, `e2e/support.ts` and every doc that names `/?board=` shall name
`/app?board=` instead.

R3 — One nav, one footer, one voice
The nav shall carry Product, Pricing, Help, Self-host, Changelog and Status, then **Sign in** and the
primary action. The footer shall carry the four groups in docs/public-site.md §The home page. Both
come from `site/layout.html` and are emitted on every page. Every page shall start with a skip link
to its main landmark, and header, nav, main and footer shall be landmarks.

R4 — Each page names itself
Every public page shall have a `<title>` unique to it, a meta description, a canonical URL built
from `SITE_URL`, Open Graph and Twitter tags, a theme colour, and the favicon set. A test walks the
built pages and fails on a duplicate title, a missing or duplicated description, a missing canonical,
or a canonical that is not absolute.

R5 — The site's own download
The site's CSS shall be its own file built from `site/site.css`, and no public page shall load the
app's JavaScript. The home page's total transfer (HTML + CSS + images) shall be at most 150 kB,
measured by a check that prints the size and fails over budget — the same discipline as
`npm run size`.

R6 — Machines
`dist/robots.txt` shall allow the public pages, disallow `/app`, and point at the sitemap.
`dist/sitemap.xml` shall list every public page with an absolute URL and a `lastmod`.
`X-Robots-Tag: noindex` shall be scoped to `/app/*` in `public/_headers` rather than applied to
everything, and no public page shall carry it. An unknown path shall answer with the 404 page and a
404 status: the single-page-application fallback shall no longer answer for every path
(`not_found_handling` in `wrangler.jsonc` and the Node entry's last route). Anything under `/app`
shall still be the app.

R7 — Nothing off-origin
No public page shall request anything from another origin — no fonts, no scripts, no images, no
analytics. The CSP in `public/_headers` shall stay `default-src 'self'` and gain `form-action 'self'`
and `frame-ancestors 'none'`. The e2e shall record every request each public page makes and fail on
one whose origin is not the site's. `npm run scan` shall stay clean.

R8 — The app is still the app
`/app` with no query shall draw the demo board exactly as `/` did. Titles, URLs, keyboard, drag, the
drawer and the admin screens shall be unchanged. The only difference shall be the base path.

WHAT THIS IS NOT
The home page's copy (152), the pricing table (153), help (158) or status (159). This task gives them
a place to exist and a build that emits them. It also does not open the site to the public: removing
the Access gate is the launch switch, and it is a checklist item in docs/public-site.md, not code.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: build; every page exists; with JavaScript disabled the home page's heading, links and images
     are in the DOM; `dist/app/index.html` loads the app.
V2 — R2: `/?board=b-atlas&view=dashboard` lands on `/app?board=b-atlas&view=dashboard`; a reload
     keeps the place; back returns to it; the other query parameters survive too.
V3 — R3: every page has the nav and the footer; the skip link is the first focusable thing and moves
     focus to main.
V4 — R4: the head test over the built pages.
V5 — R5: the size check; a page that loads the app bundle fails it.
V6 — R6: robots and sitemap contents; `/this/does/not/exist` is the 404 page with status 404;
     `/app?board=x` is 200 and the app; no noindex on the home page's response.
V7 — R7: the request audit in the e2e; `npm run scan`.
V8 — R8: the existing e2e suite, with its starting URL changed to `/app?board=b-atlas`, is green.
DELIVERED — 2026-10-24
The site owns the front door and the app lives under `/app`. `site/` holds one file per public page
and a shared layout; `scripts/build-site.ts` emits them with `sitemap.xml`, `robots.txt` and the 404;
`scripts/check-site.mjs` walks the build and fails on a duplicate title, a missing or relative
canonical, a script on a public page, a foreign origin, a home page over 150 kB, a robots or sitemap
that disagrees with what is served, or a `noindex` that is not scoped to `/app/*`.

The legacy grammar is preserved by one inline head script on the home page: `/?board=…`, `?view=`,
`?item=`, `?q=`, `?filters=`, `?lens=`, `?boundary=`, `?select=`, `?collapse=`, `?stress=` and `?edit=`
all land on `/app` with the query intact, before first paint, on any host. `useUrl` keeps the path it
was loaded on, so the app does not rewrite itself back to `/`.

An unknown path answers the 404 page with a **404**: `not_found_handling: "404-page"` on Cloudflare,
the Node entry's last route, and the same contract in `scripts/serve-dist.mjs` (which replaces
`vite preview` in the e2e's static lane, because preview answers every unknown path with one page).
`/app` and everything under it is the app: `_redirects` cannot express that on Cloudflare — a rewrite
onto `/app/index.html` matches its own rule and the API refuses it as a loop — so the Worker hands the
shell over itself, which is also the one place that already knows this deployment's routing.

Two links had to learn the new place: an invitation now points at `/app?invite=…`, and the
after-deletion redirect goes to `/app`.

Tests: the site check over the build; `e2e/site.spec.ts` (the front page readable with JavaScript off,
a legacy link landing and surviving a reload, the whole query carried, the 404 with a 404 on both
hosts, `/app` and deep paths, and no foreign request from any page); and the whole existing suite,
green from `/app?board=b-atlas`.

REVISED — 2026-10-24: the site is a project’s site
The build and the routing stand. What changed is the navigation and the footer it emits: no Pricing,
and Install in its place, with `/pricing/` deleted and `/signup/` and `/signin/` re-pointed. That is
task 164, which owns the change rather than reopening this one.
tasks.testStrategy: A static build that emits every page and the app under /app; legacy links that keep their query; no JavaScript needed to read a page and nothing fetched off-origin; a 404 that answers 404; robots and sitemap that scope the app out; and a size budget for the home page.

tasks.title: The home page says what Flowline is, and shows it running.
tasks.description: The pitch, the evidence, the real product and the questions a buyer asks — with the free account as the way in, and the portfolio as what money buys.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/public-site.md §The home page and §/product, and the promises ledger at the end of that document. SCOPE 1. `/` — the home page. 2. `/product` — how the model works, with the shipped UI. 3. The screenshots, captured from the built app rather than drawn. 4. The copy rules every page of the site inherits. CONTENT — the home page, in order 1. **Nav** and **footer** from the layout (151). 2. **Hero** — an H1 in the product's own words. The claim is *the truth is derived, not typed*; the sentence under it names the two audiences (the team's flow, management's read of it) and the one promise they share (nothing is entered twice). Actions: **Open the demo — no account** (to `/app`) and **Start free** (to `/signin`). 3. **Four checkable facts** under the hero, each linking to `/product`: one card on several boards with one identity; status rolled up from the work rather than typed; offline edits that land; no trackers and no third-party scripts. 4. **The product, shown** — one real screenshot of the shipped board, alt text describing what it shows. At most two images on this page. 5. **The three ideas** — the graph, derived facts, one truth for two audiences. Three paragraphs, each ending in the consequence for the reader. 6. **How it starts** — three steps: open the demo, shape a board, share it when it needs sharing. 7. **Who it is for** — three situations: a programme whose board no longer matches the work; a team whose column names are its own; a reader who is tired of asking for numbers. 8. **Pricing, one line per plan**, linking to `/pricing`. 9. **The unusual promises** — no trackers; your export always works; a plan that lapses falls back to the free one and nothing is ever deleted; the free plan is a real team's board with unlimited people and work; it runs on your own machine. Each links to the page that proves it. 10. **Five questions** with real answers: Do I need an account? What happens offline? Can we self-host? How do you make money? Do you train anything on our data? CONTENT — `/product`, in order One card many boards · the lane tree and the four stages · initiatives computed from the work below · dependencies that clear themselves · the same graph at three flight levels · what is deliberately not automated (no generated cards, no guesses — nothing is written that nobody wrote). Each section is one short paragraph and one screenshot. Ends with the demo and the free account. REQUIREMENTS R1 — The sections above are the page Each item in CONTENT shall exist, in that order, and be readable with JavaScript off. A section may not be dropped for convenience; if it no longer says something true, it is changed rather than deleted quietly. R2 — Nothing invented There shall be no invented logo wall, no testimonial, no customer name, no usage number and no unsourced statistic. A claim that needs evidence links to the page or the test that proves it (the promises ledger). The word "AI" shall appear only in the section that says the app does not guess. R3 — The product is the product Every screenshot shall be of the shipped build, captured by `scripts/shots.ts` into `site/img/`, with width, height and alt text. A screenshot that shows something the app does not do is a bug in the page, not in the picture. The script shall be runnable by anyone (`npm run shots`). R4 — Both actions work **Open the demo** shall land on `/app` with the seeded board drawn and no account. **Start free** shall land on `/signin`, and the page shall say what free means in one line — one team board, unlimited people and work, no card. Both shall be links, not scripts. R5 — Size and speed The home page shall stay inside 151's budget, and the largest image shall be served as a modern format with explicit dimensions so the text does not jump. R6 — Accessible and quiet One H1 per page, a logical heading order, alt text on every image, no autoplay, no motion that is not a response to the reader, contrast at WCAG 2.2 AA, and a layout that holds at 320 px wide and at 200% zoom. R7 — The voice Plain, specific, second person, sentence case; no superlatives, no competitor named, no exclamation marks. It should sound like the README, because the people who read both should not meet two different companies. TEST STRATEGY VERIFICATION V1 — R1: each required section is present, in order, in the built HTML, with JavaScript disabled. V2 — R2: a test greps the built page for a banned list (customer names, "trusted by", "AI-powered", "10,000", "% of teams"); the promises ledger has no row without a link. V3 — R3: every `` has alt, width and height; `npm run shots` reproduces them. V4 — R4: both actions resolve, and the demo draws without a session. V5 — R5: the size check of 151 includes the home page's images. V6 — R6: axe over the home and product pages, a keyboard pass, and a 320 px viewport. V7 — R7: a read-through against the banned-phrase list, recorded in the pull request. DELIVERED — 2026-10-24 **The page is the sections, in order.** Hero (*"The truth is derived, not typed."*, one sentence naming both audiences and the single promise, two actions), four checkable facts, one shipped screenshot, the three ideas each ending in its consequence, how it starts in three steps, who it is for in three situations, pricing in one line per plan, four unusual promises each linking to its proof, and five questions with real answers. `check-site.mjs` asserts the ids exist **in that order**, so a section cannot be quietly dropped. **`/product` exists**: one card many boards, the lane tree and the four stages, initiatives computed from the work below, dependencies that clear themselves, the same graph at three altitudes, and the one thing deliberately not automated — where, and only where, the word "AI" appears. **The screenshots are the app.** `npm run shots` drives the built `dist/` with Playwright, waits for the board to draw (a lane with height, not merely an element), and writes five WebP images into `site/img/`: board, lanes, initiatives, drawer, the dashboard. `sharp` is a dev dependency of that script only. Every `` carries its real width and height, so nothing jumps while it loads, and the check refuses a non-WebP image or a missing dimension. **Both actions are links.** *Open the demo — no account* is `/app` (the seeded board, no session) and *Start free* is `/signin` — a page created here as the way-in stub, because 154 is what fills it. **The copy rules, checked rather than agreed.** No "trusted by", no testimonial, no customer name, no unsourced number, no superlative and no exclamation mark — the check strips the tags from the home page and fails on the banned list. One `

` per page, a heading order that never skips a level, alt text on every image, and every promise in the list carrying a link to the page that proves it. **Size and bearing.** The home page is **87 kB compressed** — HTML, the stylesheet and the screenshot — against 150 kB. axe over `/` and `/product/` finds no serious or critical barrier, and the page holds at 320 px with the heading, the demo action and the five questions still there. Tests: the site check (section order, banned phrases, one h1 and heading order, image alt and dimensions and format, four promises each with a link, the two actions' hrefs, the budget); axe and a 320 px pass in `e2e/site.spec.ts`; and the whole suite, green. REVISED — 2026-10-24: no pricing, and the money question changes shape Section 8 (pricing, one line per plan) is replaced by **What it costs**: the software is free, the machine is yours, there is no plan to buy and nothing to cancel. The question "How do you make money?" becomes **"How is this free?"**, and a licence question is added. The four checkable facts gain the one that now matters most: *it runs on your own machine*. Everything else — the hero, the three ideas, who it is for, the unusual promises — stands, and the promises drop the lapsed-plan line. Task 164 carries the change. CANCELLED — 2026-10-24: shipped, and the money question is answered by deleting it The page was built (commit `fa7b826`) and stands. What remained here was the plan-shaped part: a pricing section and a "How do you make money?" answer. There is no cost to publish and no money question to answer, so those are **removed rather than rewritten** — and that removal, with the navigation, is task 164's. The home page now carries no cost section and no "how is this free" section, and its five questions are four.
tasks.testStrategy: The required sections present in that order with JavaScript off; nothing invented on the page; the free plan described as the account it is; screenshots reproduced from the shipped build; both actions resolving; axe clean at 320 px and 200% zoom; and a size budget.

tasks.title: Pricing is a table the product cannot contradict: free is one team board, paid is the portfolio.
tasks.description: A free account with unlimited people and unlimited work on one team board and no objectives, a paid plan for the portfolio above it, and every printed limit enforced by the server from one module.
tasks.testStrategy: Plans and limits generated from one module the server also reads; free being one team board with unlimited people and work and no objectives, enforced where the server decides; a downgrade that leaves everything readable and never deletes; and no card, clock or per-seat price the product does not honour.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/public-site.md §/pricing and §Decisions to
take (items 2 and 3), and task 126 R4 for the billing record.

SCOPE
1. `src/domain/plans.ts` — plans, prices, limits and the formatter, framework-free and unit tested.
2. `/pricing` — the page, rendered at build from that module.
3. The limits this task makes true in the product: **one team board and no objectives** on the free
   plan; unlimited people and unlimited cards and initiatives on every plan.
4. The copy for a plan ending, a downgrade, and a workspace that is over its plan.
5. No trial: the free plan is permanent and needs no card; the paid plan is chosen when it is needed.

DEFINITIONS
- **Plan**: one row of the table — free, team, self-hosted.
- **Limit**: a number or a shape the page prints and the server enforces, or a row the page does not
  print.
- **Band**: a board's flight level — team, program or portfolio.
- **Over plan**: a workspace holding more boards or objectives than its plan allows — after a
  downgrade, or after a browser workspace with several boards is copied into a new free account. It
  is a state rather than an error.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — One module, two readers
`src/domain/plans.ts` shall export the plans, their prices (monthly and annual) and every limit —
members, cards and initiatives, boards, the bands a plan may use, whether objectives exist, and the
export, audit and support rows — with a formatter for each value. The build script and the server
shall both import it. No price, limit or plan name shall be typed into the page's HTML by hand.

R2 — The page is generated from it
`/pricing` shall render every plan and every limit from the module. A test shall fail when the module
gains a limit that the page does not print, and when the page prints a number the module does not
hold.

R3 — A printed limit is an enforced limit
For each limit the page prints, the server shall refuse the action that would exceed it, in one
sentence that names the limit, the plan and what changes it (upgrade, or the account's plan screen).
The free plan's two shapes shall be enforced:

- **One board**: creating a second board is refused. Copying the browser's own workspace into a new
  account is **not** refused for count: it lands as it is, and if it holds more than one board the
  over-plan rule (R5) applies rather than a half-copied workspace.
- **A team board**: creating a board whose band is **program** or **portfolio** is refused, and so is
  changing an existing board to one of those bands.
- **No objectives**: creating or editing an objective is refused, attributing an initiative to one is
  refused, and the strategy map is not offered.

Members and cards and initiatives shall have **no counter at all**: no path may refuse an invitation,
a member or a card for count, on any plan. A table in the test names every printed limit and the
code path that enforces it, and an unlisted row fails.

R4 — Free is the whole team product
The free plan shall have no clock, no watermark and no feature gate beyond the two shapes above, and
shall ask for no card. A free account's board shall be the same board a paid one gets — lanes, splits,
WIP limits, history, invitations, the audit trail of its own work, export. What it does not have is a
second board and the portfolio above it. The app with **no account at all** — the static build and the
demo — is not a plan and is not limited by this: the limits begin at the account.

R5 — Over plan is a state, not an error
A workspace whose plan no longer covers what it holds shall keep everything readable and exportable.
The Account Admin shall choose the one team board that stays writable; the other boards and every
objective shall be read-only until the plan covers them again; and the workspace shall name which
boards and objectives are over the line and what resolves it. Nothing shall be deleted and nothing
hidden. (Task 155 owns the state and task 156 the screen; this task owns the rule and the words.)

R6 — The paid plan is the portfolio
Team shall be unlimited boards in any band, objectives across them, the strategy map, the full audit
trail, backups and support with an expectation. It shall be priced per workspace unless decision 3
says otherwise, and the page shall not print a per-seat price while members are unlimited on Free.

R7 — The edges
Annual is billed once and is cheaper by a stated amount; prices are exclusive of tax where tax
applies and the provider adds it at checkout; changing plan takes effect at the next period; **Start

task 156 shows.

R8 — The way in
Each plan's action shall be a link: free to `/signin`, the paid plan to `/signin` and then the
checkout from the account, self-hosted to `/self-host`. No form collects a card on this site.

CANCELLED — 2026-10-24: open source, and nothing is sold
Flowline is open-source software people self-host (task 163), so there is no price to publish, no
merchant to take money and no plan to manage. This task is cancelled rather than deferred: it was the

tasks.title: The way in: OIDC, a password, a magic link — and no self-service sign-up.
tasks.description: Three doors and the configuration that opens each: the operator's OIDC issuer, a password every deployment has, and a magic link where mail is configured. Invitations remain the way an account arrives, and Google and Microsoft leave the code entirely.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository — open-source software a team installs and runs itself
(task 163: one deployment is one workspace). Read `server/auth/routes.ts`, `server/config.ts`,
`server/runtime.ts` (the capability pattern `live` already uses), `src/components/AccountMenu.tsx`,
`migrations/`, `docs/configure.md`, and task 168 (SCIM, the provisioning half).

SCOPE
1. **Three doors, and the configuration that opens each**: OIDC, a password, a magic link.
2. **Invitations** stay the way an account arrives; there is no self-service registration.
3. **The first run**, on an instance with no accounts at all.
4. **Mail**, because a magic link needs it — optional, and its absence a valid deployment.
5. No vendor in the code: Google and Microsoft leave (the earlier revision of this task stands), and
   nothing replaces them by name.
6. The copy, the docs, and the tests that hold the doors to what the deployment actually has.

DEFINITIONS
- **Issuer**: the OIDC provider the operator configured. Workspace and Entra are issuers like any
  other, and neither is a name this code knows.
- **Password**: a secret the person chose, stored only as a hash, and never recoverable by anybody —
  including an administrator.
- **Magic link**: a single-use, short-lived link sent to the address on an existing account, which
  signs that person in without a password.
- **Invitation**: the link that creates the account. It is the door; a password is the key.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — The doors, and what each one needs
- **OIDC** — when `AUTH_OIDC_*` is configured (one issuer; task 154's earlier revision). It remains
  the preferred door for a team that already has an identity provider.
- **Password** — always available for an account that has one, on every deployment, with no
  configuration. It is what makes the product usable by a team that has no IdP at all.
- **Magic link** — only when mail is configured (R6). Absent otherwise: not disabled, absent.
- **Invitation** — always. It is how an account arrives (R2), and how somebody an IdP does not
  provision gets in.
- **The development switch** — only when `AUTH_DEV=1`, and never on an instance anybody can reach.

`GET /api/auth/providers` reports exactly these, so the app draws what works: a password form when any
account method exists, an issuer button when one is configured, a "send me a link" action when mail
is, and words — not a disabled control — when a deployment has no way in.

R2 — No self-service registration, ever
An account arrives in one of two ways: an **invitation**, or as the **first administrator** of an
instance with none (R3). Open registration is not a door, and `instance_settings.access`
governs who may *sign in* (an invitation, a listed domain, or an open instance) — never who may
create an account. One deployment is one team, so an account is a membership of that team: a stranger
registering one is a stranger letting themselves in.

R3 — The first run
An instance with no accounts answers with a first-run surface rather than a sign-in form: a name, an
address, and a password — or, if mail is configured, a magic link instead. Completing it makes that
person the instance's administrator and the workspace's (task 163), and closes the door behind them:
there is exactly one first run.

The surface is reached only while `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users` is zero, is rate-limited like any
other door, and there are no default credentials anywhere in the product. An instance that somehow
has accounts never shows it again.

R4 — An invitation is where a password is chosen
Opening an invitation link (address-bound, single-use, expiring) for an address with no account
offers two things, not one: **set a password**, or **sign in with a link** when mail is configured.
The account is created at that moment, with the role the invitation named, and the invitation is
spent. An invitation for an address that already has an account is an invitation to join, not to
replace a password.

R5 — Reset is a magic link, and it works without mail
"Forgot password" sends a magic link when mail is configured. When it is not, an administrator can
mint a **one-time reset link** in Admin — shown once, hashed at rest, fifteen minutes, single use,
address-bound — and hand it over out of band. There is no deployment in which a person is locked out
while an administrator exists, and no deployment in which an administrator can read a password.

R6 — Mail, and its absence
A mailer is a **runtime capability**, exactly as the live channel is (`Runtime.mail`): the Node entry
implements SMTP (`SMTP_URL`, STARTTLS required, a From address), and the Worker entry has none in this
task — the difference lives in the entry file and the bindings, never in a route or a rule.

- Unset means no magic link and no reset mail; the app says so by not offering them.
- It sends exactly two things: a magic link and a password reset. Nothing else, and nothing it was
  not configured to send.
- A console transport stands in for development and tests, so the suite never opens a socket to
  somebody's mail server.
- The message is plain text with the link, the address it was for, when it expires, and one sentence
  saying to ignore it if it was not asked for. No tracking pixel, no third-party image, no link
  shortener — the mail is as plain as the site.

R7 — Enumeration, timing and rate limits
An unknown address, a wrong password, an expired link and a used link answer with the **same sentence**
and take approximately the **same time**: a password check against a dummy hash runs for an address
that does not exist, and the magic-link screen says "if that address has an account, a link is on its
way" whether it does or not.

Sign-in, magic-link requests and resets are rate-limited per address and per client, and every refusal
is recorded in the audit the way it already is for the OIDC callback.

R8 — How a password is stored
One algorithm both runtimes can run: **PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 through WebCrypto**, at least 600 000
iterations, a 16-byte random salt per password, compared in constant time, with the iterations and
salt stored **in the hash string** (`pbkdf2$<iterations>$<salt>$<hash>`) so they can be raised later
without a migration. Argon2id would be better and is not available on both runtimes; that trade-off is
recorded rather than hidden, and the stored parameters are what let a future release raise the cost.

Nothing writes a password to a log, an audit entry or an error report. The minimum length is twelve
characters and there is no maximum below a megabyte; there is no composition rule, because a
composition rule produces `Password1!`.

R9 — The doors that leave
Google and Microsoft leave the code, the configuration, the copy and the processor list (the earlier
revision's R1 and R5, unchanged): `KNOWN` is deleted, `providers()` is built only from the deployment,
and `README.md`, `docs/configure.md`, `site/processors.json`, `site/pages/privacy.html` and the help
page stop naming them.

R10 — An identity whose issuer is gone
Identities are rows, and nothing deletes them behind a person's back. A person whose issuer is no
longer configured cannot use that door — and **now has another**: an administrator sends a magic link
or a reset link, or the person signs in with a password they set from an invitation. This is the
change the new doors make to the old problem: re-entry stops being a reconfiguration.

R11 — Copy, docs and the privacy notice
`configure.md` gains the mail variables and loses the sentence "there is no mail relay" (there is one
now, when an operator configures it). The privacy notice says what a password is stored as — a hash,
never the password — that an administrator cannot read it, and that a magic link is a row with an
expiry; the mail relay is the operator's processor and is named as such in
`site/processors.json` when configured. The help page answers "sign in with a password", "the email
never arrived", and "I forgot my password".

R12 — Both runtimes, and the tests
The Worker and the Node entry behave the same wherever a capability exists. Unit tests cover: the
first run, an invitation choosing a password, magic link single-use and expiry, reset by administrator
without mail, the dummy verify, and the PBKDF2 format. The e2e drives a password sign-in and a magic
link through a console transport — a test must not need an identity provider or a mail server.

R13 — A second factor is not this task
Passwords make a second factor worth having (task 149), and it is not smuggled in here: this task
adds the doors, and the next one can add the lock to the door.

TEST STRATEGY
V1 — R1: a deployment with nothing configured offers a password door and an invitation; one with an
     issuer offers its button; one with mail offers "send me a link"; one with none of the three says
     so in words.
V2 — R2: there is no route that creates an account without an invitation or the first run — asserted
     against the mounted routes, not just the UI.
V3 — R3: a fresh instance shows the first-run surface, the first completion is an administrator, and
     it never appears again; a second completion is refused.
V4 — R4: an invitation sets a password (or a link), the invitation is spent, and a second use is
     refused.
V5 — R5: with mail unset, an administrator's reset link is shown once, works once, and expires; with
     mail set, the same act sends the mail instead.
V6 — R6: the magic link mail is plain text with no remote image; the console transport records it in
     tests; a deployment without `mail` never attempts to send.
V7 — R7: an unknown address and a known one answer identically and in comparable time; both are
     rate-limited; the refusals are audited.
V8 — R8: a stored password is the `pbkdf2$…` string and no plaintext; a wrong password fails; the
     same password on two accounts produces two different hashes; no log or error body carries it.
V9 — R9: `grep -ri "google\|microsoft"` finds nothing outside the changelog and the history.
V10 — R10: a person with a dead issuer reaches their account through a link or a password.

REVISED — 2026-10-24: three doors, not one
The earlier revision of this task made OIDC the only way in, on the reasoning that a self-hosted team
already has an identity provider. That is true of some teams and false of others: a team that installs
Flowline on a machine with no IdP would have had no accounts at all. Passwords and magic links close
that gap, and they change three other things in this file: the first run (R3), an identity whose
issuer is gone (R10, which stops being a reconfiguration problem), and the mail relay that
`configure.md` said did not exist (R6, R11).

BROKEN DOWN — 2026-10-25: eight sub-tasks, in the order they can land
The task is one feature with a long tail, and its parts have real dependencies: nothing else can be
tested until a password can be hashed (154.2), the first run and an invitation are two different ways
an account comes to exist (154.4, 154.5), and the magic link and the reset are one mechanism with two
intents (154.7) sitting on a mail capability that may be absent (154.6).

154.1 is separable and can land first — removing the vendors is a cleanup with its own documents and
no dependency on the rest. 154.8 is last because it is the proof and the copy, and both are only
true once the doors exist.

COMPLETE — 2026-10-25: all eight sub-tasks, over nine commits
154.1 `1a5558d` · 154.2 `a5fb417` · 154.3 `a2b2c28` · 154.4 `a35edb1` (`92f6524` superseded) ·
154.5 `66814fa` · 154.6 `bddc70a` · 154.7 `d8bd9d1` · 154.8 (this commit).

A team with no identity provider and no mail relay can now install Flowline, name its workspace,
create the first administrator, invite a colleague and have them choose a password — and get back in
after forgetting it, through a link an administrator hands over. A team with a relay gets magic links
instead of passwords to remember. A team with an issuer keeps that door and can drop the others.

What is **not** here, and is deliberate: no local MFA (task 149, reopened by the password door), no
self-service registration, no password complexity rule, and no OAuth authorization server. The
consequence recorded when the KDF was chosen still stands: 600 000 PBKDF2 iterations is more CPU than
Cloudflare's free plan allows per request, so a Worker deployment that offers passwords needs the paid
plan.
tasks.testStrategy: Only configured providers offered; buttons that work without JavaScript; a return path that survives auth and never leaves the origin; the terms and the free plan linked beside the button; no trial, card or clock; and the page kept out of the index.

subtasks.title: Vendors out: OIDC is the only provider the code knows.
subtasks.description: Delete the google and microsoft endpoint table and their variables; build the provider list from AUTH_OIDC_* alone; correct the five documents and the processor list.
subtasks.details:
- `server/config.ts`: delete `KNOWN` (the two vendors' endpoints). `providers()` reads only the
  `AUTH_OIDC_*` variables, and the button's label falls back to the issuer's host parsed from
  `AUTH_OIDC_AUTHORIZE_ENDPOINT` when `AUTH_OIDC_LABEL` is unset.
- No `AUTH_GOOGLE_*` / `AUTH_MICROSOFT_*` is read anywhere; the config tests that covered them go,
  and a new one asserts that a deployment with only OIDC variables reports exactly one provider.
- `site/processors.json`: the google and microsoft rows go; `oidc` and the host and the error log
  stay. The privacy notice and `/sub-processors` render from that file, so they follow for free.
- `README.md`'s provider table, `docs/configure.md`'s table, and any prose in
  `site/pages/privacy.html` stop naming them. `AGENTS.md`'s Google Sign-In allowance becomes moot —
  record it in the task, do not rewrite the house rules.
- A grep test fails when a vendor name appears in `src/`, `server/`, `site/` or `docs/` (the site's
  history is not in those directories; the changelog page is gone).

DELIVERED — 2026-10-25 (commit below, CI green)
`KNOWN` is gone; `providers()` builds one entry from `AUTH_OIDC_*` and names it with the operator's
label or, when there is none, the issuer's host (`idp.test`, not "your provider"). The two rows left
`site/processors.json`, so the privacy notice and `/sub-processors` — which render from it — follow.
`configure.md`, the README's variable table, `compose.yaml`'s commented example and the two docs' prose
now describe one OIDC issuer; the names that remain are examples of issuers ("Workspace, Entra,
Keycloak"), not providers the product ships.

`server/providers.test.ts` holds it: no vendor endpoint table, no vendor credential variable, and the
provider list still built from the operator's endpoint. It checks the mechanism rather than the word,
because a comment naming an issuer as an example is documentation and an endpoint table is a decision.

`server/auth.test.ts` now proves the OIDC door from both sides: half a configuration offers nothing, a
labelled issuer keeps its label, and an unlabelled one is named by its host.
subtasks.testStrategy:
- one provider configured → `/api/auth/providers` reports it; none → `[]`
- the grep test fails on a reintroduced vendor name
- the built `/privacy/` and `/sub-processors/` name no vendor (the site check already reads the
  processor file)

subtasks.title: A password is stored as a hash that can be made stronger.
subtasks.description: PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 through WebCrypto, so both runtimes can run it, with the cost and salt stored in the hash string.
subtasks.details:
- `server/auth/password.ts`: `hash(password): Promise<string>` producing
  `pbkdf2$<iterations>$<salt-b64>$<hash-b64>`, and `verify(password, stored): Promise<boolean>` in
  constant time. Implemented with `crypto.subtle.deriveBits` — the one KDF Node and Workers both
  have — at 600 000 iterations with a 16-byte random salt.
- `MIN_LENGTH = 12` lives here and nowhere else; there is no composition rule and no maximum below a
  megabyte.
- The stored parameters are what let a later release raise the cost: `verify` reads the iteration
  count from the string, and a hash written by an older release keeps working.
- Nothing in this module logs, throws with the password in the message, or returns the plaintext.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-25
`server/auth/password.ts`: `hash(password, iterations = 600 000)` writes
`pbkdf2$<iterations>$<salt-b64>$<hash-b64>`; `verify` reads the cost from the string and compares in
constant time; a stored value it cannot parse is a `false` rather than a throw. The password is
normalised to NFKC before deriving, so a composed and a decomposed é are one password. `MIN_LENGTH`
(12) and `acceptable()` live here and nowhere else; an input over 1 KB is refused by length so an
absurd one costs nothing. `dummyHash()` exists for 154.3: an unknown address verifies against it, so
it costs what a wrong password costs.

Eight tests, running the real KDF at the real cost: round trip, wrong password, salts differ, a hash at
100 000 iterations still verifies (the upgrade path), ten malformed stored values all fail closed, a
megabyte is refused by rule, twelve spaces is a legitimate password, and Unicode forms agree.

Recorded in the module and in 154.3: **600 000 iterations is more CPU than Cloudflare's free plan
allows (10 ms)**. A Worker deployment that offers passwords needs the paid plan or another front door;
that is a decision for the door, not for the KDF.
subtasks.testStrategy:
- round trip; wrong password is false; two hashes of one password differ (salt)
- the format parses, an unknown prefix is refused rather than guessed
- a hash at 100 000 iterations still verifies after the default is raised (simulation)
- a 1 MB password is refused by length, not by hanging

subtasks.title: The password door.
subtasks.description: POST /api/auth/password signs in or refuses, with the same sentence and the same cost for an unknown address as for a wrong password.
subtasks.details:
- `POST /api/auth/password` `{email, password}`: looks the account up by lowercased address,
  verifies against its hash, and issues a session through the same `issueSession` the OIDC callback
  uses (including "remember me").
- **Enumeration:** an unknown address runs `verify` against a dummy hash and answers with the same
  body and status as a wrong password. The rate limiter the OIDC callback already uses applies per
  address and per client; a refusal is audited like any other (`signin.refused`, reason `password`).
- `/api/auth/providers` gains the methods that exist — `{ providers: [...], password: true }` — so the
  client draws a form only where there is one. The app's account menu renders the form and its
  sentence; no JavaScript-only path, the form posts.
- The audit gains `signin` with `targetType: 'password'`, and `password.set` for sub-task 5 and 7.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-25
`migrations/0022_passwords.sql` adds `users.password_hash` (NULL = no password, which is every
account today and stays valid); `REQUIRED_SCHEMA` is 22.

`POST /api/auth/password` `{email, password, remember}`: one sentence and one status (`401`) for an
unknown address, a wrong password and a closed account; an unknown address verifies against
`dummyHash()` so the clock says nothing either; the existing per-client limiter is charged *before*
the hash is computed, and refusals and successes both reach the audit (`signin.refused`,
`signin`, target `password`).

`GET /api/auth/providers` gains `password: <some account has one>`, so the form appears only when
somebody can actually walk through it — a control that cannot work is the thing this project refuses
to draw. The client carries it in `AuthState.password`, the account menu draws an address/password
form above the provider list (with the same "keep me signed in" choice), and `passwordSignIn()` in
`lib/auth.ts` is the session's browser half.

Six new server tests: the right password signs in and the cookie is a session; an unknown address and
a wrong password answer with the *same body*; a closed account is refused the same way; the door is
reported only once an account has a password; a body with no password is a 400 rather than a guess;
the trail records both outcomes.

The positive UI e2e is **not** here: an instance has no way to create a password account until the
first run (154.4) or an invitation (154.5), so the form's end-to-end proof belongs to 154.8, where it
can drive a real one. Until then the negative holds — no password account, no form.
subtasks.testStrategy:
- unknown address and wrong password: identical status and body; a test on the handler asserts the
  dummy verify is called
- correct password signs in; the session works on the next request
- the rate limit answers 429 after N attempts, per address
- an instance with no password accounts still answers (a viewer's hash exists for everybody, so this
  is about the address not existing)

subtasks.title: The first run: a deployment with no accounts names its administrator.
subtasks.description: A surface reachable only while there are no accounts, which creates the first administrator and then closes for good.
subtasks.details:
- `GET /api/auth/setup` → `{ available: true }` only while `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users` is zero.
- `POST /api/auth/setup` `{ name, email, password }` creates the user, `instance_members` admin, the
  workspace row if it is missing and a workspace admin seat — the same batch `identify` writes for a
  first arrival — and issues a session. A second call answers `409` whatever the state.
- The client shows it in place of the sign-in form when `available`, in the app's own words: this is
  the person who administers the instance and its one workspace (task 163).
- Rate-limited like every other door; audited as `signin.setup` with the address, never the password.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-25
`GET /api/auth/setup` and `POST /api/auth/setup` `{name, email, password}`. The POST writes, in one
transaction, the account (with its hash), `instance_members` admin, the workspace rows under
`WORKSPACE_NAME` and the admin seat — the same batch a first arrival through a provider writes — then
issues the session and records `signin.setup`.

**The first run is only offered when it is the only way in.** `setupOpen()` is true when there are no
accounts *and* no identity provider is configured *and* the development switch is off. An instance
with a provider does not need it (its first arrival is the administrator, task 163), and offering both
would put two ways to make the first account on one screen. The POST refuses with a sentence (409) on
an instance that has another door, so the rule is not just a hidden button.

`/api/auth/providers` carries `setup`, the client carries it in `AuthState.setup`, and the account
menu draws the first-run form — name, address, a password of twelve characters or more — instead of a
sign-in list, with no default credentials behind it.

A fifth e2e instance (port 4177, fresh database on every start, no development switch) proves it end
to end: the surface appears, the form creates the administrator, the deployment reports `setup:false`
afterwards, the account is an administrator of the instance and the workspace, a second attempt is
409, and the password it took signs in from a browser with no cookie.

FOLLOW-UP — 2026-10-25: the sign-in surface became its own chunk
The setup form pushed the first download to 162.2 kB against a 162 kB budget. Rather than raise the
budget, the whole signed-out surface moved to `src/components/SignInPanel.tsx`, lazily imported the
way the profile dialog already was: a person signs in once and never sees it again, so it does not
belong in the download with the board. First download is 161.1 kB (and 3 files: entry, runtime, a
shared chunk), the panel loads when the menu opens, and `e2e/place.spec.ts` now asserts *which*
screens are absent at the board rather than a bare chunk count — the count shifted by one for a
reason that has nothing to do with the promise.
subtasks.testStrategy:
- fresh database → available; completing it → signed in as instance and workspace administrator
- the second attempt is 409; afterwards `available` is false
- the workspace exists, named by `WORKSPACE_NAME`, and `GET /api/workspace` answers 200
