subtasks.title: An invitation is where a password is chosen.
subtasks.description: Accepting an invitation creates the account with the role it named and the password the person chooses — or a magic link, once sub-task 7 lands.
subtasks.details:
- `POST /api/invite/:token` currently accepts a signed-in person. It takes `{ password }` for an
  address with no account: create the account (the invitation's role), store the hash, spend the
  invitation, issue the session. A token that is used, expired or for another address answers `410`,
  as it does today.
- An address that already has an account is not given a second one: the invitation joins, and the
  password is the one they have.
- The client's invitation screen becomes a screen for a signed-out person: name, the address the
  invitation was written for (masked, not editable), a password, and the role it grants in words.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-25
`POST /api/invite/:token` now has two shapes. **With no session** the link is the proof: a `password`
(and an optional name) creates the account with the invitation's email and role, spends the invitation,
issues the session and records `invite.accepted` — the whole of how a deployment with no identity
provider and no mail admits a second person. **With a session** the old rule stands: the verified
address must be the invitation's.

Guards: an address that already has an account answers `409` ("sign in instead"), a short password is
`400` with the same sentence the setup surface uses, a used, expired or unknown token is `410` with
nothing said about which, and nothing is spent by a refusal.

The client: an invitation link opens the sign-in surface by itself, reads the invitation (masked
address and role) and asks for a name and a password — hiding the password and provider doors, which
could not work, while the development switch stays visible where an operator turned it on.

Six server tests (role from the invitation, single use, short password spends nothing, existing
address, unknown token) and a third e2e on the fresh instance: the administrator signs in with her
password, invites a Viewer, a browser that has never seen the instance joins through the link, and the
spent link answers `410` afterwards. `e2e/account-admin.spec.ts` follows the new auto-open — its leaver
uses the development door, which the invite surface no longer hides.
subtasks.testStrategy:
- an invitation creates an editor, a viewer or an administrator as it says
- a second use is 410; a forged token is 410; another address is 410
- the new account can sign in with the password it chose, once

subtasks.title: Mail, and its absence.
subtasks.description: A mail capability on the runtime, SMTP on the Node entry, a console transport for development, and nothing on the Worker — so magic links exist where they can be delivered.
subtasks.details:
- `Runtime.mail?: { send(message: { to, subject, text }) }` — the capability pattern `live` already
  uses, so the difference lives in the entry file and the bindings, never in a route or a rule.
- Node: an SMTP client (`SMTP_URL` with STARTTLS required, `MAIL_FROM`), plain text only, no images,
  no tracking pixel, no link shortener. Worker: no mail in this task; the app's method list says so.
- A console transport (`MAIL_CONSOLE=1`) writes the message to stdout for development and tests, so
  the suite never opens a socket to somebody's mail server.
- `docs/configure.md` gains the variables and loses the sentence "there is no mail relay".

DELIVERED — 2026-10-25
The capability is `Runtime.mail?` — the same shape as `live` — and the portable half is
`server/mail.ts` (the `Message`/`Mail` types and the console transport). The SMTP client is
`server/mail-smtp.ts`, excluded from the Worker project beside `index.node.ts` and `sqlite.ts`, and
`npm run portable` stays green: the core never learns about a socket.

The client is the small part of the protocol sending needs: greeting, EHLO with its capability list,
STARTTLS when offered (and **required** for anything that is not a relay on this machine — 127.0.0.1,
::1, localhost), AUTH PLAIN when credentials are in `SMTP_URL`, one `DATA`, quit. Dot-stuffing is
handled; the body is `text/plain; charset=utf-8` with no images, no tracking pixel and no shortener.

`SMTP_URL` and `MAIL_FROM` are the whole configuration; without both there is no mailer, so the door
that would need one is absent rather than broken. `MAIL_CONSOLE=1` logs each message instead, which is
what the test suite and the e2e lane use. `/api/auth/providers` reports `mail`, and `configure.md`
gained the three variables and lost the paragraph that said there was no relay.

Four tests against an in-process SMTP stub — the exact transcript (EHLO, AUTH PLAIN, MAIL, RCPT, DATA,
QUIT), the headers and body it received, dot-stuffing, a refusal when a remote server offers no
STARTTLS, and the absent case — plus the console transport's own.

Note for 154.7: the file is `mail-smtp.ts`, not `mail.node.ts`, because `./mail.node` is resolved as a
native addon by Node's loader.
subtasks.testStrategy:
- the Node mailer completes a session against an in-process SMTP stub (EHLO, STARTTLS, AUTH, DATA)
- a runtime without mail never attempts to send, and the method list omits the link door
- the message body is plain text with the link, the address and the expiry

subtasks.title: Links: a magic sign-in, and a reset that works without mail.
subtasks.description: Single-use, short-lived, address-bound links: one that signs you in when mail is configured, one an administrator mints by hand when it is not.
subtasks.details:
- `migrations/0022_magic_links.sql`: id, email, token_hash, purpose (`signin` | `reset`),
  expires_at (15 minutes), used_at, created_at, ip_hash. The token is hashed at rest exactly as a
  session is.
- `POST /api/auth/link` `{ email }` always answers `204` — "if that address has an account, a link is
  on its way" — and sends only when mail is configured and the address exists. Rate-limited per
  address and per client.
- `POST /api/auth/link/:token` consumes it: single use, expiry, and the address it was written for.
  A `signin` link issues a session; a `reset` link issues one that may only set a password, and
  setting it ends the account's other sessions.
- **Without mail**, an administrator mints a reset link in the member list: `POST
  /api/admin/workspace/members/:id/reset` returns the URL once, shown once, hashed at rest, 15
  minutes, single use — so nobody is locked out of a deployment that never sends mail.
- The client: "email me a link" beside the password form when mail exists, and the reset screen the
  link lands on.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-25
`migrations/0023_magic_links.sql` (email, hashed token, purpose, expiry, used_at, ip hash);
`REQUIRED_SCHEMA` 23. `server/auth/links.ts` is the one mechanism: `mintLink` (15 minutes, hashed,
sweeping expired rows as it goes) and `consumeLink` (claim-by-update, so two requests cannot both
spend one link).

`POST /api/auth/link` always answers `204` — the same for a member and a stranger — sends only when a
relay is configured and the account is active, and answers `404` on a deployment with no relay rather
than pretending. It is rate-limited by the limiter the provider door already uses.
`POST /api/auth/link/:token` spends it and signs the person in, answering `{ user, reset }`; `POST`
rather than `GET` because mail scanners prefetch links.

`PATCH /api/me/password` sets a password and ends every *other* session — the tab that made the change
stays. That also relaxed an old rule: unlinking the last identity is now allowed when the account has
a password, which is exactly what "there is no administrator-side reset" used to forbid.

Without mail, an administrator mints the same link from the member list: `POST
/api/admin/workspace/members/:id/reset`, shown once, hashed at rest, 15 minutes, single use.

Client: `?link=` opens the sign-in surface, consumes the token, and either signs in or asks for the
new password; "email me a link instead" sits under the password form when `auth.mail`; the member row
gains a **Reset** button that puts the link where an invitation goes.

Five server tests (send and enumeration, single use, expiry and forgery, no relay, the administrator's
link + password change + session revocation) and a fourth e2e on the fresh instance driving the
administrator's link end to end. The mail-based link is covered at the HTTP level in the unit suite;
driving it in the browser would need a relay the test could read, which is 154.8's e2e if it is worth
one.
subtasks.testStrategy:
- a link works once; a second use is 410; after 15 minutes it is 410
- an address with no account gets 204 and no mail
- the administrator's reset link is shown once, works once, and sets a password that then signs in
- setting a password ends the other sessions of that account

subtasks.title: The copy, the docs, and the proof.
subtasks.description: Every surface that describes how to get in says what is true now, and an end-to-end spec drives each door on both entries.
subtasks.details:
- `README.md` and `docs/configure.md`: the mail variables, the password and link methods, and the
  OIDC-only provider table.
- `site/pages/privacy.html` and `site/processors.json`: a password is stored as a hash nobody can read,
  and the relay is a processor when configured.
- `site/pages/security.html`: the hash, the first-run route (reachable only while there are no
  accounts) and the administrator's reset link join the scope.
- `docs/README.md` gains the identity page if 168 has written `docs/identity.md`; otherwise the paths
  are in `configure.md` and the install guide.
- The e2e (`e2e/signin.spec.ts`): first run → password sign-in → invitation with a password → magic
  link through the console transport → administrator reset without mail → an instance with no issuer
  still signs in, and one with a dead issuer signs in by password.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-25
**The copy.** The privacy notice says what a password is (a PBKDF2 hash with its own salt and cost, unreadable by anybody including an administrator) and what a sign-in link is (a row with an address, a hashed token and a fifteen-minute expiry), and notes that a deployment with a relay adds it to the processor list. The security page gains the hash, the first-run surface (reachable only while it is the only way in, no default credentials) and the reset link. `configure.md` stops saying an instance with no provider "has no way in" — a password and an administrator's reset link are both there. The README's sign-in section gained the same paragraph.

**The proof.** `e2e/mail.spec.ts` runs against a sixth instance (4178) with the console transport writing
to a file: an administrator is created, a link is requested, the mail is read from the log, the link
signs that person in from a browser that had no session, and the second use is 410. An address with no
account gets the same 204 and no message. With `e2e/setup.spec.ts` that is every door in a browser:
first run, password, invitation, magic link, administrator's reset — and the static build still
editable with no account at all.

`npm run docs:check`, `site:check`, `scan`, `portable`, the mid-run budget (161.3 kB of 162) and the
whole suite (779 unit, 68 e2e on a clean checkout) are green.
subtasks.testStrategy:
- the e2e above on the 4174 instance, plus the static build still editable with no account
- `npm run docs:check`, `site:check` and the site e2e green
- a grep for a vendor name in the copy finds nothing

tasks.title: Money is taken by a merchant of record, and the plan is decided on the server.
tasks.description: A payment provider as the seller of record, a checkout from the account, webhooks that write one subscription record, and one question every write asks — which plan, and is it in good standing — with the free plan as the default.
tasks.testStrategy: A written merchant-of-record decision; checkout only from the account; idempotent signed webhooks into one subscription record; a free plan that needs no provider; one question every write asks; and a past-due account that falls back to free rather than dying.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/public-site.md §Decisions to take item 4 and
§/pricing; task 126 R4 (billing is a record, never card data); task 153 (the plans and their limits).

SCOPE
1. The provider decision, written down in `docs/payments.md` with the comparison and the reason.
2. Checkout: a signed-in Account Admin buys a plan and returns to the account.
3. Webhooks: signature, idempotency, and one transaction that writes the subscription.
4. The plan question: which plan the account is on, and whether it is in good standing. The **limits**
   themselves are task 153's.
5. The copy for past due, grace, and a workspace over its plan.

DEFINITIONS
- **Merchant of record**: the provider is the seller, holds the card data and calculates tax; we hold
  a customer reference and a subscription state.
- **Subscription record**: plan, status, period end, provider customer and subscription ids.
- **In good standing**: paid, or past due but inside the grace period. Otherwise the account is on the
  free plan's limits.
- **Over plan**: see task 153 — a downgraded workspace holding more than the free plan covers.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — The decision is written before the code
`docs/payments.md` shall record the comparison (a merchant of record — Polar or Paddle are the
shortlist — against Stripe plus our own tax registration) and the choice, in one page, with the
reason. The code shall follow the decision rather than the other way round.

R2 — Checkout starts from the account
A signed-in Account Admin choosing the paid plan shall be sent to the provider's checkout with the
plan and the account's reference, and shall return to `/app/account/billing` — paid or declined,
either way told which. A signed-out person choosing it shall be sent to `/signin` with a return path
that brings them back. There shall be no free trial and therefore no trial state.

R3 — The webhook is the truth
A webhook shall verify the provider's signature, be idempotent by event id, and write the
subscription record in one transaction. A replayed event shall change nothing; an unknown event shall
be ignored, not crash. Nothing in the database shall be able to hold a card number, a CVC or a bank
detail — asserted against the schema, as task 126 V6 requires.

R4 — One question, asked by every write
One server-side function shall answer which plan the resolved account is on and whether it is in good
standing, read from the subscription record. Every write path — item, placement, board, lane,
objective, member, invitation, settings — shall ask it, and task 153's limits shall be applied from
the answer. A free account shall be answered without any provider call: absent a subscription, it is
free.

R5 — Failure is gradual and never a deletion
`past_due` shall be visible in the app, shall keep the paid plan for a stated grace period, and shall
then fall back to the **free plan's limits** — not to a dead workspace. A workspace that is over the
free plan at that moment follows task 153 R5: readable, exportable, one board writable, the rest
read-only with a sentence. Nothing shall be deleted for non-payment at any point, and the export stays
available in every state.

R6 — A self-hosted instance has no money in it
With no provider configured, the instance shall not be limited by a plan it cannot buy: no provider
call, no billing surface, and the free plan's board limit shall not apply. A test shall prove the
absence.

R7 — The plan question is one place
There shall not be a second notion of "subscribed" in a component, a route or a query. The plan and
the standing shall come from the one function, so that a screen, a page and a write cannot disagree
about what the account may do.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: the decision document exists and names the criterion (who is the seller of record).
V2 — R2: choosing the paid plan while signed out returns to checkout after sign-in; a declined
     payment returns with the reason; no trial state exists anywhere.
V3 — R3: a signed webhook writes the record; a replay does not; a bad signature is refused; a schema
     test finds no column that could hold a card number.
V4 — R4: a new account is free with no provider call; every write path asks the one function, and a
     source check finds no second answer.
V5 — R5: past due → grace → the free limits, with over-plan boards read-only and nothing deleted;
     export works in every state.
V6 — R6: a self-hosted instance makes no provider call, shows no billing, and is not held to one
     board.
V7 — R7: grepping for a plan comparison outside the function finds none.

CANCELLED — 2026-10-24: open source, and nothing is sold
Flowline is open-source software people self-host (task 163), so there is no price to publish, no
merchant to take money and no plan to manage. This task is cancelled rather than deferred: it was the
shape of a business this product is not.

tasks.title: The account's plan, its invoices, and the way out of a subscription.
tasks.description: One screen where an Account Admin sees what plan they are on, buys or changes it, downloads an invoice, and cancels — with the export offered first, the fall back to the free plan spelled out, and a way to choose the board that keeps working.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/public-site.md §/pricing and §The trust set;
task 126 R4 (billing record) and task 155 (subscription state and entitlement).

SCOPE
1. `/app/account/billing` — the plan screen, under the Account Admin's `account.billing`.
2. The states it must show: free, active, past due, over plan, cancelled-and-running.
3. Changing plan, and the provider's own portal for the card and the invoices.
4. Cancelling, the sentence that says what happens after, and the choice of the one board that keeps
   working on the free plan.

NOT IN SCOPE
Taking the money (155), closing the account or deleting a workspace (126), and the marketing copy
(153). This task is the screen and the promises it makes at the moment somebody leaves.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — What is true now
The screen shall show the plan — **free** included, because most accounts are on it — the people in
the workspace, the renewal date when there is one, the subscription state, and one line about what
that state means for the person reading it. The numbers shall come from the subscription record and
the plan module, not from the page. A free account shall see what it has and what the paid plan would
add, without being nagged.

R2 — The provider's own pages for money
The card, the invoices and the receipts shall be the provider's portal, opened from this screen. We
shall not build a card form, and no invoice shall be generated by us that the provider did not issue.
An invoice history shall be listed with the provider's links and its own dates.

R3 — Changing plan is one action, and it says when it lands
Upgrading and downgrading shall be possible from here, shall take effect when the provider says it
does, and shall say when that is (immediately, or at the period's end). There is no seat count to
change: people are unlimited on both plans. A downgrade that will leave the workspace over the free
plan shall say so before it happens and name the boards and objectives that will become read-only.

R4 — The way out is a real button, and it leaves an account
Cancelling shall be possible from this screen, shall say in one sentence what happens at the end of
the period — **the workspace falls back to the free plan** — shall offer the export before the
confirmation (`exportWorkspace`, already built), and shall state that nothing is deleted and the data
stays readable and downloadable. It shall not require an email to support, and it shall not use a
dark pattern: no retention offer in the way of the button.

R5 — After the end, one board keeps working
When the subscription ends the screen shall say what the free plan keeps: unlimited people and work
on **one team board**, no objectives. It shall let the Account Admin choose that board, shall say the
others and every objective become read-only rather than disappearing, shall offer the export, and
shall say how to come back. Wording shall match the rule in 153 and the refund policy in 157.

R6 — Past due is loud
`past_due` shall be visible on this screen and in the app's account control, with the grace period
and the date the workspace falls back to the free plan, and a link that fixes it. The state shall be
readable by a person, not a status code.

R7 — Nothing here is simulated
Every action shall be an action the provider took. A cancel that only changed our row shall fail the
test.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: each state renders the right plan, people and dates; the free state names what free keeps.
V2 — R2: the portal link opens the provider's page; no card field exists in our DOM or schema.
V3 — R3: an upgrade lands when the provider says; a downgrade warns about the boards it will lock
     before it is confirmed.
V4 — R4: cancel → confirmation → provider cancels; the export is offered first; the copy states what
     survives.
V5 — R5: after the end one chosen board is writable, the others and the objectives are read-only with
the reason shown, and export still works.
V6 — R6: past due shows the grace window and a working link.
V7 — R7: a provider failure stops the action and says so; our row is not changed on its own.

CANCELLED — 2026-10-24: open source, and nothing is sold
Flowline is open-source software people self-host (task 163), so there is no price to publish, no
merchant to take money and no plan to manage. This task is cancelled rather than deferred: it was the
shape of a business this product is not.
tasks.testStrategy: Every state shown truthfully, free included; money handled only on the provider’s pages; a downgrade that says which boards will lock; and a cancellation that offers the export first and leaves a working free account behind.

tasks.title: The trust set an operator can read: security, sub-processors, accessibility.
tasks.description: The pages a self-hoster checks before running it and a reader checks before trusting it: what security is claimed and what is not, which processors this demo deployment has (and why that list is not theirs), the accessibility target and its gaps, and where to report a hole.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository — open-source software a team installs and runs itself
(task 163: one deployment is one workspace). Read `docs/public-site.md` §the trust set,
`site/processors.json`, `SECURITY.md`, and task 150 (the privacy notice, terms and changelog, which
this task extends rather than repeats).

SCOPE
1. `/security` — how it is built, and what is not claimed.
2. `/subprocessors` — every processor *this demo deployment* actually has, and what a self-hoster
   does instead.
3. The accessibility statement — on `/security`, where the site's plan already puts it: the target,
   the known gaps, and where to report one. A separate page would be a twelfth page that says what
   one sentence of the eleventh already does.
4. What the licence does here — a file in the repository, not a page on the site.
5. Every page reachable, listed, and linked from the pages that promise them.

ABSENT ON PURPOSE, AND SAID OUT LOUD
There is no `/dpa`, no `/refunds`, no `/about` entity and no invoice. A self-hoster is the controller
of their own instance's data: there is no processor relationship to sign a DPA about, no charge to
refund, and no company selling anything. The pages say that plainly rather than lending a self-hoster
a contract they do not have. The privacy notice (task 150) already carries the same sentence.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Security tells the truth, including the gaps
`/security` shall describe transport and storage, how a session is carried, how a password is stored
(a PBKDF2 hash, never the password — task 154), how a SCIM token is stored (hashed, task 168), how the
error log treats addresses, what third-party code runs (nothing), whether a team's work is used to
train anything (no), how access is controlled, what the backup story is, and where to report a
vulnerability.

It shall state what is **not** claimed — no SOC 2, no ISO 27001, no penetration-test certificate until
one exists — each with a line saying whether it is planned. A claim without a test or a document
behind it does not appear.

R2 — The sub-processor list cannot go stale, and it is the demo's
`/subprocessors` shall list every processor the deployment is configured to use: the identity provider
(OIDC), the host, the database, the error log, and the mail relay when one is configured (task 154).
Name, purpose, categories of data, location, and a link to that processor's own terms.

- The list is generated at build from the same configuration that decides whether a feature is on, and
  a test fails when a configured processor is unlisted and when a listed one is no longer configured
  (`server/site.test.ts` already does this for the notice; this extends it).
- The page shall say whose list it is: **this demo instance's**. A self-hoster's processors are the
  ones they chose, they are the controller, and the page gives them the table's shape to copy rather
  than implying a relationship that does not exist.
- A change to the list is announced in the release note for the tag that changes it. There is no
  subscription route and no notice period to promise: a self-hosted instance changes when its operator
  changes it.

R3 — Accessibility is a statement, not a badge
`/security` shall carry the accessibility statement: WCAG 2.2 AA as the target (task 125 set that bar
in the app), how the public pages and the app are tested, the known gaps listed honestly, and an
address for a report with an expectation of an answer. A badge without an audit behind it is the thing
this statement exists to avoid.

R4 — The licence is a file, and the page says what it means
There is no `/licence` page: `LICENSE` is the AGPL-3.0-or-later text in the repository (task 165), and
`/install/` and the footer link it. `/security` and `/install/` shall each carry the one paragraph a
self-hoster needs: run it, change it, and a modified version run for other people over a network
offers them its source. Duplicating the licence on the site would be a second copy that can disagree.

R5 — Disclosure has an address and a promise
`security.txt` (RFC 9116: contact, policy, expiry) shall be served with an expiry in the future and
point at `SECURITY.md`, which carries the address, what to include, what the project promises and what
is out of scope. The page and the file shall agree; the file is the machine-readable copy of the page.

R6 — Every page is reachable and linked
Each page shall be in the sitemap, in the footer where it belongs, and linked from the page that
promises it — `/security` from `/install/` and the help page, `/subprocessors` from `/security`, the licence from
the footer and `/install/`. The accessibility statement is a heading on `/security`, and the site's
footer links there rather than to a page of its own. No public page shall
link a trust page that does not exist, and the site check already fails on a link that resolves to
nothing.

R7 — Read by somebody before it is relied on
The claims on these pages are the kind a person makes a decision on, so each one shall name what
backs it: a test, a file in the repository, or a sentence saying it is not claimed. The task's
completion note records the review — who read it, and when — and the site does not claim a compliance
nobody has been given.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: every claim on the security page maps to a test or a document in a table in the repo, and
     each non-claim is present.
V2 — R2: configure a processor without listing it and see the test fail; the reverse fails too; the
     page names the demo instance as the list's owner and says what a self-hoster does instead.
V3 — R3: the statement names the standard, the gaps and an address.
V4 — R4: there is no `/licence` page, the footer and `/install/` link `LICENSE`, and the paragraph
     says what the AGPL asks of a host.
V5 — R5: `security.txt` parses, has a future expiry, and points at SECURITY.md; the two agree.
V6 — R6: every trust page is in the sitemap and every link resolves.
V7 — R7: the review is recorded in the completion note, and no page claims a certification.

REWRITTEN — 2026-10-24: a buyer's trust set is not an operator's
This task was first written for a paid hosted product: a DPA with a metered processor list, a refund
policy that agreed word-for-word with a cancellation screen, an entity that invoices, and a licensing
page. None of those have a subject now — tasks 153, 155 and 156 are cancelled, 164 deleted the pages
that would have linked them, and 166 removed the billing record. Three revision notes had been stacked
on top of requirements that still asked for them, which is how a task ends up describing a product
nobody is building.

What is left is what a self-hoster and a reader actually need: what security is claimed and not
claimed, which processors this demo deployment has and why the list is not theirs, what accessibility
is targeted, where the licence lives, and where to report a hole.

DONE — 2026-10-25
`/security` and `/sub-processors` are written for this product: how a session, a role, the workspace
seal, an invitation, a report and a backup actually work; an **explicit "what is not claimed"** (no
SOC 2, no ISO 27001, no penetration-test certificate, no uptime target or status page, no bug bounty);
the **accessibility statement** — WCAG 2.2 AA as the target, how it is tested, and the two gaps that
exist — on the security page rather than a page of its own; and the licence paragraph, pointing at
`LICENSE` instead of duplicating it.

`/sub-processors` is now rendered from `site/processors.json` at build, like the privacy notice, so
there is one list; it says plainly that the list is **this demo deployment's** and that a self-hoster's
processors are their own, with no DPA to sign because there is no processing.

The site check fails when either page loses a claim, the accessibility statement, the licence, or a
processor the configuration names; `server/site.test.ts` holds the four properties directly, including
that the list comes from the placeholder rather than a second copy.

Not claimed, and now visibly not: passwords and SCIM tokens. Both belong to task 154 and 168, and the
page will gain them when they exist — it does not describe software that has not been written.
tasks.testStrategy: A DPA with the clauses a buyer checks; a sub-processor list generated from configuration that fails when it drifts; a security page that states its gaps as plainly as its measures; refund and cancellation copy that matches the app; and no dead links between them.

tasks.title: Help: the answers that keep a person out of the support inbox.
tasks.description: A small, task-shaped guide with a page for each thing a person actually does, written from the shipped UI and kept honest by the screenshots they are checked against.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/public-site.md §/help. The app's own words
(README, the drawer, the board) are the source of the vocabulary; a help page that invents a new name
for a lane is a bug.

SCOPE
1. `/help` — the index, with a sidebar that is the whole navigation.
2. Ten pages, each one task rather than one feature.
3. Screenshots captured from the built app by the existing shot script (152).
4. Links from the app and the site.

THE TEN PAGES
1. **Getting started** — the demo, the first board, where everything is. Five minutes, not a tour.
2. **A board and its lanes** — the lane tree, splitting a cell, the four stages, edit mode.
3. **Cards, hierarchy and types** — a card, a parent, children, types as labels and colour.
4. **Initiatives and the management view** — what an initiative is, why its status is derived, the
   dashboard, the timeline, the flow view.
5. **People, roles and invitations** — who may do what, inviting, removing, groups.
6. **Sharing a board read-only** — a link, what it shows, how to end it (task 123).
7. **Import, export and backups** — the workspace file, the CSV export, the backup for a self-hoster.
8. **Keyboard** — every shortcut, and the board as a keyboard user meets it.
9. **Running it yourself** — the short version, pointing at `/install/` and the docs (task 167).
10. **When something looks wrong** — a card that is read-only because somebody else has it, a write
    that was refused and the words kept, an edit made offline that is waiting, a stale tab.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — One page, one task
Each page shall open with what the reader is about to do, then the steps, then one screenshot of the
shipped UI, then "if it did not work" with the two or three things that actually go wrong. No page
shall be an alphabetical list of every control.

R2 — Written from the build
Every screenshot shall come from `npm run shots`, and every label a page names shall exist in the app
at the commit that builds the site. A help page that names a control the app does not have is a
failing test, not a stale doc: a check shall compare the labels a page quotes against the rendered UI
where it can, and a manual review list where it cannot.

R3 — The index is the navigation
The sidebar shall list the ten pages with the current one marked, and each page shall carry previous
and next. There shall be no search box: ten pages are a sidebar, and a search that returns nothing is
worse than one that does not exist.

R4 — Source and render
The pages shall be written as markdown in `site/help/` and rendered at build by the site script,
reusing `src/lib/markdown.ts` extended for headings with anchors, tables and nested lists. The render
shall escape its input, as it does today.

R5 — Reachable from where the question is asked
The app's account menu shall link Help, the site's nav and footer shall link it, and the pages that
raise a question shall link the page that answers it — `/install/` to running it yourself, the
read-only banner to "when something looks wrong", the account menu to sign-in and mail problems.

R6 — Nothing off-origin
No embedded video, no third-party screenshot host, no font. Images live in `site/img/help/`.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: each page has an intro, steps and an "if it did not work" section.
V2 — R2: every image comes from the shot script; the labels check passes; the review list is empty.
V3 — R3: the sidebar lists all ten, the current one is marked, and there is no search input.
V4 — R4: markdown renders headings, tables and lists; a script tag in a page is escaped.
V5 — R5: the three entry points resolve.
V6 — R6: the request audit of 151 covers the help pages; no third-party origin.

REVISED — 2026-10-24: the answers an operator needs
The ten answers were written for a hosted product. Three of them become the operator's: **how do I
install it**, **how do I upgrade it** (migrations, and what to do first), and **how do I back it up and
restore it**. Plans, billing and cancellation leave the list; invitations, exports and offline stay.

REVISED AGAIN — 2026-10-24: the answers are an operator's
Two of the answers become **connect your identity provider** (OIDC, task 154) and **provision from
your directory** (SCIM, task 168), and both link `docs/identity.md` rather than explaining it twice.
The help copy stops naming Google and Microsoft: the answer to "how do I sign in" is the issuer this
instance was configured with, and an instance with none says so.

REVISED AGAIN — 2026-10-24: passwords, magic links and mail that did not arrive
Three of the answers become: **sign in with a password** (where it comes from, what it is stored as,
what an administrator can and cannot do with it), **the magic link never arrived** (spam, an address
that is not the account's, a relay that is not configured, and the reset an administrator can mint
when it is not), and **connecting an identity provider** (OIDC, task 154), with **provisioning from
your directory** (SCIM, task 168) beside it. The copy stops naming Google and Microsoft.

CANCELLED — 2026-10-24: the help page is removed, and its answers have better homes
The site's `/help/` was deleted with `/status/` and `/changelog/`. What it would have carried is
already somewhere a reader trusts more: installing, configuring, upgrading and restoring are the
operator docs (task 167), which live with the code and are checked; using the board is the app's own
words, which cannot drift from the interface; and the support address is in the footer of every page.
A help page written from the app would have been a third copy of the same sentences.
tasks.testStrategy: Ten task-shaped pages with steps, a shipped-UI screenshot and a recovery section; labels and images that are checked against the build; a sidebar instead of a search box; and every entry point into it resolving.

tasks.title: The support address, and a security.txt that expires.
tasks.description: The two machine- and person-facing things that outlive the status page: a security.txt with a future expiry that points at SECURITY.md, and the support address in the footer of every page with the expectation written beside it.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read `SECURITY.md`, `site/layout.html` (the footer) and
task 157 (the security page `security.txt` points at).

SCOPE
1. `/.well-known/security.txt` — contact, policy and expiry, generated at build.
2. The support address — in the footer of every public page, with what to expect.
3. The link between them: the file is the machine-readable copy of the page.

WHAT THIS NO LONGER INCLUDES, AND WHY
The `/status` page was removed on 2026-10-24. A status page is a promise that somebody is watching:
live checks that say "now" and incidents posted during an incident. This project has no on-call rota
and no monitoring history, so the page could only ever have said "this was true when you loaded it"
— which the reader can already see for themselves by opening the site. A self-hoster's uptime is
their own machine's, and the demo's is best reported by whatever runs it.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — security.txt, generated and expiring
`/.well-known/security.txt` shall be written at build with `Contact` (the security address),
`Expires` (a date in the future), `Canonical` (its own absolute URL), `Policy` (the security page) and
`Preferred-Languages`. A test shall fail when `Expires` is in the past, because a security.txt that has
expired is worse than none: it tells a researcher not to bother.

R2 — The file and the page agree
`SECURITY.md` and `/security` carry the same address, the same promise and the same scope. The file
is generated from the same configuration the page reads, so the two cannot drift.

R3 — The support address is on every page
The footer of every public page shall carry the support address as a `mailto:`, with the expectation
in words beside it (a business day, in a named timezone) and what to include in a report. There is no
contact form: there is no inbox to spam, and a form that silently fails is worse than mail.

R4 — A self-hoster's address is their own
The address shall come from configuration, so a self-hosted instance names its own and not this
project's — and the page says whose address it is.

R5 — Nothing to keep up
There is no incident log and no check to run on page load. If a page is down, the browser says so;
this project does not pretend to watch it.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: `security.txt` parses, has a future `Expires`, and points at `/security`.
V2 — R2: the address in the file, `SECURITY.md` and `/security` are the same string.
V3 — R3: every built page's footer has the `mailto:` and the expectation.
V4 — R4: a configured address appears on a self-hosted instance.

DONE — 2026-10-25
`security.txt` is written at the root by `npm run build` — the RFC 9116 location the standard allows
as the alternative to `/.well-known/`, which Cloudflare's static assets do not serve — with `Contact`,
`Expires` (a year out), `Canonical`, `Policy` and `Preferred-Languages`, generated from
`SECURITY_EMAIL` and `SITE_URL`.

The support and security addresses are configuration now (`SUPPORT_EMAIL`, `SECURITY_EMAIL`) and the
footer of every page carries the support one with the expectation beside it ("answered within two
working days"), so the address is not on a page that can be deleted.

`scripts/check-site.mjs` fails when the file is missing, when a field is missing, when `Expires` is
not a future date, when `Canonical` is not this origin, when `Policy` is not `/security/`, or when the
page stops naming the address the file names. An e2e fetches `/security.txt` over HTTP and asserts the
same, and the privacy notice and the security page both take their addresses from the build.
tasks.testStrategy: A status page that checks now and says when; incidents a person posted rather than a history invented; support as a mailto with a stated expectation; security.txt with a future expiry; and both runtimes answering from the same code.

tasks.title: Self-host has its own page, and the licence is decided before it does.
tasks.description: The page for the buyer who wants the server on their own machine, and the licence that makes the offer legal — the decision the roadmap says must land before the repository opens.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/public-site.md §/self-host and §Decisions to
take item 5; docs/roadmap.md "The one thing that can invalidate this plan"; task 128 for the image
and the compose file.

SCOPE
1. The licence decision, recorded and applied.
2. `/self-host` — what you get, what you need, how to start, what it does not give you.
3. The links from the pricing page, the footer and the help centre.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — The licence is decided first
A licence shall be chosen (AGPL if competing hosts should share back, Apache-2.0 if adoption matters
more), added as `LICENSE`, stated in `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`'s conventions and the site's footer, and
linked from `/licence`. The page shall not be written before the choice, because its sentences depend
on it. The record of the decision names the trade-off, not just the choice.

R2 — What you actually get
`/self-host` shall say that the application is the same code, the same SQLite schema and the same
server as the hosted one; that state is one file; that the live channel is the instance's own socket;
and what an operator takes on — updates, backups, TLS, and the machine.

R3 — The commands are the ones that work
The three commands on the page shall be the ones CI proves (`npm run smoke:node` and task 128's
compose file), not a remembered variant. A test shall compare the page's command block with the
script CI runs, or the page shall link the file rather than quote it.

R4 — The limits are stated, not hidden
Single instance; the file is the database; no horizontal scale; the live channel is one process; no
hosted backups; no hosted support. A self-hoster reads this before they start, not after.

R5 — What the hosted plan adds instead
The page shall say what money buys that a self-hosted instance does not: updates without operating
them, the live channel without managing sockets, backups and restore drills, and support with an
expectation. It shall say that the self-hosted build is **not** held to the free plan's one board and
no objectives — there is nobody to sell a plan to — and shall not imply the self-hosted build is
crippled: it is the same application.

R6 — The offer is a link, not a form
Where the licence is purchased, the action goes to the provider's checkout (155) or to the repository,
whichever the licence decision made true.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: LICENSE exists, the four places name it, and /licence renders it.
V2 — R2/R4: the page names the process, the file and each limit.
V3 — R3: the command block matches CI's smoke path or links it; a changed command fails the test.
V4 — R5: the hosted extras are listed and the self-hosted build is not described as reduced.
V5 — R6: the action resolves to a real destination.

REVISED — 2026-10-24: this page is now the product
Self-hosting is not a page beside the product any more; it is the product. Raise to **high**: the page
says how to run it, what it needs, what the licence is (task 165) and where the runbook lives (task
128), and it is promoted to the second item of the navigation by task 164.

NOTE — 2026-10-24: the page now exists, and it is `/install/`
Task 164 built it and deleted `/self-host/`, so what is left here is its depth rather than its shell:
the honest limits (one instance, the file is the database, the backups are yours), the upgrade and
restore story from task 128's runbook, and the licence named and linked (task 165). Two pages about
running it would be two pages that can disagree, so this task fills `/install/` rather than adding
another one.

DONE — 2026-10-24 (commit `a4086d0`, CI green: checks, e2e, image, deploy)
`/install/` now carries both roads — `docker compose up -d` (what the image job builds and runs) above
the three commands that image performs — then the first run, what an operator takes on (TLS, updates,
backups, support), what the process reads, the honest limits, upkeep, and the licence.

Two requirements were overtaken by decisions taken since the task was written, and are recorded rather
than quietly dropped:

- **R5** asked what a paid plan adds instead. There is no paid plan (tasks 153, 155, 156 cancelled;
  166 removed the billing), so the page says the true version of it: there is no reduced edition and
  nothing to unlock.
- **R6** asked where the licence is purchased. It is not: the licence is a file in the repository, and
  the action is a clone.

R3 is held tighter than it asked: the site check now fails if either command block drifts from a
command this repository actually proves — `docker compose up -d` from the CI image job, and
`npm ci && npm run build … npm run server` from the smoke and e2e lanes — and the limits section must
name SQLite, horizontal scale and the single process.

The page had also gone stale in the opposite direction: it said there was no container image or
package, which task 128 made false. That sentence is gone.
tasks.testStrategy: A licence decided and reflected in four places; a page whose commands are the ones CI runs; the limits of one process and one file stated before someone starts; and what the paid plan adds, without pretending the free build is lesser.

tasks.title: The emails a paid account lives on: welcome, trial, receipt, failure, cancellation.
tasks.description: The transactional copy and the sending contract behind it — plain text, no tracking pixel, one send per event, and a way to run an instance with no mail at all.
tasks.details: SYSTEM Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/public-site.md §Decisions to take item 6. The invitation link already exists (`server/invite-links.ts`); this task is what happens around it. SCOPE 1. The templates and their copy. 2. The sending contract: one send per event, idempotent, no tracking. 3. The sender domain: SPF, DKIM, DMARC. 4. The no-mail mode a self-hoster runs. NOT IN SCOPE Marketing email or a newsletter. There is no list, no cadence and no consent record, and a product that does not track does not start by building one. REQUIREMENTS R1 — The set There shall be a template for each of: the first successful sign-in (what this is, where to start); an invitation (already a link, now delivered); a receipt (from the provider, linked — not re-rendered by us); a payment failure; a payment recovered; a plan change; a cancellation confirmed (what the free plan keeps at the end of the period, and how to export first); a downgrade completed (which board kept working, what became read-only); a workspace deleted; and an account closed. There is no trial mail, because there is no trial. Each shall have a subject, a plain-text body and a single action. R2 — The words are the app's words The copy shall come from one module so a template and the screen that caused it cannot disagree — "read-only", "the end of the period", "the free plan", "export" mean the same thing in the mail as in the app. The tone is the site's: plain, second person, no urgency, no exclamation marks, no guilt. R3 — No tracking, no remote assets No email shall contain a tracking pixel, a remote image, a third-party font or a link wrapper that counts clicks. Unsubscribe shall appear only on mail that is not transactional, and there is none of that in this set. A test shall reject a template containing an `` with a remote source or a one-pixel element. R4 — One send per event Sending shall be idempotent: the event that causes a mail carries a key, and a retried job or a replayed webhook shall not send a second copy. A fake transport in the tests shall count sends. R5 — The sending domain is set up properly SPF, DKIM and DMARC shall be configured for the sending domain, the From and Reply-To shall be people's addresses, bounce and complaint handling shall be stated, and the provider shall be added to the sub-processor list (157 R2). R6 — Self-host without a mail server An instance with no mail configured shall work: invitation links are shown to be copied (as today), and the pages that would have been emailed say so. Enabling mail shall be configuration, not code — and the app shall not crash, or promise a mail it cannot send. R7 — Every link resolves Each template's action shall point at a page that exists in the built site and the app, and a test shall fetch it. TEST STRATEGY VERIFICATION V1 — R1: each event renders a template with a subject, a text body and one action. V2 — R2: the copy module is the only source of the phrases the test list checks. V3 — R3: the template scan rejects a remote image and a pixel. V4 — R4: a replayed event sends once; the transport's count proves it. V5 — R5: the DNS records are present for the sending domain; the provider is listed as a sub-processor. V6 — R6: with no transport configured, the invitation flow still works and says how to share the link. V7 — R7: every action in every template resolves. CANCELLED — 2026-10-24: open source, and nothing is sold Flowline is open-source software people self-host (task 163), so there is no price to publish, no merchant to take money and no plan to manage. This task is cancelled rather than deferred: it was the shape of a business this product is not.
tasks.testStrategy: A template per transactional event with copy shared with the app; no tracking pixel or remote asset in any of them; one send per event under replay; a sending domain set up and listed as a sub-processor; and a self-hosted instance that works with no mail at all.

tasks.title: A workspace is created from a sign-up page, by the person who will own it.
tasks.description: The public front door to the act that already exists: sign in, name the workspace, land in it — with the plan and the terms beside the form, and invitations that name the workspace they are for.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read task 126 (revised) and the site plan in
`docs/public-site.md`.

SCOPE
1. The sign-up page: the place a stranger becomes an account and a workspace.
2. The act behind it — which is built (`POST /api/workspaces`), and this task puts a front door on it.
3. Invitations that name the workspace they are for.

WHAT IS ALREADY THERE (2026-10-24)
`POST /api/workspaces` creates a workspace whose **owner is the account that asked for it**, whose
administrator is the same person, with its settings row and its audit entry, in one transaction.
`GET /api/workspaces/mine` says whether the account already has one. In the app, an account with no
workspace (after deleting theirs, or being removed from one) sees **No workspace** and a **Create a
workspace** dialog: the name, and the account's own email shown as the owner — shown, not typed,
because an owner is the person who asked, not a field somebody else can be written into.
**One workspace per account**: a regular user joins the workspace they were invited to, or creates
the one they own.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — The page
A public sign-up page, reachable from the site's front door and from the sign-in page (154), that
does the whole thing in one place: sign in with a provider, name the workspace, and land in it. The
person arriving has no account, no workspace and no invitation.

R2 — The email is the account
A workspace is created by an account, and that account owns it. There is no field for "somebody
else's email": an owner who did not ask for the workspace is a transfer (126's panel), not a sign-up.
The page shows the address the provider verified, and says that it is the owner.

R3 — Admission, said plainly
Whether a stranger may sign up is the instance's setting (134): `open` admits a verified address as a
viewer and the page creates their workspace; `closed` says so on the page rather than after a failed
sign-in, and points at the invitation they need. A hosted instance runs open; a private one does not.

R4 — The plan, beside the form
The workspace is created on the plan the page says (153/155). Creating one is not a purchase, so the
page must not imply a card is needed; what it must do is state which plan this workspace starts on and
where the bill will live.

R5 — One workspace, and the way to another
An account with a workspace sees the page as "open it" rather than as a second creation, because one
workspace per account is the rule this product has decided (126). Adding a second is a separate
decision, and the page must not offer it until it exists.

R6 — Invitations carry the workspace
An invitation to join must name the workspace it is for. `invites` has a `scope` but no workspace id
— true while there was one workspace, false now that anybody may create one. Acceptance joins the
invited workspace, not "the instance's". A person who is invited to one workspace while owning
another is refused with a sentence that says so, since one workspace per account is the rule.

R7 — The emails and the terms
The welcome that follows (161) is sent once, to the owner. The terms and the notice (150) are linked
from the form, before the account exists, not after.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION

V1 — R1: a stranger with no account reaches the page, signs up with a provider, names a workspace,
     and arrives on its board; the workspace exists with them as owner and administrator.
V2 — R2: the owner is the account that signed up — asserted in the database, not in the form.
V3 — R3: on a closed instance the page refuses before the provider round trip and explains how to be
     invited; on an open one it admits.
V4 — R5: an account with a workspace is shown "open it", and a second creation is refused by the
     server whatever the page does.
V5 — R6: an invitation carries a workspace; accepting joins that one; an invitation to a second
     workspace for an account that already has one is refused.
V6 — R7: the terms and the notice are reachable from the page; the welcome email is sent to the owner
     and to nobody else.

NOTE — 2026-10-24, after the deletion correction
**Arrival is an account, not a seat.** `identify` no longer joins a stranger to the deployment's
workspace: the first person on a fresh deployment still gets it (the self-hosted first run), an
invitation still joins the workspace it is for, and everybody else arrives with **no workspace**.
That is the state this page and the in-app "Create a workspace" both address. A **group** that
carries a role is a way into a workspace, so closing the group closes the seat.

CANCELLED — 2026-10-24: the install is the sign-up
Each workspace is a separately hosted instance (task 163), so nobody signs up *for a workspace*: they
install one, and the first account to sign in is its administrator. The page this task described —
an email that owns a workspace, a plan beside the form — belonged to a hosted service. What survives
of it is task 163's first run: name the workspace, take the administrator, done.
tasks.testStrategy: A stranger signs up and arrives on a workspace they own; the owner asserted in the database; a closed instance refusing before the provider round trip; one workspace per account enforced by the server; an invitation carrying its workspace; and the terms and the welcome email wired.
tasks.complexityReasoning: A page and a form on top of an act that exists, plus one schema change: invitations must name the workspace they are for.

tasks.title: The instance is the workspace: one deployment, one team.
tasks.description: Each workspace is a separately hosted instance. One workspace per deployment, created by the install, and no path to a second. The boundary stays; the multi-tenant product does not.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read `docs/public-site.md` and task 122 (the workspace
as a container), and the decision of 2026-10-24: **Flowline is open-source software people self-host.**

SCOPE
1. One workspace per deployment — enforced, not assumed.
2. First run *is* the install: the instance names its workspace, and nobody signs up for one.
3. What stays from 122.1/122.2: the boundary (the `workspaces` row and the `workspace_id` columns,
   and the seal every route goes through) — as defence in depth, not as a multi-tenant product.
4. The vocabulary and the copy that still imply a hosted service with several workspaces.

DEFINITIONS
- **The instance**: one deployment of this software, run by one team on one machine.
- **The workspace**: that instance's own team. There is exactly one, and it is not a thing you create
  from a website.
- **The administrator**: the person who runs the instance — no longer an "owner" who pays, because
  nobody pays.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — One workspace, enforced
The server creates exactly one workspace, with the instance. `POST /api/workspaces` and every path that
could make a second are removed; a request that tries is refused with a sentence that says what this
software is. The e2e asserts a second cannot exist.

R2 — The first run is the install
A fresh deployment gets its workspace from its own installation: the name comes from configuration
(`WORKSPACE_NAME`, defaulting to something honest) or from a first-run form, and the first account to
sign in is its administrator. Nobody "signs up for a workspace"; they install one.

R3 — The boundary stays
`workspaces.id` and the `workspace_id` columns stay, and so does 122.2's seal — every read and write
resolved from the session, never from the request. One workspace makes them redundant today; they are
the shape a fork could grow into, and removing them would be churn with a risk attached. No UI ever
offers a second.

R4 — The words
"Workspace" means this instance's team. An account's own page is its **profile**. The person who runs
it is the **administrator**. "Owner", "plan", "seat", "billing", "subscription", "trial" and "upgrade
your plan" leave the product's vocabulary, and the audit sentences follow.

R5 — The copy that assumed a service
Every surface that says "your workspaces", offers a workspace switcher, invites you to "create a
workspace", or names a plan is changed or removed. The invitation flow stays: inviting a colleague to
*this* instance is the one way in.

R6 — Both runtimes, and the record
The Node entry and the Worker behave the same; the e2e runs the first-run path; `README.md` and
`docs/server-runtime.md` say "one instance, one workspace" and why.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: a second workspace cannot be created through any route, and the refusal says why.
V2 — R2: a fresh instance has one workspace, named from configuration or the first-run form, with the
     first account as its administrator.
V3 — R3: the seal still holds (the existing suite), and no surface offers a second workspace.
V4 — R4: a search of `src/` and `site/` for the retired words finds none in product copy.
V5 — R5/R6: the e2e green, both entries, and the docs read as one instance rather than a service.

DONE — 2026-10-24 (commit `d4181bd`, CI green)
`POST /api/workspaces` no longer makes anything: it answers with one sentence (`ONE_WORKSPACE`),
after the door, so a stranger gets the door and not the deployment's business. The create dialog is
deleted, and an account that is not in this workspace says so with nothing to press.

The install names the workspace (`WORKSPACE_NAME`, default `Flowline`) in both rows that hold a name,
and the first account becomes its administrator. Two rules were decided while building it, and the
e2e found the second:

- **A deleted workspace comes back the way it began.** An instance administrator arriving at a
  deployment with no workspace re-opens it — under the installation's name, seated as its
  administrator. A plain member cannot resurrect a team they were not invited into, and nobody can
  make a second. Judged on both ways through the door, because a returning identity takes the short
  path and would otherwise skip it.
- **A name a team chose is never overwritten**: only the name the row was created with is replaced.

The boundary stays untouched — the `workspace_id` columns and the seal — as R3 asked. Vocabulary:
"the instance's workspace", "administrator", "not in this workspace"; the words that remain are the
billing record's, and they are task 166's to remove (`WorkspaceAccountPanel`, `owner_id`, `plan`).
tasks.testStrategy: Per the verification list in the task.
tasks.complexityReasoning: Scoped by the task’s own verification list.

tasks.title: The site is a project’s site: install, not pricing.
tasks.description: No pricing page, no plan language. Install replaces it in the navigation, the home page and the sitemap, and the sign-up stubs go.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read `docs/public-site.md` and task 151 (the site's
build). The decision of 2026-10-24: this is **open-source software people self-host**, so there is
nothing to sell and the site is a project's site.

SCOPE
1. The navigation and the footer: no Pricing, and an Install that replaces it.
2. `/install/` — the page the navigation's action points at.
3. The home page's cost material — removed, not rewritten.
4. Three pages that go: pricing, sign-in, sign-up.
5. The navigation's **Docs** item, pointing at where the docs live (task 167).
6. Sitemap, robots, the check and the e2e.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — No pricing, anywhere
`/pricing/` is deleted; "Pricing" leaves the nav and the footer; the sitemap no longer lists it; a
request to it is the 404 page. The site check fails if the word appears in the navigation, the footer,
the sitemap or the home page's copy.

R2 — `/install/` is the page
What it is: one Node process, one SQLite file, a directory of static files. How to run it in one
command, what configuration it needs, what to do about TLS, and where the upgrade and backup
instructions live. It links task 128's runbook rather than repeating it.

R3 — The home page points at it, and stops talking about money
The primary action becomes **Install** (to `/install/`), beside **Open the demo — no account**. The
pricing section is **deleted**, and so is the "How do you make money?" question: there is nothing to
sell and nothing to explain away, and a paragraph about being free is still a paragraph about money.
The promises lose the lapsed-plan line for the same reason. What takes their place is not prose but
evidence — the licence (task 165), the install page, and the demo.

R4 — Three pages go: pricing, sign-in, sign-up
`/pricing/`, `/signin/` and `/signup/` are deleted — their files, their sitemap entries, and every
link to them, in the layout, the help page, the terms page, the home page and the product page.

No pricing is the product decision. No sign-in page is an architectural one: a person signs in **at
their own instance**, on its own domain, through the app's own door at `/app` — so a sign-in page on
the project's site could only ever be about somebody else's deployment, and the terms it would carry
would be somebody else's terms. The links that pointed at `/signin/` point at `/app`; the ones that
pointed at `/signup/` point at `/install/`, or at the demo, because those are the two things a
visitor can actually do.

R5 — The other pages stop selling
`/self-host/` is promoted to the second item of the navigation and stops saying it is "task 160"; the
help, terms and privacy pages lose plan and refund language (tasks 150, 158, 157).

R6 — The check holds it
`scripts/check-site.mjs` gains: no `/pricing`, `/signin` or `/signup` link anywhere, no plan
vocabulary, `/install` resolving, the home page's sections in their new order, and its two actions
pointing at `/app` and `/install`. The assertion that the home page carries a *Start free* link to
`/signin` becomes its opposite: no such link may exist.
Its promise floor drops from four to three, because one of the four was about plans.

R7 — Docs are a link, not a copy
The navigation and the footer carry **Docs**, and it points at where the documentation actually lives
(task 167) — the repository's markdown, rendered by GitHub, or a `docs.` subdomain generated from
those same files. The site never holds a second copy of a page that could then disagree with the one
an operator reads after cloning.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: `/pricing/` is 404; the nav, the footer, the sitemap and the home page carry no pricing.
V2 — R2: `/install/` exists, is readable with JavaScript off, and says how to run it in one command.
V3 — R3: the home page's actions are the demo and install; it carries no cost section and no money
     question, and the promises still number three.
V4 — R4: `/pricing/`, `/signin/` and `/signup/` are 404, no page links to any of them, and the
     navigation's action is Install.
V5 — R6: the site check and the e2e pass, with the new banned list and the lower promise floor.
V6 — R7: Docs resolves to the real documentation, and the site holds no page the docs also hold.

DONE — 2026-10-24 (commit `a86e89e`, CI green)
`/pricing/`, `/signin/`, `/signup/` and `/self-host/` are deleted; `/install/` is served and is the
navigation's action; the nav is Product · Install · Docs · Help · Changelog · Status; the home page's
second action is Install and its promise and its question link there; the terms stop promising a
pricing page; the check forbids a pricing, sign-in or sign-up link and any plan vocabulary, and a
deleted page is swept from a stale `dist/` when the site is built on its own.

The site's own links may leave the origin now, and only *links*: the Docs, Source and Licence items
point at the repository through one build value (`REPO_URL`, default a placeholder next to
`flowline.example`). The docs they point at are task 167's — the file does not exist yet, which is the
one link on the site that is currently a promise rather than a page.

tasks.title: An open-source project’s surface: licence, contribution, security.
tasks.description: One OSI-approved licence, CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY, a code of conduct, the templates, and a README that reads like the site.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read `AGENTS.md` (the house rules) and `README.md`.

SCOPE
1. The licence: decided, written, and pointed at from the site and the README.
2. The documents a contributor reads: CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.
3. The repository's surface: issue and pull-request templates, the README as a front door, and a
   release that can be followed.

DEFINITIONS
- **Open source**: the source is public, the licence permits use and modification, and the project has
  a stated way to contribute and a stated way to report a hole.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — The licence is decided, and it is one
One OSI-approved licence, named in `LICENSE`, in the README's first screen, in `package.json` and in
the site's footer. A copyleft licence (AGPL-3.0) is the recommendation for a product that will be run
as a service by other people; a permissive one (Apache-2.0) is the recommendation if adoption matters
more than that. **This is a decision for the owner, recorded in the task when taken** — not a detail to
be defaulted.

R2 — CONTRIBUTING says how
How to run it (`npm install`, `npm run dev`, the database), how to run the checks that gate a merge
(`npm test`, `npm run build`, `npm run test:e2e`, `npm run scan`), the house rules `AGENTS.md` states,
and what a pull request needs to contain. It links the architecture notes rather than repeating them.

R3 — SECURITY says where
`SECURITY.md` with the disclosure address, what to include in a report, what the project promises
(acknowledgement, a fix or a reason, credit if wanted), and what is in scope — the API, the sessions,
the invitation links, the server entries.

R4 — The conduct, and the templates
A CODE_OF_CONDUCT (the Contributor Covenant, unedited except for the contact), and issue templates for
a bug and a feature request that ask for the build, the runtime and the smallest reproduction.

R5 — The README is the front door
What it is in one line, one screenshot, how to run it in one command, where the docs are, the licence,
and the one rule (`AGENTS.md`). It should read like the site's home page, because the people who read
both should not meet two different projects.

R6 — A release can be followed
A version, a tag, a changelog entry in the site's own changelog (task 150), and a sentence about
migrations: which releases change the schema, and what an operator must do before upgrading.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: `LICENSE` exists, matches `package.json`, and the site footer and README name it.
V2 — R2/R3/R4: the four documents exist, are linked from the README, and `npm run scan` stays clean.
V3 — R5: the README's first screen says what it is and how to run it.
V4 — R6: the changelog names the version, and the upgrade note is true of `migrations/`.

NOTE — 2026-10-24: the docs are not this task
This is the repository's *contribution* surface — licence, conduct, disclosure, templates, and a README
that reads like the site. The operator's and the reader's documentation — install, configure, upgrade,
back up, architecture, the API — is task 167, and the README links to it rather than absorbing it.

DECIDED — 2026-10-24: **AGPL-3.0-or-later**. The owner chose it over Apache-2.0 and MIT for the
reason the task gave: Flowline is software people run as a service, and a host that runs a modified
version for other people should publish its changes. Adoption is worth less than the code coming
back.

DONE — 2026-10-24 (commit `2bb22c5`, CI green)
`LICENSE` is the AGPL v3 text verbatim; `package.json` declares `AGPL-3.0-or-later`; the README's
first screen carries the one line, the screenshot, the install commands, the licence and the links;
the site's footer and `/install/` name it; and a changelog entry says so in a person's words.

`CONTRIBUTING.md` covers run, checks, what a pull request needs, commit voice, and the release
process (version, tag, changelog, and a migration note when `migrations/` changes).
`SECURITY.md` names security@, the promises, the scope and what is out of scope.
`CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` is the Contributor Covenant 2.1 with support@ as the contact.
`.github/` has two issue forms and a pull request template that asks for the failing test and for
anything an operator needs to know.

`scripts/check-site.mjs` now fails when `LICENSE` is not the AGPL, when `package.json` disagrees with
it, when the footer or the install page stops naming it, or when the README loses a pointer to the
contributing, security, conduct, licence or docs surface.

Still open, and not this task's: the repository URL (`REPO_URL` is a placeholder) and the first tag —
a release needs the project to be published. Task 167 owns the docs the README and CONTRIBUTING link
to.

NOTE — 2026-10-24: R6's changelog entry is a release note now
The site's changelog page was removed with `/status/` and `/help/`. The release a version is
described at is the tag — `git tag -a` / the repository's releases — and `CONTRIBUTING.md` says so.
The licence, the contribution surface and the security policy are unchanged.

tasks.title: Remove the plans and the bill from the product.
tasks.description: The billing record, the plan vocabulary and the owner-as-payer leave the schema, the server and the UI, with a migration and the tests following.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read tasks 126 (the workspace's account) and 163 (one
instance, one workspace). The decision of 2026-10-24: nothing is sold, so nothing is billed.

SCOPE
1. The workspace account panel's billing record, and the word "owner" where it meant "payer".
2. The plan vocabulary in the app's copy.
3. The database columns, and the audit sentences.
4. The tests that assert the fields exist.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — No billing record
The panel loses `billing_email`, `company_name`, `billing_reference` and `plan`, and the sentence about
card numbers — there is nothing to pay. What is left of the panel is the workspace's **name** (which the
workspace panel already edits) and its **deletion**, so the panel either becomes that or is folded into
the workspace panel.

R2 — No owner as a payer
`workspaces.owner_id` was the account that would be charged. With no charge, the field has no meaning:
the workspace's **administrator** is the concept, and the membership table already records it. Remove
the field, or keep it as "the account that installed this instance" if that is useful — but stop calling
it an owner, and stop asking anyone to choose one.

R3 — The columns go, in a migration
`migrations/` gains one that drops the four billing columns and `owner_id` (or renames the last, per
R2), and the server's reads, writes, routes and tests follow. The schema version moves with it, and the
e2e proves an upgrade from the previous shape keeps every workspace.

R4 — The words
"Plan", "subscription", "billing", "invoice", "seat" and "trial" leave `src/`, `server/` and the audit
data. The check in task 163 covers the copy; this task covers the code and the trail.

R5 — The tests follow the decision
`server/workspace-account.test.ts`, the account panel's e2e and `src/domain/roles.test.ts` are updated
rather than deleted where they still assert something true (deletion, the three acts, the seal).

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION
V1 — R1/R2: no billing field, no owner picker, and the panel still deletes a workspace with its name
     typed.
V2 — R3: a database at the previous shape migrates; every workspace keeps its name, its members and
     its work; the columns are gone.
V3 — R4: a search of `src/`, `server/` and `site/` for the retired words finds none.
V4 — R5: the suite is green, and nothing was deleted that still had a true thing to say.

DONE — 2026-10-24 (commit `42bf4e4`, CI green)
`migrations/0021_no_bill.sql` drops `owner_id`, `billing_email`, `company_name`, `billing_reference`
and `plan`, and nothing else; `REQUIRED_SCHEMA` is 21, so a database still carrying the bill is
refused rather than served. The read, the patch and the write left `server/workspace/account.ts` with
the two things that are still true — the end of a workspace and the end of an account — and
`/api/workspace/account` is gone with its routes.

`WorkspaceAccountPanel` is deleted: the name, the people, the invitations and the end of the
workspace are one panel, which is what a workspace with no account actually has. The audit union
loses `workspace.account` and `workspace.create`, which no route records any more.

Two decisions taken while building it:

- **R2, the owner**: removed rather than renamed. `workspaces.owner_id` was the account that would be
  charged, there is no charge, and the authority it was standing in for is `workspace_members.role`,
  which is where it always was. Nothing in the product asks anybody to choose one.
- **History is not rewritten.** Audit rows written before this release keep their action string; the
  union is the vocabulary the server writes, not a filter over what happened.

The demo data still carries a "Billing migration" initiative and cards about a billing service. That
is work a fictional team is doing, not a plan the product sells, and R4 is about the product's
vocabulary — so it stays.

Tests: `server/workspace-account.test.ts` becomes `server/workspace-deletion.test.ts` (the deletion
cases kept, the owner/billing CRUD cases replaced by a schema test that asserts the columns are
gone), a migration test upgrades a database that still has the bill and proves the workspace, its
administrator and its board survive, and the e2e's account-admin spec now proves the panel has no
billing field, that `/api/workspace/account` is a 404, and that the name is still the team's to set.
