tasks.title: The docs live with the code, and the site points at them.
tasks.description: One home for the documentation — markdown in the repository, rendered by GitHub — covering install, configure, upgrade, backup and the architecture, linked from the site rather than copied into it.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read `README.md`, `docs/server-runtime.md`,
`docs/roadmap.md` and task 165 (the project's contribution surface).

SCOPE
1. Where the documentation lives, decided once.
2. What it contains: the operator's path and the reader's.
3. How the site and the README point at it without copying it.
4. The check that keeps the links true.

DEFINITIONS
- **The docs**: what someone needs to run this, and what someone needs to understand it. Not the
  marketing pages, not the changelog, not the terms.
- **One home**: every page exists in exactly one file, in one place. A second copy is a copy that
  can disagree.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — One home, and it is the repository
The documentation is **markdown in this repository**, under `docs/`, rendered by GitHub (or by any
static host pointed at the same files). It is readable in a clone, on a plane, and by an operator who
has never opened the website. This is the decision, recorded: GitHub-rendered markdown now; a
`docs.` subdomain only if search or versioned releases demand it, and then **generated from these
same files** — never a second copy maintained by hand.

R2 — The index is the front door
`docs/README.md` is an index a stranger can follow from nothing to a running instance: what this is,
install, configure, first sign-in, upgrade, back up, restore, then the architecture and the
contribution notes. Every file in `docs/` is listed in it, and every entry in it exists.

R3 — The operator's set
- **Install** — one command, what it needs, what it writes.
- **Configure** — every environment variable, its default, and what happens if it is unset. The
  OAuth clients stay optional (the app must run with them unset), `LIVE=0` forces polling.
- **Upgrade** — the migration step, what to do before it, and how to go back.
- **Back up and restore** — the SQLite file and the uploads, and a restore that is *drilled*, not
  described.
- **TLS and the proxy** — the one thing every operator must get right.

R4 — The reader's set
- **Architecture** — the two runtimes and why (`docs/server-runtime.md`), the schema, the domain
  rules `AGENTS.md` states, the live channel.
- **The API** — what exists, with a request and a response for each, and how a session is carried.
- **Contributing** — task 165 owns the file; the docs link to it rather than repeating it.

R5 — The site links, it does not copy
The site's **Docs** item (task 164) and the README both point at the docs. The site does not hold its
own install page *and* a docs install page: `/install/` is the short version with one command, and it
ends by sending the reader to the docs for the rest. A page that exists twice will drift.

R6 — The check
A test in the build: every relative link in `docs/` resolves to a file that exists; every file in
`docs/` is listed in `docs/README.md`; the commands the install page quotes are the commands
`package.json` actually runs; and no doc names a forbidden service (`npm run scan` already enforces
the last one, and the docs are inside it).

R7 — Last verified
Every operator doc ends with the release it was last checked against. A doc that cannot say that is
a doc nobody has run.

TEST STRATEGY
VERIFICATION
V1 — R1/R2: `docs/README.md` lists every file, every link resolves, and a reader with only the repo
     can install from it.
V2 — R3: install, configure, upgrade, backup/restore and TLS each exist and each name their release.
V3 — R4: architecture and API pages exist and describe what the code does.
V4 — R5: the site's Docs item and the README both reach the docs, and `/install/` does not repeat
     the docs' install page.
V5 — R6: the link check fails when a link is broken and when a file is unlisted.

DONE — 2026-10-24 (commit `fc2c170`, CI green)
The index, the five operator pages (install, configure, tls, upgrade, backup) and the two reader pages
(architecture, api). GitHub-rendered markdown under `docs/`, as R1 decided; the `docs.` subdomain
stays a later question, generated from these files rather than written again.

`npm run docs:check` (`scripts/check-docs.mjs`) holds R6 and runs in CI: a relative link that resolves
to nothing, a tracked file the index does not list, an index entry whose file is gone, an `npm run`
script `package.json` does not define, or an operator page that stops saying when it was last verified
— each fails. The listing rule reads `git ls-files docs`, so an untracked draft in the directory does
not block a build, and committing it without indexing it does. The site check follows R5: `/install/`
must link `docs/README.md` and the four operator pages by name.

Deliberately not duplicated: `/install/` stays the short path and ends by sending the reader to the
docs; the site holds no page the docs also hold.

Still open in this area: `docs/admin.md` is untracked (the owner's draft) and so is neither indexed
nor checked; `docs/roadmap.md` is modified in the working tree and is the owner's.

tasks.title: The identity provider provisions the team: SCIM 2.0.
tasks.description: A SCIM 2.0 endpoint an identity provider can call: users and groups, active=false as deactivation rather than deletion, a token minted once and revocable, and errors in SCIM's own shape.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository — open-source software a team installs and runs itself.
Read `server/auth/routes.ts` (the door), `server/workspace-members.ts` (invitations, deactivate,
remove), `server/groups.ts` (groups carry roles), `server/admin.ts` (the acts an administrator has),
`migrations/` and task 154 (OIDC, which this is the second half of).

SCOPE
1. A **SCIM 2.0 endpoint** (RFC 7643 / 7644) an identity provider can call, so the team's arrivals and
   departures happen where they already happen: in the IdP.
2. `/Users` — create, read, list with a filter, replace, patch, delete.
3. `/Groups` — the groups this server already has, provisioned by membership.
4. The discovery documents an IdP refuses to connect without.
5. A token to call it with, and the errors in SCIM's own shape.

DEFINITIONS
- **SCIM**: the provisioning side of an identity provider — the IdP pushes people in, and takes them
  out. Authentication is OIDC's job (task 154); lifecycle is SCIM's.
- **The token**: what an IdP sends as `Authorization: Bearer …`. It is not a person's session: it can
  provision and it cannot read a board.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — A token, minted once, shown once
An instance administrator mints a SCIM token in Admin, named (so several IdPs can be told apart, and
one can be revoked without the other). It is shown once, stored as a hash the way a session is, and
revoked with one click. It carries the **default role** a provisioned person gets — editor unless the
administrator chose otherwise — and nothing else: a SCIM token can never create an instance
administrator, and a role it was not minted with is refused.

R2 — The documents an IdP reads first
`/scim/v2/ServiceProviderConfig`, `/ResourceTypes` and `/Schemas` answer with the minimum a
provisioning client needs to accept the endpoint: patch supported, filter supported, no bulk, no
sorting, and the attributes this server honours. Providers are strict about this, and an endpoint
without them is an endpoint nobody connects to.

R3 — Users
`POST /scim/v2/Users` creates an account: `userName` is the address, `name.formatted` (or given and
family) is the display name, `externalId` is kept so the IdP can find it again. A person who already
exists by address is **returned, not duplicated** (`409` with the existing resource, or
`uniqueness` — pick one and say which in the docs). `GET /Users/:id`, `GET /Users?filter=userName eq
"…"` and by `externalId`, `PUT`, `PATCH` (name, active) and `DELETE` follow the RFC's status codes.
A SCIM `DELETE` is idempotent: `204`, and `404` the second time is not an error worth failing a sync
over.

R4 — `active` is deactivation, never deletion
`PATCH {"active": false}` is the **reversible** act this product already has (task 144): the account
stays, the work keeps their name, and their door closes. Only `DELETE` removes the account, and it
removes it the way the app does — the work stays and every reference reads "Former member". A
provisioning system that deletes by default must not be able to erase a team's history by accident.

R5 — Groups, and the boundary
`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` on `/scim/v2/Groups` map onto `groups` and `group_members`, which
is what a role can already be granted to. The line is deliberate: **an IdP provisions people and
membership; the team decides authority.** A group carries a workspace role only when an administrator
grants one in the app — SCIM can add somebody to a group, and cannot thereby make them an
administrator.

R6 — The seal holds
The workspace is resolved by the server, not by the request, so a SCIM call reaches the one workspace
this deployment has and nothing else. The token is refused without the bearer header, refused when
revoked, and rate-limited per token. It is never written to a log, and an audit entry names the token
(`scim.user.create`, token id) rather than pretending a person did it.

R7 — Errors in SCIM's shape
A refusal is
`{"schemas":["urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:Error"],"detail":"…","status":"400"}`, with the
HTTP status matching `status`. An IdP will not read our `{"error": …}`, and a sync that cannot parse
the failure retries forever.

R8 — The docs, and the test that keeps them true
A `docs/identity.md` — connect an issuer (OIDC) and provision from it (SCIM) — with the endpoints, the
token, the default role, and what each SCIM operation does to a person's account. It is linked from
the help page (task 158) and from `docs/README.md`, and `npm run docs:check` holds the links.

TEST STRATEGY
V1 — R1: a token is shown once, hashed at rest, revocable, and a revoked one is refused; a token
     cannot create an instance administrator.
V2 — R2: the three discovery documents answer with the shape an IdP validates.
V3 — R3: create, read by id, filter by `userName` and by `externalId`, replace, patch, delete; a
     second create for the same address does not duplicate the person.
V4 — R4: `active: false` closes the door and keeps the account; `DELETE` removes it, and the history
     reads "Former member"; neither reaches another workspace's work.
V5 — R5: a SCIM group add/remove changes membership, and does not change a role unless the app
     already granted that group one.
V6 — R6: no bearer header is `401`; a revoked token is `401`; the token never appears in a log line or
     an audit entry's data.
V7 — R7: every refusal is a SCIM Error with a matching status.
V8 — R8: `docs/identity.md` is listed, linked, and its endpoints match the routes.

NOTES
- SCIM and invitations coexist: an instance with no IdP still invites people by link (task 154 R4).
- The role a provisioned person gets is a decision, not an attribute: the token carries a default,
  and everything after it is the team's to change in the app.

NOTE — 2026-10-24: an account can arrive with no password
Task 154 lets a deployment live on passwords and magic links. A person provisioned by SCIM has
neither: they arrive with an account and no way to sign in until they accept an invitation-style link
or ask for a magic link. That is deliberate — the IdP just created them and the IdP is the door — but
it is a state the help page and `docs/identity.md` have to describe, and the account screen should say
"provisioned by your directory" rather than showing an empty password field.

tasks.complexityReasoning: A protocol surface with its own error shape and discovery documents, mapped onto acts that already exist (invite, deactivate, remove, group membership).

tasks.title: A REST API a script can rely on: /api/v1, and a contract that does not move.
tasks.description: A supported surface beside the app's own: boards, items, moves, objectives, people, search and the workspace file, authenticated by task 148's tokens, documented by an OpenAPI document that a test keeps true, and versioned with a written promise.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read `docs/api.md` (the internal API the app calls),
`server/app.ts`, `server/access.ts`, `server/workspace/routes.ts`, `src/domain/roles.ts`, and task 148
(the token, and the scopes this surface enforces). Task 170 (MCP) calls the same operations, and must
not grow a second set of rules.

SCOPE
1. `/api/v1/*` — a supported surface beside the app's own `/api/*`.
2. Tokens as the way in (task 148), never a session: a script has no browser.
3. The resources a script actually needs, and the acts a person already has.
4. The contract: a version, an OpenAPI document, and a written policy for what may change.

DEFINITIONS
- **Internal API**: `/api/*`, what the shipped client calls. It changes with the client in the same
  commit, and carries no promise to anybody else.
- **Public API**: `/api/v1/*`, a contract. Additive changes inside v1; anything that breaks is v2,
  with a deprecation window.
- **Operation**: one act — read a board, create an item, move a card — implemented once and used by
  the app, the REST surface and the MCP server.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Two surfaces, one implementation
Every v1 route is a thin adapter over an operation that already exists: the domain rules plus one
write. No rule lives in a route. If `moveCard` refuses a WIP breach, v1 answers with that refusal
rather than reimplementing it, and the same is true of a cycle, a stale revision and the seal. The
scope vocabulary is settled against `src/domain/roles.ts` before the first route is written (that is
task 148's R1, and it is the hour of design that gets harder later).

R2 — A token is the caller
`Authorization: Bearer <token>`, and nothing else: a session cookie is refused on `/api/v1` with a
sentence that says to use a token. The caller is the token's owner, with the token's scopes *and* the
owner's live role — both checked, on every request, exactly as the app's routes do it. The token is
**acquired by the tool**, not copied by hand (`flowline login`, task 148 R7): the first line of a
script that uses this API is a login a person approved once, and the secret lives in the keychain
rather than in the script. The workspace
is resolved by the server; there is no workspace parameter, because a deployment is one workspace
(task 163).

R3 — The resources
Reads and writes a script plausibly needs, and no more:

- **boards** — list; read one with its lanes, its workflow trees and what is placed in it.
- **items** — list (filterable), read, create, update. Items are cards and initiatives alike; the
  type is a field, not a different resource.
- **moves** — an act, not a field: `POST /boards/{boardId}/items/{itemId}/move` with the target cell,
  the position, and a reason when the lane's policy asks for one. It answers with the card's new
  place, or with the refusal.
- **objectives and key results** — read, with the rollup computed the way the app computes it.
- **people** — read, so a script can name an assignee.
- **search** — `?q=`, the app's own search, not a query language.
- **the workspace file** — export and import, so a script can take the backup that `npm run backup`
  takes a database-level copy of.

R4 — Conventions, once
Cursor pagination (`?cursor=…&limit=…`, bounded), `?updated_since=` for incremental reads, `baseRev`
on a write and `409` with the current item when it has moved, an idempotency key on create and update
(`Idempotency-Key`, answered from the same table the app's queue already uses), and one error body for
everything:

```json
{ "error": { "code": "wip_blocked", "message": "Done is at its limit of 5.", "details": { … } } }
```

`code` is stable and documented; `message` is for a person; `details` is what a script needs to act.

R5 — Rate limits
Per token, with `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining` and `RateLimit-Reset` on every answer, and a
`429` that says how long. Generous enough not to be felt by a person's script, low enough that a
runaway loop is a 429 rather than an outage. The limit is configuration, documented in
`docs/configure.md`.

R6 — The document, and the check that it is true
`GET /api/v1/openapi.json` serves an OpenAPI 3.1 document built from the same table that mounts the
routes. A test fails when a mounted route is missing from the document, when the document names a
route that is not mounted, or when a schema in it does not parse. An API nobody can generate a client
from is an API that only its author can use.

R7 — The versioning promise, in writing
`docs/rest-api.md` states it plainly: within `v1`, fields may be added and never removed or retyped; a
new required field is a breaking change; anything that breaks is `v2` beside `v1`, with a `Sunset`
header and at least one minor release of overlap. The document is in the repository, so the promise
travels with the code it describes.

R8 — Audit, without exception
A v1 write records the token's owner as the actor and names the token, the way a session write records
a person. The API is not a way to write without a trail, and it is not a way to write as somebody
else: a token belongs to one account, and its scopes are that account's to give.

R9 — The documentation
`docs/rest-api.md`: authentication, the resources, the conventions, one worked script (a shell loop
with `curl` and a small Node script), and the versioning promise. It is listed in `docs/README.md`,
and `npm run docs:check` holds its links like everything else.

TEST STRATEGY
V1 — R1: the v1 routes call the same operations the app does — a test asserts the move path reaches
     `moveCard`, not a second placement write.
V2 — R2: a token with `items:read` cannot move a card (403), and the refusal carries the scope it
     needed; a session cookie on `/api/v1` is refused with the sentence R2 promises.
V3 — R3: a move into a `justify` lane answers with the reason requirement; with a reason it lands
     where the request put it; a `block` lane refuses with the domain's sentence.
V4 — R3: an initiative cannot be moved across a section, and v1 says so in the same words the app
     would.
V5 — R4: pagination, `updated_since`, a stale `baseRev` (409 with the item), and an idempotency key
     replayed twice lands once.
V6 — R5: the headers are on every answer, and a burst hits a 429 that says when to come back.
V7 — R6: the OpenAPI document and the mounted routes agree in both directions.
V8 — R3/R7: export through v1 round-trips into a clean instance; the documented script is executed by
     a test rather than read by a person.

NOTES
- A tool and a route are the same act. If task 170 lands first, it builds the operation layer this
  task reuses; if this lands first, it builds it and 170 reuses. Neither may fork the rules.
- No webhooks in this task. They are the next thing a script asks for, and they are a task of their
  own — a delivery queue, retries and a signing secret are not a route.

DONE — 2026-10-25 (CI green: checks, image, e2e, publish, deploy)
**R1 came first, and it changed the shape of the work.** The move rule left the store for
`src/domain/move.ts` — `moveCard`, `moveInitiative`, `wipBreach`, the history entry, and the position
logic — and both the store's drag and `/api/v1` call it. The store kept only what a person hears (the
announcement, the WIP prompt) and the API keeps only the status code. Test V1 is structural, because
that is where a second implementation would hide: `server/v1/routes.ts` must import the domain module
and must contain no `INSERT`/`UPDATE` on `placements`; `src/store.ts` must import the same module. The
14 domain tests are the cases all three doors share.

The refactor also removed two duplicated helpers rather than copying them: `laneNameAt` now lives in
`src/domain/lanes.ts`, and the store's `movedEntry` is the domain's.

**R2.** A session cookie is refused with `token_required` and a sentence naming the bearer header. The
two ceilings are `403 scope_required` (with `details.scope`) and `403 role_forbidden` — the first is
the token you chose, the second is the person you are. One test demotes an editor mid-script and
watches the same token stop writing, with nothing revoked.

**R3.** boards (list, one with both lane trees + placements + items), items (list with `boardId`,
`laneId` incl. subtree, `typeId`, `q`, `updatedSince`; read with parent/placements/rollup/history;
create; update), moves, objectives (with the app's own `objectiveRollup`, `null` when nothing serves
it), people, search (the app's `searchItems`), and the workspace file both ways.

**Rules inside a route are the domain's**, not re-implementations: `canRetype`, `canSetParent`,
`canPlaceInSection`, `defaultDropLane`, `objectiveRollup`, `rollupOf`, `searchItems`, `boardTags`.
The two that the old store held inline (the parent walk, the workflow check) now call those functions.

**R4.** Cursor pagination (`limit` default 50, max 200, opaque base64url cursor — `btoa`, because the
same code runs in a Worker), `updatedSince` read from the `changes` table, `baseRev` with `409 stale`
carrying the item, `Idempotency-Key` answered from `applied_writes` (the table the app's queue already
uses), and one error body `{ error: { code, message, details } }` with a documented, stable `code`.

**R5.** Per-token, in memory, `API_RATE_LIMIT` (default 120/min), headers on every answer including
refusals, `429 rate_limited` with `details.retryAfter`. Documented in `docs/configure.md`, with the
honest note that a Worker keeps the window per isolate.

**R6.** `openapi.json` is generated from the `RouteSpec` table that mounts the routes. A test walks
Hono's own routing table for `/api/v1` and compares it with the document in both directions (the
`ALL /*` header middleware excluded, and the public document route included).

**R7/R9.** `docs/rest-api.md` — authentication, the scope table, the resources, every status and code,
the versioning promise, a `curl` loop and a Node script, and what is deliberately absent. Listed in
`docs/README.md`, linked from `docs/api.md` (which now says plainly that *it* is the internal one), and
`npm run docs:check` holds it. `docs/configure.md` gained `API_RATE_LIMIT`.

**R8.** Every write records `api.write` as the token's **owner**, naming the operation, the item and
the token id — in the same transaction as the write, through the new `audit` parameter on
`writeItemAndPlacements`.

**V8's script is executed, not read:** a test makes the documented script's calls in order — find the
board by name, file two cards with their own keys, list them, move each — against the real routes.

**Two things to know, recorded rather than buried.** (1) `/api/v1` is the **first door that persists a
move**: the server had no placement writer, so the app's own drags are still arrangement in the
browser's cache (task 118 never grew a route, and the app's other devices learn a move only on a full
reload). The next change that touches collaboration should route the app's move through the same
`writeItemAndPlacements` and the same operation. (2) `POST /workspace` refuses a workspace that
already has boards (`409 not_empty`), matching the internal import: restore is for a fresh instance,
and replacing a live workspace is not something a script should be able to do by accident.

17 tests in `server/v1.test.ts`; 836 in the suite; the first download stepped from 162 to 163 KB
because the shared move module is on it (`scripts/bundle-size.mjs` says why).
tasks.testStrategy: Per the verification list: the shared operation layer, token-only auth, the WIP and cycle refusals, conventions, rate limits, the OpenAPI drift check, and an executed example script.
tasks.complexityReasoning: A contract rather than a route list: adapters over existing operations, a document that must stay in step, and a versioning promise that constrains every later change.

tasks.title: An MCP server, so an agent reads and writes the board under the same rules.
tasks.description: The Model Context Protocol over the same operations as the app and the REST API: named tools that refuse in sentences, no write tool on a read-only token, and nothing that invents work the agent was not asked to write.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read task 148 (tokens and scopes), task 169 (the REST
surface — the same operations, a different transport), `docs/api.md`, `src/domain/` (the rules an
agent must not be able to soften) and `AGENTS.md` ("the app writes nothing nobody wrote").

SCOPE
1. An MCP server — stdio for a local agent, Streamable HTTP for a remote one.
2. Tools named after the acts a person has, not after the tables.
3. The same authority, the same rules and the same audit as every other surface.

DEFINITIONS
- **MCP**: the Model Context Protocol — a client (an agent) asks a server for *tools* it can call and
  *resources* it can read.
- **Agent**: a client that decides what to call and may be wrong. The server's job is to be safe to be
  wrong against: refuse in sentences, never half-apply, never invent.
- **Operation**: the same act the app and the REST API use — one implementation, three doors.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — One tool table, two transports
The tools are defined once. **stdio** runs the server in the agent's own process (`node
server/mcp.ts`, or a `bin` so `npx` works) and takes the instance's URL and a token from its
environment or its arguments; **Streamable HTTP** mounts at `/mcp` on the instance and takes
`Authorization: Bearer`, so an agent that cannot spawn a process still has a door. Both answer with
the same tool list, and a test asserts the two transports produce it.

Adding the tool is a click, not a config file: **Connect an agent** in Admin mints a scoped token and
writes the client's config (task 148 R8), so the JSON an agent expects is produced by the instance
that knows its own URL. The HTTP transport takes the same bearer token a script would use, and there
is no unauthenticated mode on either transport — a local agent still says who it is.

R2 — Reads, and what they are for
- `list_boards` — the boards, the band and the shape, so an agent can choose one.
- `get_board` — one board with its lanes and what is placed where; the id an agent needs before it
  writes anything.
- `search_items` — the app's own search.
- `get_item` — one card or initiative, with its parent, its placement, its revision and its rollup.
- `list_objectives` — objectives with the rollup the work gives them, and the coverage gaps.
- `list_people` — names and ids, so an assignment names a person rather than a guess.
- `workspace_summary` — counts and the board list: what an agent reads before it plans anything.

Every read is bounded (`limit`, with a default and a ceiling) and returns ids and the fields asked
for. An agent that has to page through 400 cards to answer "what is in Done" will do it wrong.

R3 — Writes, in the vocabulary of the acts
- `create_item` — a card or an initiative on a board, with a type, a parent and a placement.
- `update_item` — the fields a person writes: title, description, assignees, size, dates, type.
- `move_item` — a **move**, carrying the board, the target cell and the position; a reason when the
  lane's policy asks for one.
- `set_parent` — the hierarchy edit, judged by `canSetParent` (never its own ancestor, an item has one
  parent).

R4 — The rules are not softened for the model
`move_item` goes through `moveCard`, so `visualize` passes, `justify` answers "a reason is needed"
until one is given, and `block` refuses. `set_parent` goes through the same `canSetParent` the drop
preview uses. A revision is required on an update and a stale one is a `409` with the current item —
the model is told what changed, not silently overwritten. There is no "force" argument and no bulk
write: a batch of twenty cards is twenty calls, which is what a person would do.

R5 — Authority is the token's, and a read-only token has no write tools
A token minted read-only exposes **no write tool at all** — not a tool that errors when called, which
invites an agent to argue with it. A write tool appears only on a token with the scope. Every write is
audited as the token's owner, with the token named, exactly as a REST write is.

R6 — Nothing is invented on the agent's behalf
The server exposes no tool that generates cards, rewrites a board from a summary, or fabricates
history. The product's rule is that the app writes what somebody wrote; an agent calling
`create_item` is somebody writing, and a tool that filled a board with plausible sentences would be
the app writing what nobody wrote. This is a design constraint, not a missing tool.

R7 — Descriptions for the model, answers for the caller
Each tool's description says what it does, what it refuses, which ids it needs and what it returns.
A refusal comes back as a tool result with `isError: true` and the **server's own sentence** — "Done
is at its limit of 5", "that would make a cycle", "somebody else is editing this card" — so the
agent can tell a person why, rather than retrying a bare 500.

R8 — No free-form queries
Tools are named operations. There is no SQL passthrough, no filter expression language and no
"evaluate this". `search_items` is the app's search, and a tool that took a query language would be a
second API with none of the first one's rules.

R9 — Tests
The tool table maps every tool to one operation (a table test, so a new tool cannot arrive without
one). The stdio transport completes a session in CI against a seeded instance. The HTTP transport
refuses a request with no token, and an MCP write lands in the audit with the token named. A WIP
refusal and a cycle refusal are asserted as tool results with `isError`, not as thrown errors.

R10 — The documentation
`docs/mcp.md`: how to connect (the JSON an agent's config takes for stdio and for HTTP), the tool
list with what each refuses, the scopes a write needs, and the one rule — an agent writes what a
person asked for. Listed in `docs/README.md`; linked from the help page (task 158) and from
`docs/rest-api.md` (task 169), because they are two doors to the same acts.

TEST STRATEGY
V1 — R1: both transports answer with the same tool list; stdio completes a call in the e2e lane.
V2 — R2: each read returns bounded results, and `get_board` returns the lane ids a write needs.
V3 — R3/R4: a move into a `justify` lane refuses without a reason and lands with one; a `block` lane
     refuses; `set_parent` refuses a cycle; a stale revision is a 409 carrying the item.
V4 — R5: a read-only token's `tools/list` contains no write tool, and a write token's writes are in
     the audit with the token's name.
V5 — R6: the tool list contains no generative tool (asserted by name, so adding one is a decision).
V6 — R7: a refusal is a tool result with `isError` and the server's sentence.
V7 — R9: an unauthenticated HTTP request is refused with `401`.
V8 — R10: `docs/mcp.md` is listed, linked, and its tool names match the table.

NOTES
- The MCP server is not a second product: it is a transport over the operations the app and the REST
  API already use. If it needs a rule the other two do not have, the rule is wrong.
- Prompts and sampling are deliberately out of scope. This is a server that lets an agent read and
  write the board, not a chat product inside Flowline.
tasks.testStrategy: Per the verification list: both transports, the tool table, the rule refusals as tool results, the read-only tool list, and the audit.
tasks.complexityReasoning: A protocol transport over acts that already exist; the difficulty is the safety boundary, not the plumbing.

tasks.title: The Viewer role is read-only in the interface, not only in the API.
tasks.description: The role exists and the server enforces it; the interface has never asked. A Viewer is offered drag, add-card, board design and settings today and answered with a 403. Wire the matrix into the surfaces a person actually touches, and say read-only where it is.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read `src/domain/roles.ts` (the matrix — the decision), `src/lib/permissions.ts` (the
interface's half, added 2026-10-25), and `src/components/BoardView.tsx`, `BoardCanvas.tsx`,
`ItemPanel.tsx`, `BoardWorkspace.tsx`, `Toolbar`/`CommandPalette.tsx`, `CardMenu.tsx`.

WHY THIS EXISTS
The server refuses a write from a Viewer on every route, and the matrix has said so since task 131.
The interface never asked: `can()` is called only inside `roles.ts` itself, so a Viewer is offered
"Add card", drag, "Edit board", board settings and workspace actions, and each one answers 403. A
control that cannot work is a lie about what the product does.

DEFINITIONS
- **Viewer**: reads every board, searches, and comments. Writes nothing else — not a title, not a
  move, not a lane, not a board.
- **Anonymous**: a browser with no account. It is a workspace in `localStorage`, not a Viewer: there is
  no server and no role to enforce, and the demo must stay editable (`may()` already says so).

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — One question, asked everywhere
Every component asks `may(action)` from `@/lib/permissions`; no component re-implements a rule. The
matrix stays the only place a permission is decided, and a test asserts that the helper answers
`undefined` (signed out) as editable.

R2 — The board surface
Done in part on 2026-10-25: `interactive` follows `item.write`, so drag, the add-card button, lane
editing and the initiatives/workflows surfaces are inert; "archive done" is gone without
`item.delete`; a `read-only · viewer` chip says why. Finish the surface: the **Edit board** toggle and
board settings entry points hide without `board.design` / `board.settings`, and the card kebab menu
offers only what the role may do.

R3 — The item panel
The panel is where a card is written. For a Viewer: every field renders read-only (title, description,
people, size, dates, type, parent, tags), the save and delete controls are absent rather than disabled
alone, and the **comment composer stays** — `item.comment` is a Viewer's, and a viewer who can read a
board can tell the team what they think. The panel says, in one line, that it is read-only and why.

R4 — The workspace home
`BoardWorkspace` hides New board, Duplicate, Archive, the template editor and the import for a role
without `board.create`, `board.settings` or `workspace.import`. Reading a board, switching boards,
searching and exporting stay.

R5 — The command palette and the menus
Palette commands that write (`New card`, board design, settings) are absent for a Viewer, not present
and failing. Same for `CardMenu` and any kebab that lists a write.

R6 — Nothing else changes for an Editor or an Administrator
The guards are `may(...)` questions, not new roles: Editor and Administrator see exactly what they saw,
and the existing suite stays green.

R7 — The e2e that proves it
A Viewer signs in (a second account on the 4174 instance, its role set through the workspace members
route), then: no add-card control, drag does nothing, the item panel has no save, the comment composer
works, and a direct write to the API answers 403 with the domain's sentence.

TEST STRATEGY
V1 — R1: the helper's unit tests (done) plus a grep-level assertion that no component calls `can()`
     directly.
V2 — R2/R3: the viewer e2e — no control, no save, comment allowed.
V3 — R4/R5: a viewer's workspace home has no New board; the palette has no New card.
V4 — R6: the whole existing suite green, unchanged.
V5 — R7: the API still refuses the write, so the interface and the server agree.

NOTES
- The chip is the one place the interface explains a refusal in advance; without it a Viewer sees a
  board with no controls and wonders whether the app is broken.
- This is a courtesy, not the security boundary. If a guard here were wrong, the server would still
  refuse — which is why the e2e asserts both.

DONE — 2026-10-25 (CI green: checks, image, e2e, publish, deploy)
**R1** — `may()`/`useMay()` is the only door. A new test reads every `src/components/*.tsx` and
fails if one imports `can` from `@/domain/roles` or calls it: prose may say "you can", a control
may not decide. Anonymous stays editable, as the unit tests already said.

**R2** — finished. The card kebab no longer opens for a Viewer (`Overlays` asks `item.write`, so the
menu is not rendered at all rather than rendered empty); `Edit board` and board settings were
already hidden in `TopBar`; `CommandPalette` keeps every reading verb and drops the four writing
ones (New card, New initiative, Edit board design, Board settings).

**R3** — the item panel. Two things were wrong: the body's `<fieldset disabled>` also covered the
comment composer, and the header's controls sat outside it. The fieldset now closes before the
composer, its `disabled` is `held || !may('item.write')`, and the header's More menu, block/unblock
and title follow the same answer. One line above the body says why: *"You are a Viewer here, so
this card is read-only. A note at the bottom is yours to leave."*

**The comment is real, which meant a server change.** A note travels the item endpoint, so a
Viewer's comment used to be refused with `item.write`. `PATCH /api/workspace/items/:id` now opens on
`item.comment` — the least a change to a card can need — and the *change* decides whether that is
enough (`commentOnly`): every field but the log must equal what is stored, the stored log must be an
unchanged prefix, and appended entries must be notes attributed to the caller or to nobody. Judged
after the revision check, so a Viewer whose base is stale is told to catch up (409) rather than
refused. Five tests in `server/acceptance.test.ts`: a note accepted (and the revision moves like any
other change), an unsigned note accepted, a note carrying a title refused, a rewritten or forged
history refused, a creation refused.

**R4** — `BoardWorkspace`: New board follows `board.create`; Duplicate `board.create`, Archive
`board.settings`, Delete `board.delete` (the kebab does not render if none applies); the Templates
section is `template.manage`'s; Import is `workspace.import`'s. Search, the band filter, reading a
board and Export stay.

**R5** — palette and `CardMenu`, above.

**R6** — unchanged for Editor and Administrator: every guard is a `may(...)` question, and the
suite that existed before this task still passes untouched (785 tests, 62 files).

**R7 — deviated, on purpose.** The task asked for a Viewer on the 4174 instance with a role set
through the members route. The e2e instead uses the **4177 fresh instance**, where Grace was *invited
as a Viewer and chose her own password* two tests earlier — the real road, not a shortcut through
the API — and it asserts on top of the interface claims that the server agrees: the note she leaves
is in the item's log afterwards, and a direct `PATCH` with her cookie answers `403 a viewer may not
item.write`. The drag is attempted (pointer, 12 steps, at the Done column) and the Backlog's order is
unchanged. `e2e/setup.spec.ts`, fifth test, serial after the invitation and the reset.

**Not touched:** the Admin screen's own writing controls (snapshots/restore, import) — outside this
task's surface; `workspace.restore` is a separate action and its own task if it needs one.
tasks.testStrategy: Per the verification list: the helper, a viewer e2e across the board, the panel and the palette, and the API still refusing the write.
tasks.complexityReasoning: Mechanical once the helper exists, but it touches four large components and every control that writes.

tasks.title: A published image, so nobody has to build one.
tasks.description: CI already builds the instance image on every push; publish it to a registry, tagged by commit and by version, so a self-hoster runs one command instead of cloning and waiting for a build.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read `.github/workflows/ci.yml` (the `image` job),
`Dockerfile`, `compose.yaml`, `docs/install.md`, `docs/docker.md` and task 173 (an instance is the
application, not the project's site).

WHAT THIS IS, AND IS NOT
The image is **one instance of the application**: the API, the built client and the migrations. It is
not the project's website and not its documentation — the site is what this repository deploys, and the
docs are markdown in `docs/`, read on GitHub. Task 173 makes the image honest about that; this task
makes it downloadable.

SCOPE
1. The `image` job publishes what it already builds and tests.
2. Tags that mean something: the commit, the version, and `latest` from `main` only.
3. Two architectures, because a self-hoster may be on ARM.
4. The one command, and a compose file that can use the image instead of building it.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Publish the image the job already proves
The `image` job builds, runs through compose and asserts health, the unprivileged uid, the database it
creates and the first sign-in. It then logs in to the registry and pushes that same image — never a
separately-built one, because a published artifact nobody tested is the failure mode this task exists
to avoid.

R2 — Tags
- `ghcr.io/<owner>/flowline:<commit-sha>` — always, so a deployment can pin what it ran.
- `ghcr.io/<owner>/flowline:<version>` from the version in `package.json`, on `main`.
- `latest` on `main` only, and documented as "the last green `main`", not as "the stable release".
A tag is never overwritten except `latest`; a published tag is a fact somebody may have pinned.

R3 — Two architectures
`linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64`, built with buildx in one job. A team's small ARM server (a Pi, an
Ampere instance, an Apple machine) is exactly the kind of machine this product is for. If the build
cannot do both in the job's time budget, say so in the task's completion note rather than shipping one
and pretending.

R4 — The password door, on the published image
Nothing changes: the image runs the Node entry, which is where hashing belongs, and 600 000 iterations
is fine there. The CPU note in `docs/server-runtime.md` is about deploying on Workers, not about this.

R5 — One command, and no clone
```bash
docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:8787:8787 -v flowline-data:/data ghcr.io/<owner>/flowline:latest
```
and the same via compose, where `image:` sits beside `build:` so a reader can choose. `docs/install.md`
and `docs/docker.md` lead with the published image and keep the build-from-checkout path for people who
want to read the source first.

R6 — An image is a version, and says which
The running container reports the version it is (`/api/health` or the boot line), so an operator with
three instances can tell them apart. `package.json`'s version is the source of truth.

TEST STRATEGY
V1 — R1: the published digest is the image the job ran; a failing assertion in the job publishes nothing.
V2 — R2: the three tags exist after a `main` push, and `latest` does not move on a tag build.
V3 — R3: `docker run` on both architectures starts and answers `/api/health`.
V4 — R5: the documented command, from a machine with nothing but Docker, reaches the first-run surface.
V5 — R6: the version the container reports equals `package.json`'s.

NOTES
- Publishing needs a registry the repository can write to (ghcr with `GITHUB_TOKEN` is the obvious
  choice) and a **public** repository before anonymous pulls work; until then the docs say "build it
  from the checkout", which is what they say today.
- This task is last in the install path on purpose: an image that contains the wrong thing, published
  widely, is worse than a build step.

DONE — 2026-10-25 (commit `d350b6b`, CI green: checks, image, e2e, **publish**, deploy)
A `publish` job takes the build to `ghcr.io/malcolm/…` on every `main` push — see the run's annotation
for the digest — for **linux/amd64 and linux/arm64**, with three tags that each mean one thing:

| tag | what it is |
| --- | --- |
| `<commit>` | that exact commit; what a deployment should pin |
| `<version>` | the release, from `package.json` |
| `latest` | the last green `main` — not a release |

**R1, deviated and stated:** a multi-platform manifest cannot be the single-architecture image the
`image` job ran, so the published digest is **verified after publishing** — the job pulls
`name@digest` and repeats the assertions (health, the version it reports, uid 10001, its own database,
and the first sign-in becoming the workspace). Same assertions, different order; the note is in the
workflow beside the job.

**R6** is in: `/api/health` reports `{"ok":true,"database":"ok","version":"0.1.0"}`, read once from the
`package.json` the image already carries, so three containers can be told apart by curling them.

**R5, partly:** `docs/docker.md` gained *The published image* — the `docker run` command, the compose
`image:` alternative, and the table of tags — and `docs/install.md` points at it. It does **not** lead
with it, for an honest reason:

> **The repository is private today, so the package is private too.** Pulling needs a GitHub token
> until the repository is public — so the clone-and-build road stays first, because it works without
> one.

When the repository is made public the package becomes pullable by anybody, and the two pages flip
their order. That is the only thing left of this task, and it is a repository setting rather than code.

**R3, on the time budget:** both architectures built and pushed inside the job's 30-minute ceiling on
the first attempt, with a GitHub Actions layer cache so a rebuild of an unchanged Dockerfile is quick.

tasks.title: An instance is the application, not the project’s site.
tasks.description: The Node entry serves the app at /app and nothing else: no marketing pages, no project 404, no project security.txt — and the image ships only what an instance needs.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read `server/index.node.ts` (the instance entry),
`Dockerfile`, `scripts/smoke-node.mjs`, `src/components/SignInPanel.tsx` (the terms links) and
`docs/install.md`.

THE POINT
Building the image builds **an instance of the application**. It does not build the project's website,
and it never had anything to do with the documentation: the site is what this repository deploys to its
own origin, and the docs are markdown in `docs/`, read on GitHub. Today the container carries the site
pages anyway — `dist/index.html`, `/install/`, `/privacy/`, `/security/`, `robots.txt`,
`sitemap.xml`, `security.txt` — because it copies the whole build and the Node entry serves it.

So a team that installs Flowline and opens `https://flowline.their-company.com/` gets **this project's**
marketing page, whose privacy notice describes *the demo deployment*, whose `/security.txt` names
`flowline.example`, and whose footer links back to the project. None of that belongs to their instance.

SCOPE
1. What the Node entry serves.
2. What the image carries.
3. What an instance's own `/` and 404 are.
4. The two links in the app that assume the project's pages exist.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — The entry serves the application
`/` answers a redirect to `/app` (302). `/app` and everything beneath it is the app's document.
`/assets/*` and the app's own static files are served. `/api/*` is the API. **Nothing else resolves** —
not `/install/`, not `/privacy/`, not `/product/`, not the project's `robots.txt`, `sitemap.xml` or
`security.txt`.

R2 — An instance's 404 is its own
An unknown path answers `404` with a small, self-contained page in the app's own styling — not the
project's 404 page, which links to the site. It says the path was wrong, offers `/app`, and names the
instance (`WORKSPACE_NAME`) so it is obviously *this* deployment's page.

R3 — The image carries what an instance needs
`dist/app/`, `dist/assets/`, the app's favicon and app icon. Not the site's pages, images, stylesheet,
sitemap or `security.txt`. `STATIC_DIR` keeps its meaning: the root the entry serves from.

R4 — The app's two links stop pointing at the project
The sign-in surface says "by continuing you agree to the terms and the privacy notice" and links
`/terms/` and `/privacy/`. On an instance those pages are the operator's, and after R1 they do not
exist. Two ways out, and the task must pick one and say why:
- an instance serves a minimal, operator-owned `/terms/` and `/privacy/` (configurable text, or a
  placeholder that says "your operator has not published these"); or
- the sentence links nothing on an instance and says who to ask.
Whichever is chosen, a link in the app must never reach a page the instance does not serve.

R5 — The project's own deployment is unchanged
The Worker keeps serving the site and the demo (that is what `wrangler.jsonc` is for), and the static
tier (`dist/` on any host) is unchanged — a plain SPA is still a valid way to read a board. This task is
about the **Node instance** and the image.

R6 — Proved by the smoke and the e2e
`npm run smoke:node` asserts `/` redirects to `/app`, `/app` serves the app, an unknown path is a 404
with the instance's name, and `/install/` (a site page) is 404 on an instance. The e2e keeps passing:
its servers serve `dist/`, and the app's own routes do not change.

TEST STRATEGY
V1 — R1: `/` is a 302 to `/app`; `/app` and `/assets/*` are 200; `/install/`, `/privacy/`,
     `/robots.txt`, `/sitemap.xml`, `/security.txt` are all 404 on the Node entry.
V2 — R2: the 404 names the workspace and offers `/app`; it is not the project's page.
V3 — R3: `docker run` the image and list `dist/` — no site pages, no site.css, no img/.
V4 — R4: no link in the app reaches a page the instance does not serve; the chosen behaviour is
     asserted.
V5 — R5: the Worker deployment and the static build are unchanged (site check, deploy job).
V6 — R6: `smoke:node` green, the e2e green, and the image job's assertions still pass.

NOTES
- This is the change that makes task 172 safe to publish: an image that carries the project's marketing
  site is an image that would put *our* privacy notice on somebody else's domain.
- The site keeps its `/install/` page and its docs — those are the project's, and they are how somebody
  finds the image in the first place.

DONE — 2026-10-25 (commit `8d647ed`, CI green: checks, image, e2e, deploy)
The Node entry serves the application and nothing else. `/` redirects to `/app`; `/app` and
everything under it is the app's document; `/assets/*` and `/favicon.svg` are served; `/api/*` is the
API; `/robots.txt` answers `Disallow: /` because an instance is one team's private work. Everything
else is the instance's **own** 404 — self-contained, naming the workspace from `WORKSPACE_NAME`, and
offering `/app`. The project's pages (`/install/`, `/product/`, `/privacy/`, `/terms/`, `/sitemap.xml`,
`/security.txt`) are in the same build and are deliberately unreachable there.

The image carries what an instance is: it builds with `build:app` (the client, not the site) and copies
`dist/app`, `dist/assets` and the icon. Verified by listing the container's `dist/` — three entries, no
site pages, no stylesheet, no sitemap.

**R4, decided:** an instance links **the project's** terms and privacy notice, hosted on the project's
site, through a new runtime `PROJECT_URL`. Set, the sign-in surface links them and says they cover the
software rather than this instance; unset, the sentence says whose policies apply and links nothing,
because a link to a domain nobody serves is worse than a sentence. The e2e's instance is told
`PROJECT_URL=http://localhost:4173`, so the test proves the link resolves *there* while `/terms/` on
the instance is 404.

Proved by `smoke:node` (22 checks: the redirect, the app's chunk, the icon, robots, seven project pages
answering 404, and the 404 naming the workspace), by the image job through compose, and by the site
e2e. The Worker deployment and the static tier are untouched, as R5 required.

Not done, and deliberately: the Worker still serves the site — that is this project's own deployment,
which is what `wrangler.jsonc` is for. Task 172 (a published image) is now unblocked.
tasks.testStrategy: Per the verification list: the entry serves only the app, the 404 is the instance’s, the image carries no site pages, and the app has no link to a page the instance does not serve.
tasks.complexityReasoning: A routing change in one entry plus a decision about the terms links; the care is in not breaking the two other deployments.
